Conceptual Framework for Strategic Management

Unit I · Topic 1

1. Overview

Strategic management is the ongoing process by which an organization determines what it wants to achieve, analyses the environment it competes in, decides how it will compete, and puts that decision into action. It sits above day-to-day operational management: operational decisions ask "how do we do this task well?", while strategic decisions ask "are we doing the right things, in the right businesses, in the right way, to build a lasting competitive advantage?"

The topic matters because most business failure is not a failure of execution alone — it is a failure to choose a viable strategic direction in the first place, or a failure to adapt that direction as the environment changes.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Defining strategic management

Hill & Jones define strategic management as "the analyses, decisions, and actions an organization undertakes in order to create and sustain competitive advantages." Three ideas are packed into this definition:

  • Analysis — of the external environment (industry, competitors, macro forces) and the internal environment (resources, capabilities, structure).
  • Decisions — choices about mission, goals, and the strategies used to pursue them.
  • Actions — allocating resources, designing structures and systems, and executing the chosen strategy.

Competitive advantage — the central goal of the process — exists when a firm's profitability is higher than the average profitability of other firms competing for the same customers.

2.2 Levels of strategy

LevelResponsible forKey question
CorporateThe overall scope of the organization — which businesses/industries to compete inWhat businesses should we be in?
Business (SBU)How to compete within a particular industry or market segmentHow do we win in this market?
FunctionalMarketing, operations, finance, HR, R&D — building the capabilities that support the business-level strategyHow does this function support our competitive position?

2.3 The strategic management process

Although scholars phrase the steps differently, the process is generally presented as a cycle rather than a one-time event:

Mission, Vision & Goals
→
External Analysis (Opportunities & Threats)
→
Internal Analysis (Strengths & Weaknesses)
→
Strategy Formulation (SWOT-based choice)
→
Strategy Implementation
→
Evaluation & Control

The loop is continuous: evaluation and control feed back into the mission/goals stage, because performance outcomes and environmental change constantly prompt reconsideration of the strategy.

2.4 Who are "strategic managers"?

  • Corporate-level managers (e.g. CEO, Board, corporate staff) — oversee the whole portfolio of businesses, allocate resources across them, and are the ultimate guardians of shareholder value.
  • Business-level managers (e.g. divisional heads, general managers) — translate corporate direction into a competitive strategy for their specific business/market.
  • Functional-level managers — responsible for a specific operation (production, marketing, finance) and for building the distinctive competencies that give the business its edge.

2.5 Planned vs. emergent perspectives

The classical/design school (Andrews, Ansoff) treats strategy formation as a deliberate, rational, top-down planning exercise. Henry Mintzberg challenged this with the idea of emergent strategy — strategy that develops incrementally from the pattern of decisions actually taken, including unplanned responses to unforeseen events. In practice, realized strategy in most organizations is a blend of deliberate intentions and emergent adaptation.

3. Key Terms

Strategic management
The set of analyses, decisions, and actions an organization undertakes to create and sustain competitive advantage.
Competitive advantage
Above-average profitability relative to the average profitability of other firms in the same industry.
Strategic business unit (SBU)
A self-contained division or unit that formulates its own business-level strategy.
Deliberate strategy
Strategy that is planned in advance and implemented as intended.
Emergent strategy
Strategy that arises from an unplanned pattern of decisions/actions over time, often as a response to change.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Strategic management = analysis + decisions + actions aimed at building competitive advantage.
  • Three levels: corporate (which businesses), business (how to compete), functional (capability-building).
  • Process is a continuous cycle: mission/goals → external analysis → internal analysis → strategy formulation → implementation → evaluation/control → feedback loop.
  • Strategic managers exist at all three levels; corporate managers own portfolio-wide decisions.
  • Mintzberg's distinction: deliberate (planned) vs. emergent (unplanned, adaptive) strategy — real strategy is usually a mix.

Practice Questions

  1. Define strategic management and explain how it differs from operational management. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Strategic management is the set of analyses, decisions, and actions an organization undertakes to create and sustain competitive advantage (Hill & Jones) — it addresses "are we doing the right things" at the level of mission, goals, and long-term direction. Operational management, by contrast, focuses on "how do we do this task well" — the day-to-day execution of processes within a chosen strategy. Strategic management sets the direction; operational management executes within it.
  2. Describe the strategic management process as a continuous cycle, using a diagram. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    The process runs: Mission, Vision & Goals → External Analysis (opportunities/threats) → Internal Analysis (strengths/weaknesses) → Strategy Formulation (SWOT-based choice) → Strategy Implementation → Evaluation & Control, which feeds back into the mission/goals stage. It is continuous because performance results and environmental change constantly prompt reconsideration of the strategy (see the diagram in section 2.3 above).
  3. Distinguish between corporate-level, business-level, and functional-level strategy with examples. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Corporate-level strategy decides which businesses/industries to compete in (e.g. a conglomerate choosing to operate across steel, IT, and hospitality). Business-level strategy decides how to compete within a given industry or market segment (e.g. a car model competing on cost vs. differentiation). Functional-level strategy builds the capabilities — marketing, operations, HR — that support that business-level choice (e.g. a lean manufacturing process supporting a low-cost strategy).
  4. "Strategy is never purely planned nor purely emergent." Discuss with reference to Mintzberg's view. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Mintzberg argued that realized strategy = deliberate strategy (intended and implemented as planned) + emergent strategy (unplanned patterns arising from autonomous action, serendipity, or unplanned shifts by top managers). Purely planned strategy ignores that some intentions go unrealized due to unforeseen change; purely emergent strategy ignores that organizations do set deliberate direction. In practice, most realized strategies — such as Honda's entry into the US motorcycle market — blend both.
  5. What is competitive advantage, and how does it relate to the goal of strategic management? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Competitive advantage exists when a firm's profitability is higher than the average profitability of other firms competing for the same customers. It is the central goal that strategic management — analysis, decisions, and actions together — is organized around achieving and sustaining.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define strategic management. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The set of analyses, decisions, and actions an organization undertakes to create and sustain competitive advantage (Hill & Jones).
  2. What is a Strategic Business Unit (SBU)? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A self-contained division or unit within a larger organization that formulates and executes its own business-level strategy.
  3. What is emergent strategy? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Strategy that arises from an unplanned pattern of decisions and actions over time, often as an adaptive response to change, as distinguished by Mintzberg from deliberate (planned) strategy.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain the three levels of strategy with their key responsibilities. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Corporate-level strategy decides the overall scope of the organization — which businesses/industries to compete in. Business-level strategy (often set at the SBU) decides how to compete within a given industry or market segment. Functional-level strategy covers marketing, operations, finance, HR, and R&D — building the capabilities that support the business-level choice. The three levels form a cascading hierarchy: corporate direction shapes business strategy, which in turn shapes functional priorities.
  2. Describe the strategic management process as a continuous cycle. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    The process runs: Mission, Vision & Goals → External Analysis (opportunities/threats) → Internal Analysis (strengths/weaknesses) → Strategy Formulation (SWOT-based choice) → Strategy Implementation → Evaluation & Control, which feeds back into the mission/goals stage. It is continuous rather than a one-time event because performance outcomes and environmental change constantly prompt reconsideration of the strategy.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the concept of strategic management, its continuous process cycle, the strategic managers who drive it at different organizational levels, and Mintzberg's distinction between deliberate and emergent strategy. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Concept: Strategic management is the set of analyses, decisions, and actions an organization undertakes to create and sustain competitive advantage (Hill & Jones) — analysis of the external/internal environment, decisions on mission/goals/strategy, and actions to allocate resources and execute. It sits above operational management, addressing "are we doing the right things" rather than "are we doing things right." Competitive advantage — the central goal — exists when a firm's profitability exceeds the average profitability of firms competing for the same customers.

    Process cycle: Mission, Vision & Goals → External Analysis → Internal Analysis → Strategy Formulation (SWOT-based) → Strategy Implementation → Evaluation & Control, feeding back continuously as performance and environmental conditions change.

    Strategic managers at each level: Corporate-level managers (CEO, Board) oversee the whole business portfolio and are the ultimate guardians of shareholder value; business-level managers (divisional heads) translate corporate direction into competitive strategy for their specific market; functional-level managers build the distinctive competencies (production, marketing, finance) that give the business its edge.

    Deliberate vs. emergent (Mintzberg): Deliberate strategy is planned in advance and implemented as intended; emergent strategy develops incrementally from the actual pattern of decisions taken, including unplanned responses to unforeseen events. Realized strategy in most organizations blends both — pure top-down planning ignores real-world adaptation, while pure emergence ignores that organizations do set deliberate direction.

The Concept of Strategy and the Strategy Formation Process

Unit I · Topic 2

1. Overview

"Strategy" is one of the most used and most loosely defined words in management. Before an organization can manage its strategy, it needs a working definition of what strategy actually is — and an understanding of how strategies actually come into being inside real organizations, which is rarely a single, tidy planning exercise.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Defining strategy

ThinkerDefinition / emphasis
Alfred Chandler (1962)"The determination of the basic long-term goals and objectives of an enterprise, and the adoption of courses of action and the allocation of resources necessary for carrying out these goals." — strategy as long-term goal-setting plus resource allocation.
Michael PorterStrategy is about being different — deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value, and creating "fit" among a firm's activities so they reinforce one another and are hard to imitate.
Henry MintzbergStrategy cannot be captured in one definition — he offers five complementary views, the "5 Ps."

2.2 Mintzberg's 5 Ps of strategy

Plan
A consciously intended course of action for dealing with a situation, decided in advance.
Ploy
A specific maneuver intended to outwit a competitor (e.g. a threatened price cut to deter entry).
Pattern
Consistency in behavior over time, whether or not it was intended — "a realized pattern in a stream of actions."
Position
The way the organization locates itself in its environment — the match between organization and industry context.
Perspective
The organization's ingrained way of perceiving the world — its shared concepts and culture, "the organization's personality."

2.3 Intended, deliberate, realized, and emergent strategy

Mintzberg's model of strategy formation distinguishes between what an organization plans to do and what it actually ends up doing:

Intended Strategy
→
Deliberate Strategy
(intentions that get realized)
→
Realized Strategy

also feeding into Realized Strategy:

Emergent Strategy
(unplanned patterns that develop)
→
Realized Strategy

Unrealized Strategy = the part of the intended strategy that was never carried out.

2.4 Scientific vs. artistic perspectives on strategy formation (Parnell)

Parnell frames a second, complementary debate about how strategy should be formed:

  • Scientific perspective — most strategy scholars endorse this view: the environment is largely objective and analyzable, so managers should follow a systematic process of environmental, competitive, and internal analysis and build strategy on that foundation. It minimizes the role of intuition.
  • Artistic perspective — given how unpredictable and fast-moving the environment really is, elaborate formal planning is treated with suspicion; strategists instead rely on creativity and intuition. Mintzberg's image of the strategist as a craftsman — molding strategy the way a potter molds clay, through skill, feel, and mastery of detail — embodies this view.

Most courses (including this one, following Parnell) treat the scientific approach as the primary foundation while still valuing creativity and intuition within that systematic process — echoing the earlier point that realized strategy blends deliberate planning with emergent, unplanned adaptation.

2.5 The strategy formation process — stages

  1. Strategic intent / goal setting — clarifying mission, vision, and long-term aspirations.
  2. Environmental scanning — external analysis (industry structure, macro-environment, competitors) and internal analysis (resources, capabilities, value chain).
  3. Strategy formulation — generating and evaluating strategic options at corporate, business, and functional levels; selecting the strategy that best matches internal capability to external opportunity (the classic SWOT logic).
  4. Strategy implementation — translating the chosen strategy into organizational structure, systems, resource allocation, and day-to-day action.
  5. Strategic control and evaluation — monitoring performance against goals and feeding results back into the next cycle of strategy formation.

Because environments change and plans meet real-world friction, this process is iterative rather than linear — the "formation" of strategy is really a continuous interplay between deliberate planning and emergent learning.

3. Key Terms

Strategy
The long-term direction and scope of an organization, and the pattern of resource allocation and action by which it seeks to achieve competitive advantage.
Intended strategy
What the organization planned to do.
Realized strategy
What the organization actually did, combining deliberate and emergent elements.
Strategic fit
Porter's idea that a strategy's activities reinforce each other, making the whole system hard for rivals to copy.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Chandler: strategy = long-term goals + action + resource allocation. Porter: strategy = deliberate choice to be different + fit among activities. Mintzberg: strategy has 5 faces — Plan, Ploy, Pattern, Position, Perspective.
  • Realized strategy = Deliberate strategy (planned and executed) + Emergent strategy (unplanned patterns) − Unrealized strategy (planned but abandoned).
  • Parnell's Scientific perspective (systematic, analytical planning) vs. Artistic perspective (Mintzberg's "craftsman" — intuition and creativity) on how strategy should be formed.
  • Strategy formation process: strategic intent → environmental scanning (external + internal) → formulation → implementation → control/evaluation, feeding back continuously.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain Mintzberg's "5 Ps" of strategy with an example for each. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Plan — a consciously intended course of action (e.g. a 5-year expansion plan). Ploy — a maneuver to outwit a rival (e.g. announcing a price cut to deter a competitor's entry). Pattern — consistency in actions over time, intended or not (e.g. a firm that has consistently grown by acquiring smaller rivals). Position — how the firm locates itself relative to its environment (e.g. occupying the low-cost position in a price-sensitive market). Perspective — the organization's ingrained way of seeing the world (e.g. an engineering-led culture that always solves problems through R&D).
  2. Differentiate between deliberate and emergent strategy, and explain how the two combine into realized strategy. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Deliberate strategy is an intended strategy that is actually implemented as planned. Emergent strategy is an unplanned pattern that develops from autonomous action, serendipity, or unplanned shifts in response to changing circumstances. Realized strategy — what a company actually ends up doing — is the deliberate strategy that gets carried out plus the emergent strategy that develops along the way; whatever part of the original intended strategy is abandoned becomes unrealized strategy.
  3. Compare Chandler's and Porter's definitions of strategy. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Chandler defined strategy as the determination of long-term goals and objectives, plus the courses of action and resource allocation needed to carry them out — an emphasis on goal-setting and resourcing. Porter defined strategy as deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique value mix, with "fit" among those activities creating a system that is hard for rivals to imitate — an emphasis on differentiation and activity systems rather than goals alone.
  4. Outline the stages of the strategy formation process. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) Strategic intent/goal setting — clarifying mission and vision; (2) Environmental scanning — external and internal analysis; (3) Strategy formulation — generating and selecting options at corporate, business, and functional levels; (4) Strategy implementation — translating the choice into structure, systems, and action; (5) Strategic control and evaluation — monitoring performance and feeding results back into the next cycle.
  5. Compare the scientific and artistic perspectives on strategy formation, as described by Parnell. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The scientific perspective treats the environment as largely objective and analyzable, so managers should follow a systematic process of environmental, competitive, and internal analysis before formulating strategy. The artistic perspective distrusts elaborate formal planning given how unpredictable environments really are, and instead emphasizes creativity and intuition — Mintzberg's image of the strategist as a "craftsman" molding strategy the way a potter molds clay.
  6. "Strategy formation is as much about learning as it is about planning." Comment. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    This reflects Mintzberg's emergent-strategy insight: organizations often discover successful strategies through action and feedback rather than through prior planning alone (e.g. Honda's accidental success with 50cc bikes in the US). Effective strategic managers combine systematic planning with the willingness to recognize and nurture good emergent patterns as they surface, rather than rigidly executing only what was originally planned.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define strategy as per Alfred Chandler. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The determination of the basic long-term goals and objectives of an enterprise, and the adoption of courses of action and allocation of resources necessary for carrying out these goals.
  2. What is a "ploy" in Mintzberg's 5 Ps of strategy? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A specific maneuver intended to outwit a competitor, such as a threatened price cut to deter a rival's entry into a market.
  3. What is unrealized strategy? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The part of an organization's intended strategy that was planned but never actually carried out.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain Mintzberg's "5 Ps" of strategy briefly. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Plan — a consciously intended course of action. Ploy — a maneuver to outwit a rival. Pattern — consistency in behavior over time, intended or not. Position — how the firm locates itself relative to its environment. Perspective — the organization's ingrained way of perceiving the world, its shared culture. Together these five views show that strategy cannot be captured by a single definition.
  2. Compare the scientific and artistic perspectives on strategy formation. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    The scientific perspective treats the environment as largely objective and analyzable, so managers should follow a systematic process of environmental, competitive, and internal analysis before formulating strategy — it minimizes the role of intuition. The artistic perspective distrusts elaborate formal planning given how unpredictable environments really are, relying instead on creativity and intuition, captured in Mintzberg's image of the strategist as a "craftsman" molding strategy like a potter molds clay.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the various definitions of strategy, Mintzberg's model of intended/deliberate/emergent/realized strategy, and the stages of the strategy formation process. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Definitions: Chandler defines strategy as long-term goal-setting plus the resource allocation needed to pursue it. Porter frames strategy as deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver unique value, with "fit" among activities making the system hard to imitate. Mintzberg argues strategy cannot be captured in one definition, offering five complementary views — the 5 Ps: Plan, Ploy, Pattern, Position, Perspective.

    Intended/deliberate/emergent/realized model: An organization's intended strategy splits into deliberate strategy (the part actually implemented as planned) and unrealized strategy (the part abandoned). Separately, emergent strategy — unplanned patterns arising from autonomous action or unforeseen circumstances — also feeds into what the firm actually does. Realized strategy = deliberate strategy + emergent strategy.

    Strategy formation process: (1) Strategic intent/goal setting — clarifying mission and vision; (2) Environmental scanning — external analysis (industry, macro-environment, competitors) and internal analysis (resources, capabilities); (3) Strategy formulation — generating and evaluating options at corporate, business, and functional levels using SWOT logic; (4) Strategy implementation — translating the chosen strategy into structure, systems, and resource allocation; (5) Strategic control and evaluation — monitoring performance and feeding results back into the next cycle. The process is iterative, not linear, blending Parnell's scientific (systematic analysis) and artistic (intuitive, craftsman-like) perspectives on how strategy should actually be formed.

Stakeholders in Business

Unit I · Topic 3

1. Overview

No organization sets or pursues its strategy in isolation — it operates within a web of individuals and groups who affect, or are affected by, its decisions. Understanding who these stakeholders are, what they want, and how much influence they have is a precondition for setting a workable mission and objectives (the next two topics).

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Defining stakeholders

R. Edward Freeman's classic definition: a stakeholder is "any group or individual who can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organization's objectives." This is broader than the older shareholder-only view of the firm — it recognizes that sustainable strategy must account for a wider set of claims on the business.

2.2 Internal vs. external stakeholders

Internal stakeholdersExternal stakeholders
Shareholders / ownersCustomers
Board of directorsSuppliers
ManagersGovernment & regulators
EmployeesLocal communities
 Creditors / lenders
 Competitors, trade unions, pressure groups, the media

A closely related distinction is between market/economic stakeholders (parties in a direct economic relationship with the firm — shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, creditors) and non-market/social stakeholders (government, communities, pressure groups, the media) who influence the firm through public, legal, or social channels rather than market transactions.

2.3 The stakeholder exchange relationship (Hill & Jones)

Hill & Jones frame every stakeholder relationship as an exchange: each stakeholder group supplies the organization with a resource or contribution, and in exchange expects its interests to be satisfied through an inducement.

StakeholderProvides (contribution)Expects in return (inducement)
StockholdersRisk capitalMaximized return on investment
Creditors / bondholdersDebt capitalTimely repayment with interest
EmployeesLabor and skillsFair income, job satisfaction, security, good conditions
CustomersRevenueHigh-quality, reliable, value-for-money products
SuppliersInputsRevenue and dependable, ongoing business
GovernmentRules maintaining fair competitionCompliance with those rules
UnionsProductive, organized employeesBenefits proportional to members' contribution
Local communitiesLocal infrastructureResponsible corporate citizenship
General publicNational infrastructureAn improved quality of life

If a firm fails to honor a stakeholder's claim, that stakeholder can withdraw support — stockholders sell shares, employees quit, customers switch suppliers, unions strike, communities block expansion, government imposes fines. This is why stakeholder claims must be factored directly into strategy formulation, not treated as a side issue.

2.4 Stakeholder Impact Analysis (Hill & Jones)

Because a company can rarely satisfy every stakeholder claim at once — claims often conflict, e.g. union demands for higher wages vs. shareholder demands for returns vs. customer demands for lower prices — Hill & Jones prescribe a five-step stakeholder impact analysis to decide which claims to prioritize:

  1. Identify stakeholders.
  2. Identify stakeholders' interests and concerns.
  3. Identify what claims stakeholders are likely to make on the organization.
  4. Identify the stakeholders who are most important from the organization's perspective.
  5. Identify the resulting strategic challenges.

Most companies that carry out this analysis conclude that three stakeholder groups must be satisfied above all others for the firm to survive and prosper: customers, employees, and stockholders. Stockholders are usually treated as a distinct class because they supply risk capital — capital with no guarantee of being recouped — so managers generally give priority to strategies that maximize long-run profitability (ROIC) and profit growth for stockholders, while still meeting the claims of other key stakeholders.

2.5 Stakeholder mapping — the Power/Interest Matrix

A complementary tool widely taught alongside stakeholder impact analysis is to plot stakeholders on two dimensions: their power to influence the organization, and their interest in its activities.

Low InterestHigh Interest
High PowerKeep Satisfied — meet their needs, don't over-communicateKey Players — manage closely, engage actively in decisions
Low PowerMinimal Effort — monitor onlyKeep Informed — consult and update regularly

This mapping is a practical way to operationalize step 4 of stakeholder impact analysis (identifying the most important stakeholders) and to decide where to invest limited time and communication effort.

2.6 Common stakeholder goals (Parnell)

StakeholderTypical goal
CustomersHigh-quality products/services at the most reasonable prices
General publicMinimum environmental cost, more employment, contribution to social/charitable causes
SuppliersLong-term relationships and prices that let suppliers stay profitable
EmployeesGood working conditions, equitable compensation, advancement opportunities
CreditorsA healthy financial position and on-time debt repayment
ShareholdersA higher-than-average return on equity
Board of directorsRetention and protection from legal liability
ManagersFinancial benefit from the firm's growth and success

These claims frequently conflict (e.g. shareholders wanting cost cuts vs. employees wanting job security), which is why balancing stakeholder goals is a core strategic — not just ethical — task: unresolved conflicts can derail strategy execution.

3. Key Terms

Stakeholder
Any group or individual that can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organization's objectives (Freeman).
Internal stakeholder
A stakeholder that is part of the organization itself (e.g. employees, managers, shareholders).
External stakeholder
A stakeholder outside the organization who has a claim on its behavior (e.g. customers, government, community).
Stakeholder impact analysis
Hill & Jones' five-step process for identifying stakeholders, their claims, and which claims to prioritize.
Risk capital
Capital provided by stockholders with no guarantee it will be recouped — the basis for treating stockholders as a distinct stakeholder class.
Stakeholder mapping
Classifying stakeholders (e.g. by power and interest) to decide how to manage relationships with each.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Stakeholder = any party who affects or is affected by the firm's objectives (Freeman).
  • Internal: shareholders, board, managers, employees. External: customers, suppliers, government, community, and more.
  • Every stakeholder relationship is an exchange: a contribution to the firm in return for an inducement (Hill & Jones).
  • Stakeholder impact analysis (5 steps): identify stakeholders → their interests/concerns → their likely claims → the most important stakeholders → the resulting strategic challenges.
  • Three groups usually rank as most critical to survival: customers, employees, stockholders. Stockholders are distinct because they supply risk capital.
  • Power/Interest matrix: Power × Interest → Key Players / Keep Satisfied / Keep Informed / Minimal Effort — a practical tool for step 4 of the analysis.
  • Stakeholder claims often conflict (Parnell's Table 5.1) — strategic managers must prioritize and balance them.

Practice Questions

  1. Define "stakeholder" and distinguish between internal and external stakeholders with examples. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    A stakeholder is any group or individual who can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organization's objectives (Freeman). Internal stakeholders are part of the organization itself — shareholders, the board, managers, employees. External stakeholders sit outside it but still hold a claim on its behavior — customers, suppliers, government, local communities.
  2. Explain Hill & Jones' concept of the stakeholder "exchange relationship" with an example. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Every stakeholder relationship is framed as an exchange: the stakeholder supplies the firm with a resource/contribution and expects an inducement in return. Example: employees supply labor and skills and expect fair income, job security, and good working conditions in exchange; if that inducement isn't honored, employees can withdraw their contribution by quitting.
  3. Describe the five steps of stakeholder impact analysis and explain why it is needed. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) Identify stakeholders; (2) identify their interests/concerns; (3) identify their likely claims; (4) identify the most important stakeholders; (5) identify the resulting strategic challenges. It is needed because a firm can rarely satisfy every stakeholder's claim simultaneously (e.g. union wage demands vs. shareholder return demands), so managers must systematically prioritize.
  4. Why are stockholders usually treated as a distinct class of stakeholder? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Stockholders provide risk capital — capital with no guarantee it will ever be recouped — which distinguishes them from stakeholders like employees or suppliers who face less open-ended risk. Because of this, managers generally give priority to strategies that maximize long-run profitability and profit growth for stockholders, alongside satisfying other key stakeholders like customers and employees.
  5. Explain the power/interest matrix and how it complements stakeholder impact analysis. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    The matrix plots stakeholders on power (ability to influence the organization) and interest (level of concern in its activities), producing four categories: Key Players (high power/high interest — manage closely), Keep Satisfied (high power/low interest), Keep Informed (low power/high interest), and Minimal Effort (low power/low interest). It operationalizes step 4 of stakeholder impact analysis — identifying the most important stakeholders — by giving managers a practical way to decide where to focus engagement.
  6. Discuss a situation in which shareholder interests and employee interests might conflict, and how a firm could balance them. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    A common conflict arises during cost-cutting: shareholders may want layoffs or wage freezes to protect short-term profitability, while employees want job security and fair compensation. A firm can balance this by communicating transparently about the trade-off, favoring temporary measures (hiring freezes, voluntary retirement) over layoffs where possible, and tying part of returns to long-term measures that also reflect workforce stability, rather than treating the conflict as zero-sum.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define "stakeholder" as per Freeman. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Any group or individual who can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organization's objectives.
  2. What is risk capital? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Capital provided by stockholders with no guarantee it will ever be recouped — the basis for treating stockholders as a distinct stakeholder class.
  3. Name the four quadrants of the Power/Interest stakeholder matrix. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Key Players (high power, high interest), Keep Satisfied (high power, low interest), Keep Informed (low power, high interest), and Minimal Effort (low power, low interest).

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain Hill & Jones' concept of the stakeholder exchange relationship. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Every stakeholder relationship is framed as an exchange: the stakeholder supplies the firm with a resource or contribution and expects an inducement in return — e.g. employees supply labor and skills and expect fair income, security, and good conditions; customers supply revenue and expect quality, reliable, value-for-money products. If a firm fails to honor a stakeholder's claim, that stakeholder can withdraw support (employees quit, customers switch suppliers, shareholders sell shares), which is why claims must be factored directly into strategy.
  2. Describe the five steps of stakeholder impact analysis. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    (1) Identify stakeholders; (2) identify their interests and concerns; (3) identify the claims they are likely to make on the organization; (4) identify the stakeholders who are most important from the organization's perspective; (5) identify the resulting strategic challenges. It is used because a firm can rarely satisfy every stakeholder claim simultaneously, so managers must systematically decide which to prioritize.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the concept of stakeholders, the internal/external classification, the stakeholder exchange relationship, and stakeholder impact analysis with the power/interest matrix. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Concept: Freeman defines a stakeholder as any group or individual who can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organization's objectives — broader than the older shareholder-only view of the firm.

    Internal vs. external: Internal stakeholders are part of the organization — shareholders/owners, the board of directors, managers, and employees. External stakeholders sit outside it but still hold a claim on its behavior — customers, suppliers, government and regulators, local communities, creditors, competitors, unions, and the media. A related split is market/economic stakeholders (direct economic relationship) vs. non-market/social stakeholders (influence via public, legal, or social channels).

    Exchange relationship: Each stakeholder supplies a contribution and expects an inducement in return (e.g. stockholders provide risk capital and expect maximized return; employees provide labor and expect fair income and security; suppliers provide inputs and expect dependable ongoing business). Failure to honor a claim lets the stakeholder withdraw support.

    Stakeholder impact analysis: A five-step process — identify stakeholders, their interests/concerns, their likely claims, the most important stakeholders, and the resulting strategic challenges — needed because claims often conflict (e.g. union wage demands vs. shareholder return demands). Most firms conclude customers, employees, and stockholders must be satisfied above all others to survive, with stockholders distinct because they bear risk capital.

    Power/Interest matrix: Plots stakeholders on power (ability to influence) and interest (concern in activities), producing Key Players, Keep Satisfied, Keep Informed, and Minimal Effort quadrants — a practical tool for operationalizing step 4 of the impact analysis and deciding where to focus limited engagement effort.

Vision, Mission and Purpose

Unit I · Topic 4

1. Overview

Once an organization understands its stakeholders, it must articulate why it exists and where it is headed. Vision, mission, and purpose statements are the formal expression of this — they set the boundaries and direction within which every subsequent objective, strategy, and decision is made.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Vision vs. mission vs. purpose vs. values

TermAnswersTime horizonNature
Vision"What do we want to become?"Long-term, aspirationalA future-oriented, inspiring picture of success
Mission"What is our business, and who do we serve?"Present / ongoingA statement of current purpose, scope, and reason for being
Purpose"Why do we exist, beyond making money?"EnduringThe deeper, often social, reason for the organization's existence
Values"What do we stand for/how do we behave?"EnduringCore principles guiding behavior and decisions

In practice these terms often overlap and companies use them inconsistently — but exam answers should keep the distinctions above clear: vision is aspirational/future, mission is operational/present, purpose is the underlying "why."

2.2 Characteristics of an effective mission statement

  • Clear and focused — not so broad it is meaningless, not so narrow it limits legitimate opportunities.
  • Distinctive — communicates what makes the organization different.
  • Feasible — realistic given the organization's resources and environment.
  • Motivating — inspires employees and stakeholders.
  • Flexible enough to endure — durable but not so rigid it prevents adaptation.

2.3 Components of a mission statement

Supplementary framework

The Pearce & David checklist below is a widely taught way to audit a mission statement's completeness. It is not from Hill & Jones or Parnell specifically, but is a useful practical tool alongside their definitions in 2.1–2.2.

A commonly taught framework (Pearce & David) lists the elements a comprehensive mission statement should address:

  1. Customers — who are they?
  2. Products/services — what does the firm offer?
  3. Markets — where does it compete geographically?
  4. Technology — is the firm technologically current?
  5. Concern for survival, growth, and profitability
  6. Philosophy — beliefs, values, and ethical priorities
  7. Self-concept — the firm's own view of its distinctive competence
  8. Concern for public image
  9. Concern for employees

2.4 Business definition — Abell's three dimensions

Derek Abell's framework is often used to sharpen how a mission defines "what business are we in?" along three axes:

  • Customer groups — who is being served?
  • Customer needs/functions — what needs are being satisfied?
  • Technology/means — how are those needs being satisfied?

This is used to avoid two classic mistakes: defining a mission too narrowly around a single product (Levitt's "marketing myopia" — e.g. railroads defining themselves as being "in the railroad business" instead of "the transportation business," missing the rise of trucking and air travel), or too broadly to be actionable.

2.5 Why vision/mission matter strategically

The mission and vision act as a filter for strategic choice: they guide which opportunities the organization pursues and which it declines, they provide a shared sense of direction across business units, and they form the starting point from which measurable objectives and goals (Topic 5) are derived.

3. Key Terms

Vision
An aspirational statement of what the organization wants to become in the future.
Mission
A statement of the organization's current purpose, scope, and reason for being — what business it is in and who it serves.
Purpose
The organization's fundamental reason for existing, beyond financial performance.
Marketing myopia
Levitt's term for defining a business too narrowly around a product rather than the customer need it satisfies, causing firms to miss broader threats and opportunities.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Vision = future aspiration; Mission = present purpose & scope; Purpose = deeper "why"; Values = behavioral principles.
  • Good mission statements are clear, distinctive, feasible, motivating, and durable yet adaptable.
  • Pearce & David's 9 components: customers, products/services, markets, technology, survival/growth/profitability, philosophy, self-concept, public image, employees.
  • Abell's 3 dimensions of business definition: customer groups, customer needs, technology/means.
  • Marketing myopia = defining the business too narrowly around a product instead of the underlying customer need (classic example: railroads).

Practice Questions

  1. Distinguish between vision, mission, and purpose, giving an example of each. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Vision is an aspirational statement of what the organization wants to become (e.g. Nokia's "If it can go mobile, it will!"). Mission is a statement of current purpose and scope — what business the company is in and who it serves (e.g. Kodak's mission to provide imaging solutions). Purpose is the deeper, enduring reason the organization exists beyond profit (e.g. a company's stated purpose "to improve quality of life in the communities we serve").
  2. What are the characteristics of an effective mission statement? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    It should be clear and focused (not so broad it's meaningless, not so narrow it limits opportunity), distinctive, feasible given the firm's resources, motivating to employees and stakeholders, and flexible enough to endure environmental change without needing constant rewriting.
  3. Explain Abell's three-dimensional framework for defining a business, and illustrate with an example of "marketing myopia." (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Abell's framework defines a business along three dimensions: customer groups (who is being satisfied), customer needs (what is being satisfied), and technology/distinctive competencies (how needs are satisfied). Myopia occurs when a firm defines itself around its product rather than the customer need it serves — the classic case is 1950s–60s typewriter makers like Smith Corona, who defined their business as "making typewriters" rather than "information processing," and were wiped out by computers; IBM survived by defining its business the broader way.
  4. Draft a mission statement for a hypothetical company and justify it against Pearce & David's nine components. (Applied / Essay)
    Show model answer
    Open-ended — no single correct answer. A strong response states a mission statement (e.g. for a campus food-delivery startup) and then explicitly maps it against each of the nine components — customers, products/services, markets, technology, survival/growth/profitability, philosophy, self-concept, public image, employees — showing where each is addressed and where the statement is deliberately silent, and why.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define vision statement. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    An aspirational statement of what the organization wants to become in the future — long-term and future-oriented.
  2. What is marketing myopia? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Levitt's term for defining a business too narrowly around a product rather than the customer need it satisfies, causing firms to miss broader threats and opportunities.
  3. Name Abell's three dimensions for defining a business. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Customer groups (who is served), customer needs/functions (what needs are satisfied), and technology/means (how those needs are satisfied).

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Distinguish between vision, mission, purpose, and values. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Vision answers "what do we want to become?" — long-term and aspirational. Mission answers "what is our business, and who do we serve?" — present and operational. Purpose answers "why do we exist, beyond profit?" — an enduring, often social, reason for being. Values answer "what do we stand for?" — enduring core principles guiding behavior and decisions.
  2. What are the characteristics of an effective mission statement? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    It should be clear and focused (neither so broad it's meaningless nor so narrow it limits legitimate opportunity), distinctive (communicates what makes the firm different), feasible given the organization's resources and environment, motivating to employees and stakeholders, and flexible enough to endure environmental change without needing constant rewriting.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Explain the distinction between vision, mission, and purpose; the Pearce & David checklist for mission statements; and Abell's three-dimensional framework for defining a business, with reference to marketing myopia. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Vision vs. mission vs. purpose: Vision is a long-term, aspirational picture of what the organization wants to become. Mission is a present-tense statement of current purpose, scope, and reason for being — what business the firm is in and who it serves. Purpose is the enduring, deeper reason for existing beyond financial performance. In practice these terms overlap in company usage, but exam answers should keep them conceptually distinct.

    Pearce & David's nine components of a comprehensive mission statement: customers, products/services, markets, technology, concern for survival/growth/profitability, philosophy, self-concept (the firm's view of its distinctive competence), concern for public image, and concern for employees. This checklist is used to audit whether a mission statement is complete.

    Abell's three dimensions: customer groups (who is served), customer needs/functions (what need is satisfied), and technology/means (how it is satisfied). This framework helps a firm avoid two classic mistakes: defining its mission too narrowly around a single product — Levitt's "marketing myopia," illustrated by railroads that saw themselves as being "in the railroad business" instead of "the transportation business" and missed the rise of trucking and air travel — or defining it too broadly to be actionable. Vision and mission together act as a filter for strategic choice, guiding which opportunities the firm pursues and forming the starting point from which measurable objectives (Topic 5) are derived.

Business Objectives and Goals

Unit I · Topic 5

1. Overview

Mission and vision (Topic 4) set the broad direction; objectives and goals translate that direction into specific, measurable targets that guide strategy formulation and let performance actually be evaluated. Without them, a mission statement remains an aspiration with no way to check whether the organization is on track.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Goals vs. objectives

Per Parnell, the organization's goals represent the desired general ends toward which effort is directed; objectives are specific and often quantified versions of those goals. Goals alone are hard to verify because they are usually not quantified — objectives are what make performance actually measurable.

GoalObjective
SpecificityGeneral, broad desired endSpecific, quantified, verifiable
Example"Be known as the innovative leader in the industry""Have 30% of sales each year come from products developed in the preceding four years"
RoleStates the directionGives management a measurable target to track progress against that direction

Note: Hill & Jones use "goal" somewhat differently — for them, a well-constructed goal itself should already be precise and measurable (see 2.3 below). For exam purposes, use Parnell's goal/objective distinction unless your instructor specifies otherwise.

2.2 Official vs. operative goals

  • Official goals — the formally stated aims in mission statements and annual reports (often broad, e.g. "delivering shareholder value").
  • Operative goals — the actual targets that guide day-to-day decisions, which may differ from official goals (e.g. a stated goal of "customer first" but operative pressure to hit quarterly sales numbers).

A gap between official and operative goals is a common source of organizational tension and a useful analytical lens for case studies.

2.3 Characteristics of well-constructed goals (Hill & Jones)

Hill & Jones set out four characteristics that well-constructed goals should have:

  1. Precise and measurable — giving managers a yardstick against which to judge performance.
  2. Address crucial issues — a limited number of major, important goals, so focus is not lost.
  3. Challenging but realistic — unrealistic goals cause employees to give up; goals that are too easy fail to motivate.
  4. Specify a time period, where appropriate — deadlines inject urgency and act as a motivator.

Supplementary mnemonic

Many courses also teach the general management shorthand SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) for writing good objectives — it captures the same four ideas above and is useful as a memorable checklist, even though it is not the specific terminology used in Hill & Jones or Parnell.

2.4 Types of objectives

BasisTypes
Time horizonLong-term (strategic, 3–5+ years) vs. short-term (operational, <1 year)
NatureFinancial objectives (profitability, revenue growth, ROI, shareholder return) vs. strategic objectives (market share, quality, innovation, brand reputation)
LevelCorporate objectives → business-unit objectives → functional/departmental objectives (a cascading hierarchy)

Financial and strategic objectives can conflict in the short run (e.g. cutting R&D spending improves short-term profit but weakens long-term strategic position) — a well-run strategic planning process makes this trade-off explicit rather than letting financial pressure silently override strategic intent.

2.5 The Balanced Scorecard

Kaplan & Norton's Balanced Scorecard is a widely used tool for setting and tracking objectives beyond pure financial measures, across four perspectives:

PerspectiveTypical question
FinancialHow do we look to shareholders?
CustomerHow do customers see us?
Internal business processWhat must we excel at internally?
Learning & growthCan we continue to improve and create value?

This ensures objective-setting does not become narrowly financial, which can encourage short-termism at the expense of the mission's longer-term intent.

3. Key Terms

Goal
A desired general end toward which organizational effort is directed (Parnell) — broad and usually not quantified.
Objective
A specific, verifiable, often quantified version of a goal, used to measure whether the goal is being met (Parnell).
Official goals
Formally stated organizational aims.
Operative goals
The goals actually pursued through day-to-day decisions and resource allocation.
Balanced Scorecard
Kaplan & Norton's performance-management framework tracking strategic objectives and measures across financial, customer, internal process, and learning/growth perspectives.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Goals = general desired ends (Parnell); Objectives = specific, quantified, verifiable versions of a goal.
  • Hill & Jones' 4 characteristics of a well-constructed goal: precise/measurable, addresses crucial issues, challenging but realistic, time-bound where appropriate.
  • Official goals (stated) can diverge from operative goals (actually pursued) — a key case-study analysis point.
  • Goals/objectives cascade: corporate → business unit → functional, and split into financial vs. strategic types.
  • Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan & Norton) broadens objective-setting to 4 perspectives: Financial, Customer, Internal Process, Learning & Growth.

Practice Questions

  1. Differentiate between goals and objectives as defined by Parnell, with an example of each. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Goals are general, usually unquantified desired ends (e.g. "be known as the innovation leader in the industry"). Objectives are the specific, verifiable, often quantified versions of a goal used to measure whether it's being met (e.g. "30% of annual sales from products launched in the last four years").
  2. List and explain the four characteristics of well-constructed goals according to Hill & Jones. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) Precise and measurable — gives managers a yardstick for performance; (2) address crucial issues — a limited number of important goals, to maintain focus; (3) challenging but realistic — unrealistic goals cause employees to give up, too-easy goals fail to motivate; (4) specify a time period where appropriate — deadlines create urgency.
  3. Distinguish between official and operative goals, and explain why the gap between them matters strategically. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Official goals are the formally stated aims in mission statements/annual reports (often broad, e.g. "customer first"). Operative goals are what actually drives day-to-day decisions (e.g. hitting quarterly sales targets). The gap matters because it's a common source of organizational tension and a useful lens for case analysis — a firm whose operative goals contradict its official goals risks both ethical and strategic problems.
  4. Describe the four perspectives of the Balanced Scorecard and explain why relying only on financial objectives can be risky. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Financial ("how do we look to shareholders?"), Customer ("how do customers see us?"), Internal Business Process ("what must we excel at internally?"), and Learning & Growth ("can we continue to improve and create value?"). Relying only on financial objectives is risky because it encourages short-termism — e.g. cutting R&D or marketing to hit this quarter's profit number — since financial results are a lagging indicator of decisions already made elsewhere in the business.
  5. "Financial objectives and strategic objectives can conflict." Discuss with an example. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Financial objectives (e.g. maximizing current-year ROIC) can tempt managers to cut "non-essential" spending like R&D, marketing, or capital investment, boosting short-term profitability. But strategic objectives (e.g. innovation, customer satisfaction, long-run competitiveness) depend on exactly that spending. A firm that repeatedly favors financial targets over strategic investment risks eroding the capabilities that generate future profit.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Distinguish "goal" from "objective" in one line each, as per Parnell. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A goal is a general, usually unquantified desired end; an objective is a specific, verifiable, often quantified version of a goal.
  2. What does the "S" and "M" in SMART objectives stand for? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    S = Specific, M = Measurable (the full mnemonic is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound).
  3. What is an operative goal? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The actual target that guides day-to-day decisions, which may differ from the organization's formally stated official goals.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. List and explain Hill & Jones' four characteristics of well-constructed goals. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    (1) Precise and measurable — gives managers a yardstick to judge performance; (2) address crucial issues — a limited number of major goals, so focus is not lost; (3) challenging but realistic — unrealistic goals cause employees to give up, too-easy goals fail to motivate; (4) specify a time period where appropriate — deadlines inject urgency and act as a motivator.
  2. Describe the four perspectives of the Balanced Scorecard. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Kaplan & Norton's Balanced Scorecard tracks objectives across four perspectives: Financial ("how do we look to shareholders?"), Customer ("how do customers see us?"), Internal Business Process ("what must we excel at internally?"), and Learning & Growth ("can we continue to improve and create value?"). This prevents objective-setting from becoming narrowly financial, which can encourage short-termism.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the distinction between goals and objectives, official vs. operative goals, Hill & Jones' characteristics of well-constructed goals, the types of objectives, and the Balanced Scorecard framework. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Goals vs. objectives: Per Parnell, goals represent the desired general ends toward which effort is directed (e.g. "be known as the innovation leader"); objectives are specific, quantified versions of those goals (e.g. "30% of annual sales from products launched in the last four years") that make performance actually measurable.

    Official vs. operative goals: Official goals are the formally stated aims in mission statements and annual reports, often broad (e.g. "delivering shareholder value"). Operative goals are the actual targets guiding day-to-day decisions, which can diverge from official goals (e.g. stated "customer first" vs. operative pressure to hit quarterly numbers) — a common source of organizational tension.

    Characteristics of well-constructed goals (Hill & Jones): precise and measurable, addressing crucial issues, challenging but realistic, and time-bound where appropriate — echoed in the general SMART mnemonic.

    Types of objectives: long-term (strategic) vs. short-term (operational) by time horizon; financial (profitability, ROI) vs. strategic (market share, quality, innovation) by nature; and a cascading hierarchy of corporate → business-unit → functional objectives by level. Financial and strategic objectives can conflict in the short run — e.g. cutting R&D improves short-term profit but weakens long-term strategic position.

    Balanced Scorecard: Kaplan & Norton's framework tracks objectives across Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, and Learning & Growth perspectives, ensuring objective-setting does not become narrowly financial and short-termist.
