Corporate Governance and Social Responsibility

Unit I · Topic 6

1. Overview

Strategic decisions are made by managers on behalf of owners and in a context shaped by wider society. Corporate governance is the system of checks that ensures managers act in the interests of shareholders (and other stakeholders); corporate social responsibility (CSR) is the broader question of what obligations a business has to society beyond its shareholders. Both directly constrain and shape the strategic choices covered in Topics 1–5.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Corporate governance — definition

Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices, and processes by which a company is directed and controlled, defining the relationships and balance of power among shareholders, the board of directors, and management.

2.2 The agency problem

Modern corporations separate ownership (shareholders) from control (professional managers). This creates an agency relationship: shareholders (principals) hire managers ("agents" of the owners) to run the company on their behalf. Per Parnell, the agency problem refers to a situation in which a firm's managers fail to act in the best interests of the shareholders. It stems from two related conditions:

  • Moral hazard — a situation where the parties in an arrangement do not share equally in the risks and benefits; owners risk their capital while managers seek other benefits and enjoy only a limited share of the returns.
  • Adverse selection — the inability of shareholders to precisely identify the competencies and true intentions of the managers they hire, since owners can never be fully certain the professionals running the firm have the owners' best interests at heart.

Two competing views exist on how serious this is in practice: one view holds that management serves its own interests (e.g. growing the firm to increase managerial salary/prestige even when growth isn't the optimal strategy — a pattern researchers link to excessive CEO compensation); the other holds that management and stockholders largely share the same interests, particularly where compensation is tied to firm performance.

Why this matters for strategy

Agency problems can distort strategic choices — e.g. managers preferring safe, low-growth strategies that protect their position over riskier strategies that would better serve shareholders, or pursuing acquisitions/growth that increase firm size (and managerial pay) without creating shareholder value.

2.3 Governance mechanisms

Corporate governance (Parnell) refers to the board of directors, institutional investors (pension/retirement funds, mutual funds, banks, insurers), and large shareholders ("blockholders") who monitor firm strategy to ensure effective management. Key mechanisms include:

  • Board of directors — elected by shareholders to select/terminate the CEO, set compensation, advise on strategy, and monitor performance. Boards include inside directors (firm executives, who bring company knowledge) and outside directors (who bring independence).
  • CEO duality — when the CEO also chairs the board. This can weaken oversight, since insiders' career prospects depend on the CEO, making a "rubber stamp" board more likely. Hill & Jones list separating the CEO and chairman roles as a cornerstone of strong governance.
  • Independent compensation and audit committees — composed of outside directors, to limit self-dealing in executive pay and ensure rigorous, independent review of financial statements.
  • Independent outside auditors — auditors without a conflicting consulting relationship with the firm, so they can question management's numbers without fear of losing other business.
  • Regulation — the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) — passed after major accounting scandals (Enron, WorldCom); requires more independent directors, disclosure of internal controls/ethics codes/audit-committee composition, CEO and CFO certification of financial statements, and bans personal loans from firms to their directors/executives.
  • Institutional investors and activist shareholders — large holders (pension/mutual funds) and activist investors who pressure boards to act in shareholders' interests.
  • Market for corporate control — the threat of takeover disciplines underperforming management.

Hill & Jones' five cornerstones of strong governance

(1) A board with a majority of independent outside directors; (2) separate individuals as CEO and board chairman (chairman being an outside director); (3) a compensation committee composed entirely of outside directors; (4) an audit committee composed entirely of outside directors; (5) truly independent outside auditors with no conflicting consulting relationship.

2.4 Corporate social responsibility (CSR) — definition

CSR refers to the obligations a firm has toward the society in which it operates, beyond what is required by law and beyond the pursuit of profit alone.

2.5 Carroll's CSR Pyramid

Archie Carroll's widely taught model organizes a firm's social responsibilities into four layers, built from the base up:

Layer (top = most discretionary)ResponsibilityExpectation
4. PhilanthropicBe a good corporate citizenDesired by society
3. EthicalDo what is right, fair, and just, even beyond legal minimumsExpected by society
2. LegalObey laws and regulationsRequired by society
1. EconomicBe profitable — the foundation on which all other layers restRequired by society

Carroll's key insight is that economic performance is not opposed to social responsibility — it is its foundation. A firm cannot sustain ethical or philanthropic activity without first being economically viable. Carroll also stressed the four dimensions are not mutually exclusive: managers are constantly balancing these competing obligations together, not moving through them in strict sequence.

2.6 The CSR debate, and Porter & Kramer's Strategic CSR (Parnell)

Parnell frames CSR as a live debate rather than a settled matter:

  • Pro-CSR view — firms owe society more than legal compliance; advocates often invoke the triple bottom line — the idea that firms should maintain and improve social and ecological performance alongside economic performance, not just financial results.
  • Critics (e.g. Milton Friedman) — argue CSR is not management's role: firms should behave ethically and maximize shareholder returns within the law; spending shareholder funds on social causes substitutes managers' judgment for that of individual shareholders and can make the firm less competitive.

Building on this debate, Porter & Kramer (2006) proposed that CSR and competitive advantage need not be a zero-sum trade-off, describing a continuum:

  • Responsive CSR — acting as a good corporate citizen responsive to stakeholders' social concerns, and mitigating existing/anticipated harm from the firm's own operations.
  • Strategic CSR — going further, launching initiatives whose social and business benefits are both large and distinctive to the firm — CSR designed to reinforce, not merely offset, competitive advantage.

2.7 CSR vs. corporate governance — how they relate

Governance is primarily about accountability and control mechanisms (protecting shareholders and ensuring proper conduct); CSR is about the scope of obligations the firm voluntarily accepts toward broader society. Good governance is increasingly seen as itself a component of social responsibility, and many governance codes now require boards to consider stakeholder and environmental impact, not just shareholder return — a link often labeled "ESG" (Environmental, Social, Governance).

3. Key Terms

Corporate governance
The board of directors, institutional investors, and blockholders who monitor firm strategy to ensure effective management (Parnell); more broadly, the system of rules and processes by which a company is directed and controlled.
Agency problem
A situation in which a firm's managers (agents) fail to act in the best interests of shareholders (principals).
Moral hazard
A situation where the parties in an arrangement do not share equally in the risks and benefits (owners bear the capital risk; managers capture disproportionate benefits).
Adverse selection
Shareholders' inability to precisely identify the true competencies and intentions of the managers they hire.
CEO duality
When one person holds both the CEO and board chairman roles, weakening independent board oversight.
Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002)
U.S. legislation requiring more independent directors, greater financial/ethics disclosure, and CEO/CFO certification of financial statements, passed after major accounting scandals.
Corporate social responsibility (CSR)
The expectation and obligation that business firms should serve both society and the financial interests of shareholders (Parnell).
Triple bottom line
The idea that firms should maintain and improve social and ecological performance alongside economic performance.
Carroll's CSR Pyramid
A model of four layered responsibilities: economic, legal, ethical, and philanthropic.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Agency problem = managers not acting in shareholders' best interest; rooted in moral hazard (unequal risk/reward sharing) and adverse selection (owners can't verify managers' true competence/intent).
  • Two views on severity: management serves its own interests vs. management and shareholders share the same interests.
  • Hill & Jones' 5 cornerstones of strong governance: majority-outsider board, separate CEO/chairman (no CEO duality), independent compensation committee, independent audit committee, independent outside auditors.
  • Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002): more independent directors, more disclosure, CEO/CFO certify financials, no personal loans to directors/executives — passed after Enron/WorldCom-type scandals.
  • CSR debate: pro-CSR (triple bottom line: economic + social + ecological) vs. Friedman-style critics (CSR isn't management's role; focus on legal, ethical profit-seeking).
  • Porter & Kramer: Responsive CSR (good citizenship, mitigate harm) → Strategic CSR (initiatives with large, distinctive social *and* business benefit).
  • Carroll's CSR Pyramid (bottom to top): Economic → Legal → Ethical → Philanthropic — economic responsibility is the foundation; the four are balanced together, not pursued in strict sequence.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the agency problem? Explain how moral hazard and adverse selection contribute to it. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    The agency problem is a situation where a firm's managers (agents) fail to act in shareholders' (principals') best interest. Moral hazard contributes because owners bear the capital risk while managers capture disproportionate benefits (salary, prestige) without sharing equally in the downside. Adverse selection contributes because shareholders can never fully verify a manager's true competence and intentions before hiring them, so managers who don't share owners' priorities can still be appointed.
  2. Explain CEO duality and why Hill & Jones consider separating the CEO and chairman roles a governance cornerstone. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    CEO duality is when one person holds both the CEO and board-chairman roles. This weakens oversight because insider directors' career prospects depend on the CEO, making a "rubber-stamp" board more likely, and the CEO can control the board's agenda to limit scrutiny of their own decisions. Separate CEO/chairman roles (chairman being an outside director) preserve independent oversight.
  3. List and briefly explain Hill & Jones' five cornerstones of strong corporate governance. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) A board with a majority of independent outside directors; (2) separate individuals as CEO and chairman; (3) a compensation committee composed entirely of outside directors; (4) an audit committee composed entirely of outside directors; (5) truly independent outside auditors with no conflicting consulting relationship with the firm. Together these limit self-dealing and information manipulation by top management.
  4. What was the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and what governance problems was it designed to address? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Sarbanes-Oxley (2002) is U.S. legislation passed after major accounting scandals (Enron, WorldCom) that requires firms to include more independent directors, disclose internal controls/ethics codes/audit-committee composition, have the CEO and CFO personally certify financial statements, and prohibits firms from extending personal loans to directors/executives — all aimed at reducing self-dealing and restoring investor confidence in financial reporting.
  5. Explain Carroll's CSR Pyramid with an example for each layer. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Economic (be profitable — the foundation, e.g. running a sustainably profitable core business). Legal (obey the law, e.g. complying with environmental regulations). Ethical (do what is right/fair even beyond legal minimums, e.g. paying suppliers fairly even where not legally required). Philanthropic (be a good corporate citizen, e.g. funding community education programs). Carroll stressed these are balanced together, not pursued strictly in sequence.
  6. Summarize the CSR debate between pro-CSR advocates and critics such as Friedman. Where does Porter & Kramer's "Strategic CSR" fit into this debate? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Pro-CSR advocates argue firms owe society more than legal compliance, often invoking the triple bottom line (economic + social + ecological performance). Critics like Friedman argue CSR isn't management's role — firms should behave ethically and maximize shareholder returns within the law, since spending shareholder funds on social causes substitutes managers' judgment for shareholders' own choices. Porter & Kramer's Strategic CSR tries to bridge the debate: rather than treating CSR spending as a cost against shareholder returns, it designs social initiatives that also reinforce competitive advantage, making the trade-off non-zero-sum.
  7. "A firm cannot be socially responsible without first being economically successful." Discuss in relation to Carroll's model. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    This reflects Carroll's core claim that economic responsibility is the foundation of the CSR pyramid — legal, ethical, and philanthropic responsibilities all depend on a firm first generating sustainable profit. However, Carroll also stressed the four layers are balanced simultaneously in practice, not pursued in strict sequence — so profitability is necessary but not sufficient for genuine social responsibility.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define the agency problem. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A situation in which a firm's managers (agents) fail to act in the best interests of the shareholders (principals) who hired them.
  2. What is CEO duality? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    When one person holds both the CEO and board-chairman roles, which can weaken independent board oversight.
  3. What is the triple bottom line? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The idea that firms should maintain and improve social and ecological performance alongside economic (financial) performance, not just profit.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain moral hazard and adverse selection as they relate to the agency problem. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Moral hazard is a situation where the parties in an arrangement do not share equally in risk and benefit — owners risk their capital while managers seek other benefits (salary, prestige) and enjoy only a limited share of the returns. Adverse selection is the inability of shareholders to precisely identify a manager's true competencies and intentions before hiring them, since owners can never be fully certain the professionals running the firm share their priorities. Together these explain why managers can end up not acting in shareholders' best interests.
  2. Explain Carroll's CSR Pyramid with its four layers. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Built bottom-up: Economic (be profitable — the foundation), Legal (obey laws and regulations), Ethical (do what is right and fair, even beyond legal minimums), and Philanthropic (be a good corporate citizen). Carroll's key insight is that economic performance is not opposed to social responsibility — it is its foundation — and the four layers are balanced together in practice, not pursued in strict sequence.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the agency problem and Hill & Jones' five cornerstones of strong corporate governance, including the role of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Agency problem: Modern corporations separate ownership (shareholders) from control (professional managers), creating an agency relationship in which managers act as agents of the owner-principals. The agency problem arises when managers fail to act in shareholders' best interests, rooted in moral hazard (owners bear capital risk while managers capture disproportionate benefits) and adverse selection (owners cannot fully verify a manager's true competence and intent before hiring). Two views exist on its severity: that management serves its own interests (e.g. empire-building to grow salary/prestige), or that management and shareholders largely share the same interests, particularly where pay is tied to performance.

    Five cornerstones (Hill & Jones): (1) a board with a majority of independent outside directors; (2) separate individuals as CEO and chairman, avoiding CEO duality which weakens oversight since insiders' careers depend on the CEO; (3) a compensation committee composed entirely of outside directors, limiting self-dealing in executive pay; (4) an audit committee composed entirely of outside directors, ensuring rigorous independent review of financial statements; (5) truly independent outside auditors with no conflicting consulting relationship.

    Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002): passed after major accounting scandals (Enron, WorldCom), it requires more independent directors, disclosure of internal controls/ethics codes/audit-committee composition, CEO and CFO certification of financial statements, and bans personal loans from firms to their directors/executives — directly reinforcing the five cornerstones through regulation.
  2. Discuss the concept of corporate social responsibility, the CSR debate between pro-CSR advocates and critics, Porter & Kramer's Strategic CSR, and Carroll's CSR Pyramid. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    CSR defined: the obligations a firm has toward the society in which it operates, beyond what is required by law and beyond the pursuit of profit alone.

    The debate: Pro-CSR advocates argue firms owe society more than legal compliance, often invoking the triple bottom line — social and ecological performance alongside economic results. Critics such as Milton Friedman argue CSR is not management's role: firms should behave ethically and maximize shareholder returns within the law, since spending shareholder funds on social causes substitutes managers' judgment for that of individual shareholders and can weaken competitiveness.

    Porter & Kramer's Strategic CSR: proposes CSR and competitive advantage need not trade off against each other, describing a continuum from Responsive CSR (acting as a good corporate citizen, mitigating harm from operations) to Strategic CSR (initiatives whose social and business benefits are both large and distinctive to the firm, reinforcing rather than merely offsetting competitive advantage).

    Carroll's CSR Pyramid: four layers built bottom-up — Economic (profitability, the foundation), Legal (compliance), Ethical (fairness beyond legal minimums), and Philanthropic (good citizenship). Economic responsibility is required before the others become sustainable, but Carroll stressed all four are balanced simultaneously by managers, not pursued in strict sequence. Together, governance and CSR increasingly overlap under the "ESG" (Environmental, Social, Governance) framework, since good governance is itself now seen as part of social responsibility.

Unit I — Assignments

Two assignments: an applied case-analysis task and a mission-statement design task.

Assignment 1: Company Case Analysis

Task: Choose a real company you are familiar with. Apply the six-step case-analysis framework from the Unit I case study to it:

  1. Identify its mission, vision, and objectives — stated or implied.
  2. Map its stakeholders and apply the power/interest matrix to identify key players.
  3. Identify one current strategic issue it faces (formulation or implementation/governance).
  4. Analyze its governance and accountability — board structure, any agency-problem risk.
  5. Evaluate its social responsibility using Carroll's CSR Pyramid.
  6. Recommend a course of action grounded in its mission and key stakeholders' interests.

Format: 800–1,200 words, or equivalent structured slide deck. Cite specific facts about the company (public statements, annual report, news coverage) — generic claims without evidence will be marked down.

Assignment 2: Draft a Mission Statement

Task: Invent a hypothetical company (or use a real one with no public mission statement). Draft a mission statement for it, then justify each sentence against Pearce & David's nine components (Topic 4): customers, products/services, markets, technology, survival/growth/profitability, philosophy, self-concept, public image, employees.

Format: The mission statement itself (3–6 sentences) plus a component-by-component justification (400–600 words). Explicitly note any component you chose to leave out, and why.

Grading Rubric (applies to both assignments)

CriterionWeightWhat it looks for
Concept understanding25%Correct, precise use of Unit I terminology and frameworks (not vague paraphrasing).
Application to the chosen company30%Specific, evidence-based mapping of the framework to real facts — not generic statements that could apply to any firm.
Critical analysis25%Goes beyond describing to evaluating — trade-offs, tensions between stakeholders, honest weaknesses.
Structure & clarity10%Follows the framework's steps in order; clearly organized and easy to follow.
Use of course material10%Explicit references back to the relevant Unit I topics and frameworks used.

Unit I — Quiz

10 questions, one attempt shown at a time. Select an answer for each, then click Submit to see your score and which answers were correct.

1. According to Hill & Jones, strategic management is best defined as:

Correct answer: B. This is Hill & Jones' core definition — analysis, decisions, and actions together, aimed at competitive advantage.

2. In Mintzberg's model, strategy that is planned in advance AND actually implemented as intended is called:

Correct answer: C. Deliberate strategy is intended strategy that gets carried out as planned.

3. Which of Mintzberg's "5 Ps" refers to a specific maneuver intended to outwit a competitor?

Correct answer: B. A Ploy is a maneuver aimed at outwitting a rival, e.g. a threatened price cut to deter entry.

4. Which stakeholder group does Hill & Jones identify as supplying the firm with "risk capital"?

Correct answer: C. Stockholders provide risk capital with no guarantee of being recouped, which is why they're treated as a distinct stakeholder class.

5. In the power/interest matrix, a stakeholder with HIGH power but LOW interest should be:

Correct answer: B. High power/low interest → Keep Satisfied — meet their needs without over-communicating.

6. Abell's three-dimensional framework defines a business according to:

Correct answer: B. Who is satisfied (customer groups), what is satisfied (customer needs), and how (technology/competencies).

7. According to Parnell, which correctly distinguishes a goal from an objective?

Correct answer: B. Parnell: goals = general, unquantified ends; objectives = specific, verifiable versions of a goal.

8. The agency problem arises primarily because:

Correct answer: B. The agency problem is a conflict of interest between managers (agents) and shareholders (principals).

9. In Carroll's CSR Pyramid, which responsibility forms the foundation on which all others rest?

Correct answer: D. Economic responsibility (being profitable) is the foundation the other three layers rest on.

10. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) was passed primarily in response to:

Correct answer: B. Sarbanes-Oxley followed major accounting scandals, requiring more independent directors and financial disclosure.

Case Study — Applying Unit I

Unit I · Topic 7

Note for instructors

The syllabus lists "Case study" without naming a specific case, so this page provides (1) a reusable case-analysis framework and (2) a short worked example applying it, using the Tata Group as an illustration because its mission, governance structure, and CSR activities are well documented and widely taught. Swap in any preferred case (a textbook case from Hill & Jones or Parnell, or a current news case) using the same framework.

Seminar Discussion Agenda (~45–50 min session)

  1. Framing (5 min) — presenter introduces the Tata Group background (section 2.1) and today's guiding question: how do mission, stakeholders, governance, and CSR interact in one real organization?
  2. Walk the framework (15 min) — presenter works through case-analysis steps 1–6 in order (section 1), pausing after each step to check the class agrees with the analysis before moving to the next.
  3. Open discussion — Question 1 (8 min) — stakeholder mapping and the power/interest matrix applied to Tata Sons' ownership structure.
  4. Open discussion — Question 2 (8 min) — how trust-ownership changes the usual shareholder-return vs. CSR trade-off.
  5. Open discussion — Question 3 (8 min) — what the 2016–2017 governance dispute reveals about the limits of a strong mission alone.
  6. Wrap-up (5 min) — class collectively answers Question 4: pick a different company and sketch how steps 1–5 would apply to it.

1. Case Analysis Framework

Use this sequence to analyze any strategic management case, drawing on Topics 1–6:

  1. Identify the mission, vision, and objectives in play — stated or implied. Are they clear, feasible, and aligned with each other?
  2. Map the stakeholders — who are the internal and external stakeholders in this situation? Apply the power/interest matrix to identify the key players.
  3. Identify the strategic issue — what decision, conflict, or problem is the organization facing? Is it a formulation issue (choosing a strategy) or an implementation/governance issue (executing or overseeing one)?
  4. Analyze governance and accountability — who has decision-making authority? Is there an agency problem? Are governance mechanisms (board, shareholders, disclosure) functioning as intended?
  5. Evaluate social responsibility dimensions — using Carroll's pyramid, assess how the organization balances economic, legal, ethical, and philanthropic responsibilities.
  6. Recommend a course of action — grounded in the mission and the interests of the key stakeholders identified in step 2.

2. Worked Example: Tata Group

2.1 Background

The Tata Group is one of India's largest and oldest business conglomerates, operating across steel, automobiles, information technology, hospitality, and consumer products, among other sectors.

2.2 Mission and purpose

The Tata Group has long articulated a purpose that goes beyond profit: to improve the quality of life of the communities it serves, alongside conducting business responsibly and with fairness to all stakeholders. This framing (purpose stated ahead of pure financial ambition) is a useful contrast case to a purely shareholder-value-first mission statement — good discussion material for Topic 4.

2.3 Stakeholder structure

A distinctive feature of the Tata Group is its ownership structure: the majority of shares in Tata Sons (the group's principal holding company) are held by philanthropic trusts (the Tata Trusts), which channel a large share of dividend income into charitable causes such as healthcare, education, and rural development. This directly links the "shareholder" stakeholder category to the "community/CSR" stakeholder category — an unusually direct structural connection between ownership and philanthropy.

2.4 Governance dimension

The group's governance structure — trust-majority ownership of a holding company that in turn holds stakes across many operating companies — has been the subject of public discussion, including a well-publicized 2016–2017 boardroom dispute over the removal of a group chairman, which raised questions about board authority, the role of promoter/trust influence, and minority shareholder rights in operating companies. This is a useful real illustration of the agency and governance concepts in Topic 6: even organizations with a strong stated social purpose still need clear, functioning governance mechanisms to resolve conflicts over control.

2.5 CSR dimension

Group companies run extensive CSR programs (e.g. in health, education, water, and livelihood), and the trust-ownership structure means a meaningful share of group profits is directed toward these programs by design rather than as a discretionary add-on — a strong real-world example of Carroll's philanthropic layer being structurally embedded rather than optional.

3. Discussion / Practice Questions

  1. Using the case-analysis framework above, identify the key stakeholders in the Tata Group's ownership structure and classify them using the power/interest matrix. (Applied)
    Show model answer
    Key stakeholders include the Tata Trusts (majority shareholder — high power, high interest — Key Player), Tata Sons' board and operating-company minority shareholders (high interest, variable power depending on shareholding), employees and communities served by CSR programs (high interest, typically lower formal power — Keep Informed), and regulators/government (high power over compliance, moderate day-to-day interest — Keep Satisfied).
  2. How does linking ownership (via trusts) to philanthropy change the usual tension between shareholder returns and CSR spending? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    In a typical firm, CSR spending competes with shareholder returns for the same profit pool. Because Tata Trusts — a philanthropic entity — are the majority shareholder of Tata Sons, a large share of "shareholder returns" (dividends) are by design routed into CSR/philanthropic causes rather than private wealth, so growing profitability directly grows the philanthropic budget rather than trading off against it.
  3. What does the 2016–2017 governance dispute illustrate about the limits of governance mechanisms, even in an organization with a strong stated mission? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    It illustrates that a strong mission/purpose statement does not by itself guarantee smooth governance — disputes over board authority, promoter/trust influence, and minority shareholder rights can still surface even in organizations widely regarded as ethically-minded. Governance mechanisms (clear board authority, defined removal procedures, minority protections) need to be explicit and tested, not assumed from a firm's reputation.
  4. Choose a company you are familiar with and repeat steps 1–5 of the case-analysis framework for it. (Applied / open-ended)
    Show model answer
    Open-ended — no single correct answer. A strong response works through each step in turn: state the company's mission/vision/objectives, map its key stakeholders by power/interest, name the central strategic issue it faces, assess its governance and accountability structure, and evaluate its social responsibility using Carroll's pyramid.

Unit II — Competitive Advantage

Six topics covering where competitive advantage comes from: the external industry environment, the internal capabilities that build advantage, and how firms sustain (or lose) it.

  1. 1
    External Environment and Porter's Five Forces Model

    Defining an industry, the five competitive forces, and entry barriers.

  2. 2
    Competitive Changes during Industry Evolution

    The industry life cycle — embryonic/introduction, growth, shakeout, maturity, decline — and how competitive forces shift at each stage.

  3. 3
    Globalisation, Industry Structure and National Context

    How globalisation reshapes industry structure, and Porter's Diamond of national competitive advantage.

  4. 4
    Core Competencies and the Building Blocks of Competitive Advantage

    Resources, capabilities, and distinctive competencies; the four generic building blocks — efficiency, quality, innovation, customer responsiveness.

  5. 5
    Low Cost and Differentiation

    The generic business-level strategies and the value creation frontier.

  6. 6
    Distinctive Competencies: Avoiding Failure and Sustaining Competitive Advantage

    Assignments

External Environment and Porter's Five Forces Model

Unit II · Topic 1

1. Overview

Before a firm can decide how to compete, it must understand the structure of the industry it competes in — how intense competition is, and why. Porter's Five Forces model is the standard tool for this: it explains why some industries are consistently more profitable than others, regardless of how well any single firm is managed.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Defining an industry

An industry is a group of companies offering products or services that are close substitutes for each other — that satisfy the same basic customer need (Hill & Jones). Industry boundaries must be defined from the customer's need, not the product itself: Coca-Cola long saw itself as being in the "soda" business rather than the broader "soft drink" business, and was caught off guard by the rise of bottled water and juices.

Related distinctions: a sector is a group of closely related industries (e.g. the "computer sector" spans component, hardware, and software industries); a market segment is a distinct group of customers within an industry with specific demands (e.g. mass-market vs. craft beer). Industry boundaries also shift over time as technology and customer needs evolve — e.g. telecom and computing industries converging as phones became handheld computers.

2.2 Porter's Five Forces

Once an industry's boundaries are defined, Porter's five forces model analyzes the forces shaping competition and profitability within it. The stronger each force, the more it limits established companies' ability to raise prices and earn profits — so a strong force is a threat, a weak force is an opportunity.

Risk of Entry by Potential Competitors
Rivalry Among Established Firms
Bargaining Power of Buyers
Bargaining Power of Suppliers
Threat of Substitutes
  1. Risk of entry by potential competitors — governed by the height of barriers to entry: economies of scale, brand loyalty, absolute cost advantages, customer switching costs, and government regulation. High barriers keep out new entrants even when industry profits are attractive.
  2. Rivalry among established companies — intensity depends on industry competitive structure (e.g. number/size of competitors), demand conditions, and how easily companies can exit (exit barriers).
  3. Bargaining power of buyers — buyers who are large, concentrated, or face low switching costs can force down prices and demand better quality/service, capturing more of an industry's value.
  4. Bargaining power of suppliers — powerful suppliers (few in number, no substitutes for their input, or able to threaten forward integration) can raise input prices and squeeze industry profitability.
  5. Threat of substitutes — products from another industry that meet the same customer need cap the prices a firm can charge (e.g. tea/coffee as substitutes for soft drinks).

A sixth force is sometimes added: complementors — companies whose products increase the value of an industry's own products (e.g. app developers for a smartphone platform). Strong complementors can expand an industry's profit pool; weak or absent complementors can constrain it.

2.3 Barriers to entry, in detail

BarrierHow it deters entry
Economies of scaleUnit costs fall as output rises; a small-scale entrant suffers a cost disadvantage, while large-scale entry requires heavy capital and risks retaliation.
Brand loyaltyBuilt through advertising, patents, R&D-driven innovation, quality, and service — makes it costly for entrants to win customers away.
Absolute cost advantagesEstablished firms may have lower costs from accumulated experience/patents, control over key inputs, or access to cheaper capital — advantages entrants simply cannot match.
Customer switching costsThe one-time cost a customer bears when switching supplier discourages them from trying a new entrant's product.
Government regulationLicensing, safety, or other regulatory requirements can directly restrict entry.

2.4 Limitations of the Five Forces model (Parnell)

Parnell highlights that the model, rooted in the industrial-organization (IO) perspective, has real limits: (1) it assumes a clear, identifiable industry, which is often hard to define in practice; (2) it does not account for firms cooperating through partnerships/alliances; (3) it does not account for large firms actively reshaping industry structure in their favor (e.g. lobbying for regulations that raise entry barriers); (4) it treats industry structure, not firm-specific resources, as the primary driver of profit — a view contested by the resource-based perspective; and (5) firms competing across many countries face multiple, differing industry structures simultaneously, which the basic model does not capture.

3. Key Terms

Industry
A group of companies offering products/services that are close substitutes, serving the same basic customer need.
Sector
A group of closely related industries.
Market segment
A distinct group of customers within a market, differentiated by their specific needs/attributes.
Barriers to entry
Factors that make it costly for new companies to enter an industry.
Complementors
Companies whose products add value to an industry's own products — the "sixth force."

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Industry = group of close substitutes serving the same customer need; define from customer need, not product, to avoid missing threats (Coca-Cola/bottled water example).
  • Five forces: risk of entry, rivalry among incumbents, buyer power, supplier power, threat of substitutes. Strong force = threat; weak force = opportunity.
  • Entry barriers: economies of scale, brand loyalty, absolute cost advantages, switching costs, government regulation.
  • Sixth force (supplementary): complementors.
  • Parnell's critique: the model assumes clear industry boundaries, ignores alliances, ignores firms reshaping structure themselves, over-weights industry vs. firm resources, and doesn't handle multi-country competition well.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain Porter's Five Forces model and how it helps identify opportunities and threats. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    The model analyzes five forces — risk of entry, rivalry among established firms, buyer power, supplier power, and threat of substitutes — that jointly determine how much of an industry's value firms can capture as profit. A strong force limits firms' ability to raise prices (a threat); a weak force allows greater pricing power and profit (an opportunity). Managers use the model to diagnose why an industry is attractive or unattractive and to identify which forces their strategy should try to weaken.
  2. List and explain the five barriers to entry discussed by Hill & Jones. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Economies of scale (cost advantage from large-scale production), brand loyalty (built through advertising, R&D, quality, service), absolute cost advantages (from experience, input control, or cheaper capital), customer switching costs (cost of moving to a new supplier), and government regulation (licensing/safety rules that restrict entry). Each raises the cost of entering an industry, protecting incumbents' profitability.
  3. Why is it important to define an industry from the customer's need rather than the product itself? Illustrate with an example. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    A product-based definition can blind a firm to competitors serving the same underlying need through a different product. Coca-Cola defined itself narrowly as being in the "soda" business rather than the "soft drink" business, and was caught off guard in the 1990s by rising demand for bottled water and fruit drinks — competitors it hadn't been watching because they didn't sell soda.
  4. What is meant by "complementors" as a sixth force, and how do they affect an industry's profit pool? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Complementors are companies whose products increase the value of an industry's own products — e.g. app developers increasing the value of a smartphone platform. Strong, abundant complementors expand the total value (and profit pool) available in an industry; weak or absent complementors constrain it.
  5. Discuss Parnell's critique of the limitations of the Five Forces model. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Parnell argues the model: (1) assumes industries can be clearly defined, which is often difficult; (2) ignores firm partnerships/alliances that don't fit neatly into a "rivals" framework; (3) ignores that large firms can actively reshape industry structure (e.g. lobbying for entry-restricting regulation); (4) reflects the industrial-organization view that industry structure — not firm-specific resources — drives profit, a claim the resource-based view disputes; (5) doesn't easily handle firms facing different industry structures across multiple countries simultaneously.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define "industry" as per Hill & Jones. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A group of companies offering products or services that are close substitutes for each other, satisfying the same basic customer need.
  2. What are complementors? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Companies whose products increase the value of an industry's own products — sometimes called the "sixth force" (e.g. app developers for a smartphone platform).
  3. Name any two barriers to entry. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Any two of: economies of scale, brand loyalty, absolute cost advantages, customer switching costs, government regulation.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. List and briefly explain Porter's five forces. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Risk of entry by potential competitors (governed by barrier height), rivalry among established firms (depends on competitive structure and exit barriers), bargaining power of buyers (large/concentrated buyers force down prices), bargaining power of suppliers (powerful suppliers raise input prices), and threat of substitutes (products from another industry capping prices). A strong force limits firm profitability (a threat); a weak force allows greater profit (an opportunity).
  2. Explain the barriers to entry that protect established firms in an industry. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Economies of scale (unit costs fall as output rises, disadvantaging small-scale entrants), brand loyalty (built through advertising, R&D, quality, service), absolute cost advantages (from experience, input control, or cheaper capital), customer switching costs (the cost a buyer bears moving to a new supplier), and government regulation (licensing/safety rules restricting entry). Each raises the cost of entering, protecting incumbent profitability.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Explain Porter's Five Forces model in detail, including the barriers to entry and the model's limitations as identified by Parnell. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Defining an industry: a group of companies offering close substitutes serving the same basic customer need — defined by customer need, not the product itself, to avoid missing threats (e.g. Coca-Cola narrowly seeing itself as a "soda" business, missing the rise of bottled water).

    The five forces: (1) Risk of entry by potential competitors, governed by barrier height; (2) Rivalry among established firms, depending on competitive structure, demand conditions, and exit barriers; (3) Bargaining power of buyers, who can force down prices if large, concentrated, or facing low switching costs; (4) Bargaining power of suppliers, who can raise prices if few in number or hard to substitute; (5) Threat of substitutes, which caps the prices a firm can charge. A sixth force, complementors, is sometimes added.

    Barriers to entry: economies of scale, brand loyalty, absolute cost advantages, customer switching costs, and government regulation — each raising the cost of entering an industry.

    Limitations (Parnell): the model assumes a clear, identifiable industry, which is often hard to define; it does not account for firms cooperating through alliances; it ignores large firms actively reshaping industry structure (e.g. lobbying for entry-restricting regulation); it treats industry structure, not firm-specific resources, as the primary driver of profit — contested by the resource-based view; and it does not capture firms facing multiple, differing industry structures across countries simultaneously.

Competitive Changes during Industry Evolution

Unit II · Topic 2

1. Overview

The five forces are not static — their strength shifts predictably as an industry ages. The industry life cycle model tracks this evolution through five stages, helping managers anticipate how competitive intensity will change and adjust strategy ahead of time rather than reactively.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The five stages

Embryonic
(Parnell: Introduction)
→
Growth
→
Shakeout
→
Mature
→
Decline

Note the terminology difference: Hill & Jones label the first stage embryonic; Parnell labels the same stage introduction. Both describe the identical early phase of a young, forming industry.

StageCharacteristicsCompetitive forces
Embryonic / IntroductionSlow growth — buyers unfamiliar with the product, high prices (no economies of scale yet), poorly developed distribution. Rivalry centers on educating customers and perfecting product design, not price.Entry barriers based on access to technological know-how; can be high if that know-how is complex.
GrowthFirst-time demand expands rapidly as customers become familiar with the product; prices fall as experience/scale economies are attained.Entry barriers (scale, brand loyalty) not yet built up, so threat of entry is high — but rapid growth absorbs new entrants without intensifying rivalry much.
ShakeoutGrowth slows toward saturation; companies that added capacity at growth-era rates now face excess capacity.Rivalry intensifies sharply; price wars can erupt, driving inefficient firms into bankruptcy.
MatureMarket is saturated; demand is mostly replacement demand. Surviving firms typically have brand loyalty and efficient low-cost operations; industries often consolidate into oligopolies.Entry barriers rise (brand loyalty + efficiency scale), so threat of entry falls; firms may recognize mutual interdependence and avoid price wars.
DeclineDemand falls, often as substitute industries emerge (e.g. typewriters giving way to computers) or as the macro-environment shifts.Growth is hard to sustain; firms typically divest or attempt to "reinvent" around a related product/market.

2.2 Caveats on using the model (Parnell)

  • Not all industries pass through the stages at predictable intervals — e.g. the U.S. railroad industry took over 100 years to reach decline, while the PC industry showed signs of maturity after only 7 years.
  • An industry's stage can vary by country/market (the same industry can be "mature" in one country and "growth" in another).
  • Decline is not always permanent — changes in the macro-environment can revitalize a declining industry (e.g. the bicycle industry's revival driven by health/fitness trends).
  • Hypercompetition: some industries evolve so rapidly that trying to pin down a single life-cycle stage is neither possible nor strategically useful — executives should be cautious about over-relying on the model in such settings.

3. Key Terms

Industry life cycle
A model identifying five sequential stages an industry typically passes through as demand and competitive structure evolve.
Shakeout
The stage where growth slows sharply, excess capacity emerges, and intense rivalry (often price wars) drives weaker competitors out.
Hypercompetition
A condition in which industries evolve so rapidly that traditional life-cycle stages become unreliable guides to strategy.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • 5 stages: Embryonic/Introduction → Growth → Shakeout → Mature → Decline.
  • Terminology note: Hill & Jones = "Embryonic"; Parnell = "Introduction" — same stage, different label.
  • Threat of entry is highest in Growth (low barriers, few incumbents built up yet); rivalry peaks in Shakeout (excess capacity, price wars); Mature industries often consolidate into oligopolies with high entry barriers.
  • Caveats: stages don't occur at fixed intervals, vary by country, decline can be reversed, and hypercompetitive industries may defy the model altogether.

Practice Questions

  1. Describe the five stages of the industry life cycle and how the strength of competitive forces changes at each stage. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Embryonic/Introduction: slow growth, high entry barriers based on technical know-how, rivalry over product design rather than price. Growth: rapid first-time demand, low entry barriers so threat of entry is high, but rivalry stays low because growth absorbs new entrants. Shakeout: growth slows, excess capacity emerges, rivalry intensifies into price wars. Mature: demand saturates, brand loyalty and efficiency become the surviving firms' hallmark, entry barriers rise, industries often consolidate into oligopolies. Decline: demand falls, often due to substitutes; firms divest or reinvent.
  2. Why does the threat of entry tend to be highest during the growth stage, even though rivalry stays relatively low? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Early in growth, few firms have yet built up economies of scale or brand loyalty, so entry barriers are still low — making entry attractive. But because demand itself is expanding rapidly, new entrants can be absorbed and grow their own sales without having to take market share away from existing competitors, so rivalry between firms stays relatively low despite the higher entry threat.
  3. What causes the shakeout stage, and why does it often lead to price wars? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Firms accustomed to rapid growth continue adding capacity at historic rates even as demand growth slows toward saturation, creating excess productive capacity. To use up that capacity, firms cut prices, triggering a price war that drives the least efficient competitors into bankruptcy — which is itself enough to deter new entrants.
  4. What is hypercompetition, and why does it complicate the use of the industry life cycle model? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Hypercompetition describes industries that emerge, develop, and evolve so rapidly that pinning them to a single life-cycle stage is neither possible nor strategically useful, since the "rules" a firm might rely on at a given stage no longer hold long enough to act on. It's a caution against over-relying on the life-cycle model in fast-moving industries.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Name the five stages of the industry life cycle. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Embryonic (Introduction), Growth, Shakeout, Mature, and Decline.
  2. What is the shakeout stage? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The stage where growth slows sharply, excess capacity emerges, and intense rivalry — often price wars — drives weaker competitors out of the industry.
  3. What is hypercompetition? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A condition in which industries evolve so rapidly that pinning them to a single life-cycle stage is neither possible nor strategically useful.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Describe how competitive forces change across the five stages of industry evolution. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Embryonic: high entry barriers from technical know-how, rivalry over product design. Growth: low entry barriers so entry threat is high, but rivalry stays low as expanding demand absorbs new entrants. Shakeout: rivalry intensifies sharply into price wars as growth slows and excess capacity appears. Mature: entry barriers rise (brand loyalty, efficiency), industries often consolidate into oligopolies. Decline: demand falls, often due to substitutes; firms divest or reinvent.
  2. Explain the caveats Parnell raises about applying the industry life cycle model. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Industries don't pass through stages at predictable intervals (railroads took over 100 years to decline; PCs matured in about 7 years); an industry's stage can differ by country; decline is not always permanent (e.g. the bicycle industry's revival via health/fitness trends); and hypercompetitive industries evolve so fast that the model may not offer a reliable single stage to act on.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the industry life cycle model in detail, describing each stage's characteristics and competitive forces, and the caveats to applying it. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    The industry life cycle tracks five sequential stages an industry typically passes through as demand and competitive structure evolve (note: Hill & Jones label the first stage "Embryonic," Parnell labels it "Introduction" — same stage).

    Embryonic/Introduction: slow growth, buyers unfamiliar with the product, high prices (no scale economies yet), poorly developed distribution; rivalry centers on educating customers and product design rather than price; entry barriers depend on access to technological know-how.

    Growth: first-time demand expands rapidly, prices fall as experience/scale economies are attained; entry barriers not yet built up so threat of entry is high, but rapid growth absorbs new entrants without much intensifying rivalry.

    Shakeout: growth slows toward saturation, firms that added capacity at growth-era rates face excess capacity; rivalry intensifies sharply and price wars can erupt, driving inefficient firms into bankruptcy.

    Mature: market saturates, demand becomes mostly replacement demand; surviving firms typically have brand loyalty and efficient operations, industries often consolidate into oligopolies; entry barriers rise so threat of entry falls.

    Decline: demand falls, often as substitute industries emerge or the macro-environment shifts; firms typically divest or attempt to reinvent around a related product/market.

    Caveats: stages don't occur at fixed, predictable intervals and can vary by country/market; decline is not always permanent; and hypercompetitive industries evolve so rapidly that pinning down a single stage is neither possible nor strategically useful, so managers should apply the model with caution rather than mechanically.

Globalisation, Industry Structure and National Context

Unit II · Topic 3

1. Overview

Industry analysis cannot stop at national borders. Globalisation changes industry structure directly — merging previously separate national markets into single global ones, changing the five forces in the process — and, perhaps surprisingly, the world's leading firms in a given industry are still often clustered in just one or two countries. Porter's Diamond explains why.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 How globalisation reshapes industry structure

The globalization of production and markets means firms increasingly source inputs and sell output worldwide rather than within one country. This has direct five-forces consequences: it can lower entry barriers globally (new entrants can attack from any country), intensify rivalry (domestic firms now compete with global players), increase buyer/supplier power (customers and suppliers can source internationally), and reshape which substitutes are relevant. Industries that were once a patchwork of separate national markets — each with its own local competitors — increasingly consolidate into single global industries with a smaller number of global-scale competitors.

2.2 National Competitive Advantage — Porter's Diamond

Despite globalisation, many of the world's most successful companies in a given industry remain clustered in a small number of countries (e.g. biotechnology and computing in the US; consumer electronics in Japan/South Korea; chemicals/engineering in Germany). Michael Porter identified four attributes of a nation's environment that explain this — together forming "the diamond":

AttributeWhat it means
Factor endowmentsA nation's position in factors of production — basic factors (land, labor, capital, raw materials) and advanced factors (technological know-how, managerial sophistication, infrastructure) relevant to the industry.
Local demand conditionsThe nature of home-market demand for the industry's product — sophisticated, demanding home customers push firms to innovate and improve quality ahead of foreign rivals.
Competitiveness of related and supporting industriesWhether internationally competitive supplier and related industries exist domestically, creating efficient input networks and knowledge spillovers.
Intensity of rivalryHow companies are created, organized, and managed domestically, and how intense domestic rivalry is — fierce home rivalry tends to force firms to become fitter global competitors.

Porter argues these four attributes form a mutually reinforcing system — the effect of any one attribute depends on the state of the others — and that firms from a given nation are most likely to succeed internationally in industries/strategic groups where all four are favorable.

Illustration: Nokia and Finland

Finland's harsh geography made wireless telephony cheaper than wired infrastructure (factor endowments/local demand), its market had no telephone monopoly so Nokia faced fierce domestic price competition from the start (intensity of rivalry), and Nordic countries jointly built the world's first international wireless network (related infrastructure) — together explaining how Nokia, from a small country with no obvious tech pedigree, became a global leader in wireless equipment.

3. Key Terms

Globalization of production and markets
The trend of firms sourcing inputs and selling output worldwide, merging previously separate national markets into single global industries.
Porter's Diamond
A framework identifying four national attributes — factor endowments, local demand conditions, related/supporting industries, and intensity of rivalry — that explain why a nation's firms succeed in particular global industries.
Factor endowments
A nation's basic and advanced factors of production relevant to competing in an industry.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Globalisation merges national markets into global ones, directly altering all five forces (lower entry barriers globally, higher rivalry, wider buyer/supplier options).
  • Porter's Diamond: 4 attributes — factor endowments, local demand conditions, related & supporting industries, intensity of rivalry — forming a mutually reinforcing system.
  • Favorable conditions across all four attributes predict where a nation's firms are likely to achieve global competitive advantage in a given industry.
  • Nokia/Finland is the textbook illustration of the diamond in action.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain Porter's Diamond model of national competitive advantage, with its four attributes. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Porter identified four attributes of a nation's environment that shape its firms' global competitiveness in an industry: factor endowments (basic and advanced factors of production), local demand conditions (the sophistication and nature of home-market demand), competitiveness of related and supporting industries (strong domestic supplier/related industries), and intensity of domestic rivalry (fierce home competition toughens firms for global competition). These four form a mutually reinforcing "diamond" — each attribute's effect depends on the state of the others.
  2. Why does intense domestic rivalry tend to help, rather than hurt, a nation's firms in global competition? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Fierce domestic competition forces firms to continuously improve efficiency, quality, and innovation just to survive at home. Firms that emerge from such an environment are better prepared and more competitive when they expand internationally than firms that faced little domestic pressure.
  3. How does globalisation change the strength of the five competitive forces within an industry? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Globalisation typically lowers effective entry barriers (entrants can come from anywhere in the world), intensifies rivalry (domestic firms now face global competitors), and increases buyer and supplier power (both can source internationally rather than being limited to domestic partners). It can also change which products count as substitutes, as global product categories converge. Overall, industries that were once fragmented into separate national markets tend to consolidate into a single global industry structure with fewer, larger-scale competitors.
  4. Using the Nokia/Finland example, illustrate how the four diamond attributes worked together. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Finland's harsh, sparsely populated geography made wireless telecommunications cheaper than wired infrastructure, creating strong local demand for wireless solutions early (local demand conditions/factor endowments). Because Finland had no national telephone monopoly, Nokia faced intense domestic price competition from the start, forcing it to be cost-efficient (intensity of rivalry). Nordic nations jointly built the world's first international wireless network, providing supporting infrastructure and expertise (related and supporting industries). Together, these reinforced each other and produced a globally dominant wireless equipment maker from a small nation with no prior reputation in cutting-edge technology.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Name the four attributes of Porter's Diamond. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Factor endowments, local demand conditions, competitiveness of related and supporting industries, and intensity of domestic rivalry.
  2. What are factor endowments? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A nation's basic factors (land, labor, capital, raw materials) and advanced factors (technological know-how, managerial sophistication, infrastructure) relevant to an industry.
  3. What is the globalization of production and markets? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The trend of firms increasingly sourcing inputs and selling output worldwide rather than within one country, merging previously separate national markets into single global industries.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain how globalisation changes the strength of the five competitive forces within an industry. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Globalisation typically lowers effective entry barriers (entrants can come from anywhere), intensifies rivalry (domestic firms face global competitors), and increases buyer and supplier power (both can source internationally). It also changes which products count as substitutes as global categories converge. Industries once fragmented into separate national markets tend to consolidate into a single global structure with fewer, larger competitors.
  2. Why does intense domestic rivalry tend to help a nation's firms compete globally? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Fierce domestic competition forces firms to continuously improve efficiency, quality, and innovation just to survive at home. Firms that emerge from such an environment are better prepared and more competitive when they expand internationally than firms that faced little domestic pressure — one of Porter's four diamond attributes, and part of why nations with intense home rivalry (e.g. Finland's telecom sector) often produce globally dominant firms.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Explain Porter's Diamond model of national competitive advantage in detail, illustrating with the Nokia/Finland example, and discuss how globalisation reshapes industry structure. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Why national clustering persists: despite globalisation, many world-leading firms in a given industry remain clustered in a small number of countries (biotechnology/computing in the US, consumer electronics in Japan/Korea, chemicals/engineering in Germany). Porter's Diamond explains this through four mutually reinforcing attributes: factor endowments (basic and advanced factors of production relevant to the industry), local demand conditions (sophisticated home customers push firms to innovate ahead of foreign rivals), competitiveness of related and supporting industries (strong domestic supplier networks and knowledge spillovers), and intensity of domestic rivalry (fierce home competition toughens firms for global competition). The effect of any one attribute depends on the state of the others.

    Nokia/Finland illustration: Finland's harsh geography made wireless telephony cheaper than wired infrastructure, creating strong early local demand; the absence of a national telephone monopoly meant Nokia faced fierce domestic price competition from the start; and Nordic countries jointly built the world's first international wireless network, providing supporting infrastructure. Together these explain how Nokia, from a small country with no obvious tech pedigree, became a global leader in wireless equipment.

    Globalisation's effect on industry structure: merging previously separate national markets into single global ones directly alters the five forces — lowering effective entry barriers (entrants can attack from any country), intensifying rivalry (domestic firms now compete with global players), and increasing buyer/supplier power (both can source internationally). Industries that were once fragmented into national markets consolidate into global industries with fewer, larger-scale competitors.

Core Competencies and the Building Blocks of Competitive Advantage

Unit II · Topic 4

1. Overview

Unit II's first three topics analyzed the external environment. This topic turns inward: where does competitive advantage actually come from inside the firm? Hill & Jones ground the answer in distinctive competencies, built from resources and capabilities, which in turn express themselves through four generic "building blocks."

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The roots of competitive advantage

A company has a competitive advantage when its profitability exceeds the industry average, and a sustained competitive advantage when it maintains above-average profitability over a number of years. Competitive advantage is based on distinctive competencies — firm-specific strengths that let a company differentiate its products and/or achieve substantially lower costs than rivals.

2.2 Resources and capabilities

Distinctive competencies arise from two complementary sources:

  • Resources — the assets of a company. Tangible resources are physical (land, buildings, equipment, money); intangible resources are nonphysical (brand names, reputation, accumulated employee know-how, patents/copyrights/trademarks).
  • Capabilities — a company's skills at coordinating resources and putting them to productive use; they reside in an organization's structure, processes, control systems, and culture, not in any one individual.

A resource is more likely to produce a sustainable advantage if it is valuable, rare (competitors don't possess it), and protected by barriers to imitation. A company needs either (1) a valuable, firm-specific resource plus the capability to exploit it, or (2) a firm-specific capability to manage even ordinary resources unusually well (e.g. Nucor's low-cost steelmaking comes from managerial capability, not unique resources — it uses the same plant/equipment as rivals).

2.3 The four generic building blocks of competitive advantage

Superior Efficiency
Superior Quality
Superior Innovation
Superior Customer Responsiveness

↓

Low Cost and/or Differentiation → Competitive Advantage

  • Efficiency — commonly measured via employee productivity (output per employee); higher efficiency lowers a firm's cost structure.
  • Quality — has two dimensions: quality as excellence (design, styling, features, aesthetic appeal — e.g. a Rolex) and quality as reliability (a product consistently does its job without breaking down — e.g. Toyota). High quality both lets a firm charge a premium (excellence) and lowers unit costs (reliability reduces waste/rework — central to Total Quality Management).
  • Innovation — creating new products (product innovation, e.g. the iPod) or new processes (process innovation, e.g. Toyota's lean production system). Innovation is arguably the single most important building block long-run, since a successful innovation gives a firm something unique that rivals lack, at least until imitated.
  • Customer responsiveness — identifying and satisfying customer needs better than rivals, including customizing products to individual/segment demands and minimizing customer response time (e.g. order-to-delivery time). Superior quality and innovation both feed into superior responsiveness.

These four building blocks are not independent alternatives — a firm typically pursues a combination of them to reach the "value creation frontier" (see Topic 5), positioning itself toward either a low-cost or a differentiation advantage.

3. Key Terms

Distinctive competency
A firm-specific strength, built from resources and capabilities, that allows a company to differentiate its products and/or achieve lower costs than rivals.
Resources
A company's tangible and intangible assets.
Capabilities
A company's skills at coordinating resources and putting them to productive use.
Quality as excellence
Superiority in a product's design, features, and aesthetic appeal.
Quality as reliability
A product consistently performing its function without failure.
Customer response time
The time taken to deliver a good or perform a service for a customer.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Competitive advantage = above-average industry profitability; sustained when maintained over years.
  • Distinctive competencies = Resources (tangible/intangible) + Capabilities. Sustainable advantage requires resources/capabilities to be valuable, rare, and hard to imitate.
  • 4 generic building blocks: Efficiency, Quality (excellence + reliability), Innovation, Customer Responsiveness → feed into Low Cost and/or Differentiation.
  • Innovation is often the most important building block long-run, since it creates temporary uniqueness.

Practice Questions

  1. Define distinctive competency and explain how it is built from resources and capabilities. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    A distinctive competency is a firm-specific strength that lets a company differentiate its products and/or achieve lower costs than rivals. It arises from resources (tangible assets like plant/equipment, or intangible assets like brand and know-how) combined with capabilities (the organization's skill at coordinating those resources through its structure, processes, and culture). A firm needs either a valuable resource plus the capability to exploit it, or a superior capability to manage even ordinary resources — as with Nucor's low-cost steelmaking, which comes from managerial capability rather than unique resources.
  2. List and explain the four generic building blocks of competitive advantage. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Efficiency (output per employee — lowers cost structure), Quality (excellence — design/features that raise willingness to pay; reliability — consistent performance that also lowers costs by reducing waste), Innovation (product or process innovation that creates temporary uniqueness), and Customer Responsiveness (identifying and meeting customer needs better/faster than rivals). Together these feed into a low-cost and/or differentiation advantage.
  3. Distinguish between quality as excellence and quality as reliability, with an example of each. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Quality as excellence refers to a product's design, styling, features, and aesthetic appeal (e.g. a Rolex watch). Quality as reliability refers to a product consistently performing its function without breaking down (e.g. Toyota's high reliability ratings). A product can be high on one dimension and low on the other — a Lexus is high on both; a Toyota Corolla is highly reliable but less "excellent" than a Lexus.
  4. Why must a resource be both rare and protected by barriers to imitation to produce a sustainable competitive advantage? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    If a valuable resource is common (not rare), competitors already have it and it cannot differentiate the firm. If it is rare but easy for rivals to copy or acquire, any advantage it creates will quickly be competed away. Only a resource that is both rare and hard to imitate can sustain an advantage over time.
  5. Why is innovation often considered the most important building block of competitive advantage in the long run? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    A successful innovation gives a firm something genuinely unique that competitors lack, at least until they manage to imitate it — creating a window of differentiation or cost advantage no other building block can offer as directly. Because competition can be viewed as a process driven by innovation, firms that consistently innovate stay ahead of imitators, while firms that rely only on efficiency or quality without innovating risk having those advantages copied over time.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define distinctive competency. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A firm-specific strength, built from resources and capabilities, that allows a company to differentiate its products and/or achieve lower costs than rivals.
  2. Distinguish resources from capabilities in one line each. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Resources are a company's tangible and intangible assets; capabilities are its skills at coordinating those resources and putting them to productive use.
  3. Name the four generic building blocks of competitive advantage. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Superior efficiency, superior quality, superior innovation, and superior customer responsiveness.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Distinguish between quality as excellence and quality as reliability, with examples. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Quality as excellence refers to a product's design, styling, features, and aesthetic appeal (e.g. a Rolex watch), letting a firm charge a premium. Quality as reliability refers to a product consistently performing its function without breaking down (e.g. Toyota), which also lowers unit costs by reducing waste and rework — central to Total Quality Management. A product can score high on one dimension and lower on the other.
  2. What conditions must a resource meet to produce a sustainable competitive advantage? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    A resource is more likely to produce a sustainable advantage if it is valuable, rare (competitors don't possess it), and protected by barriers to imitation. A firm needs either a valuable, firm-specific resource plus the capability to exploit it, or a firm-specific capability to manage even ordinary resources unusually well — e.g. Nucor's low-cost steelmaking comes from managerial capability, not unique resources, since it uses the same plant and equipment as rivals.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the roots of competitive advantage — resources and capabilities — and explain the four generic building blocks of competitive advantage in detail. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Roots of advantage: a company has a competitive advantage when its profitability exceeds the industry average, and a sustained advantage when it maintains this over years. Advantage is based on distinctive competencies, arising from two complementary sources: resources (tangible assets like plant/equipment, and intangible assets like brand, reputation, and know-how) and capabilities (skills at coordinating resources, residing in an organization's structure, processes, and culture rather than any one individual). A resource is more likely to sustain advantage if it is valuable, rare, and protected by barriers to imitation.

    Four building blocks: (1) Efficiency — commonly measured via output per employee, which lowers a firm's cost structure; (2) Quality — has two dimensions, excellence (design, features, aesthetics, letting a firm charge a premium) and reliability (consistent performance, which lowers costs by reducing waste); (3) Innovation — creating new products or new processes, arguably the single most important building block long-run since it gives a firm something unique rivals lack, at least until imitated; (4) Customer responsiveness — identifying and satisfying customer needs better/faster than rivals, fed by superior quality and innovation.

    These four building blocks are not independent alternatives — a firm typically pursues a combination to reach the "value creation frontier," positioning itself toward a low-cost and/or differentiation advantage (developed further in Topic 5).
