Managing Growth and ETOP

Unit III · Topic 5

Source note

"Managing growth" draws on themes already grounded in Hill & Jones and Parnell elsewhere in this course (growth-strategy risk, overexpansion failure). ETOP is not covered in either of the two core textbooks — it is a framework from the broader Indian strategic-management curriculum (e.g. Kazmi, listed as a reference text in your syllabus). It's presented here for syllabus completeness, clearly marked as supplementary.

1. Overview

Growth is often treated as an unqualified good, but Topic 1 already showed growth is only worth pursuing if it increases firm value — and Unit II's Topic 6 showed how overexpansion can destroy the very competitive advantage that made growth possible in the first place. This topic pulls those threads together explicitly around "managing" growth, then introduces ETOP as a structured way to scan the environment before committing to a growth path.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The discipline problem in growth

Growth strains an organization in predictable ways: it can outpace the firm's operational and service capacity (JetBlue's 2007 crisis, Topic 1), push a focused competitor into acquisitions that don't fit its original model and destroy its cost/differentiation advantage (People Express, Unit II Topic 6), and create integration problems when growth comes through M&A rather than organically (failed "synergy" cases like AOL–Time Warner, Topic 1). Successfully managing growth means pacing expansion to the organization's actual capacity to absorb it — preserving the strategic fit between competencies, customer groups, and customer needs (Unit II, Topic 5) even as the firm gets larger — rather than treating growth as self-evidently good and dealing with the consequences afterward.

Southwest Airlines' roughly two-decade, deliberately paced national expansion (contrasted with People Express's rapid overreach) is the clearest illustration already covered in this course of growth managed with discipline rather than growth pursued for its own sake.

2.2 ETOP — Environmental Threat and Opportunity Profile (supplementary)

ETOP is a structured technique for summarizing how favorable or unfavorable an organization's environment is before committing to a growth (or any other) strategy. It works by:

  1. Dividing the environment into relevant sectors (e.g. economic, political-legal, social, technological, competitive, supplier, customer).
  2. Identifying specific factors within each sector and classifying each as an opportunity or a threat.
  3. Assigning each factor a qualitative or numerical rating for how favorable/unfavorable it is, and often its probability or impact.
  4. Summarizing the sectors into an overall profile — an at-a-glance picture of how hospitable the environment currently is to the firm's strategy.

ETOP is conceptually a more structured, sector-by-sector cousin of the Opportunities/Threats half of a SWOT analysis (Topic 4) — the same underlying idea (identify O's and T's from the macro-environment and industry) organized into an explicit environmental "profile" rather than a simple list.

3. Key Terms

Managing growth
Pacing expansion to match an organization's actual operational and strategic capacity, to avoid overexpansion failure.
ETOP (Environmental Threat and Opportunity Profile)
A structured, sector-by-sector technique for rating how favorable or unfavorable an organization's environment is to its strategy. Supplementary framework, not covered in Hill & Jones or Parnell.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Growth must be paced to organizational capacity — unmanaged growth risks operational strain (JetBlue), loss of strategic fit (People Express), or failed integration (AOL–Time Warner).
  • Southwest's deliberate ~20-year expansion is the model example of disciplined growth management already covered in this course.
  • ETOP (supplementary, not in Hill & Jones/Parnell): environment divided into sectors → factors rated as opportunities/threats → summarized into an overall environmental profile. Conceptually a structured extension of SWOT's O/T half.

Practice Questions

  1. What does it mean to "manage" growth, and why is unmanaged growth risky? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Managing growth means pacing expansion to the organization's actual capacity to absorb it, preserving the fit between its competencies, customer groups, and customer needs as it scales. Unmanaged growth is risky because it can outpace operational/service capacity (as with JetBlue's 2007 crisis), push a firm into acquisitions that don't fit its original competitive model (People Express), or create integration problems when growth is pursued through M&A without the anticipated synergy materializing (AOL–Time Warner).
  2. Describe the ETOP technique and how it relates to a standard SWOT analysis. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    ETOP (Environmental Threat and Opportunity Profile) divides the environment into sectors (economic, political-legal, social, technological, etc.), identifies specific factors within each as opportunities or threats, rates their favorability, and summarizes them into an overall environmental profile. It is conceptually similar to the Opportunities/Threats half of SWOT analysis, but organizes that analysis more formally by environmental sector rather than as a simple combined list.
  3. Using Southwest Airlines and People Express, contrast disciplined versus undisciplined growth management. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Southwest expanded gradually over roughly two decades, staying disciplined to its cost-leadership model throughout — a textbook case of managed growth. People Express, by contrast, rushed to expand through acquisitions of differentiator airlines that didn't fit its focused cost-leadership model, raising its cost structure and destroying its competitive advantage, ultimately leading to its takeover. The contrast shows that the pace and coherence of growth matter as much as the underlying opportunity for growth itself.

    Show answer
    Environmental Threat and Opportunity Profile.
  2. What does "managing growth" mean? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Pacing expansion to match an organization's actual operational and strategic capacity, to avoid overexpansion failure.
  3. Name one example of a firm that expanded with discipline, as covered in this course. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Southwest Airlines, which expanded gradually over roughly two decades while staying disciplined to its cost-leadership model.

It is conceptually a more structured, sector-by-sector cousin of the Opportunities/Threats half of SWOT analysis.
  2. Why is unmanaged growth risky? Give examples. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Unmanaged growth can outpace a firm's operational and service capacity (JetBlue's 2007 crisis), push a focused competitor into acquisitions that don't fit its original model and destroy its advantage (People Express), or create integration problems when growth comes through M&A without the anticipated synergy materializing (AOL–Time Warner). Managing growth means pacing expansion to preserve strategic fit even as the firm scales.

    Show answer
    The discipline problem: growth is often treated as an unqualified good, but it is only worth pursuing if it increases firm value, and overexpansion can destroy the very competitive advantage that made growth possible. Growth strains an organization predictably: it can outpace operational and service capacity (JetBlue's 2007 crisis), push a focused competitor into acquisitions that don't fit its original model, destroying cost/differentiation advantage (People Express), and create integration problems when growth comes through M&A without anticipated synergy materializing (AOL–Time Warner). Successfully managing growth means pacing expansion to the organization's actual capacity to absorb it, preserving the strategic fit between competencies, customer groups, and customer needs even as the firm gets larger. Southwest Airlines' roughly two-decade, deliberately paced national expansion — contrasted with People Express's rapid overreach — is the clearest illustration of growth managed with discipline.

    ETOP: a structured technique (supplementary to Hill & Jones/Parnell, from the broader Indian strategic-management curriculum) for summarizing how favorable or unfavorable an organization's environment is before committing to a growth strategy. It works by dividing the environment into relevant sectors, identifying specific factors within each sector and classifying each as an opportunity or threat, assigning each factor a qualitative or numerical rating for favorability/impact, and summarizing the sectors into an overall profile — an at-a-glance picture of how hospitable the environment currently is. It is conceptually a more structured, sector-by-sector cousin of the Opportunities/Threats half of a SWOT analysis.

Corporate Portfolio Analysis I: SWOT, GAP Analysis and the BCG Matrix

Unit III · Topic 6

1. Overview

A corporation with multiple business units needs tools that go beyond analyzing one business at a time — tools that help allocate resources sensibly across the whole portfolio. This topic covers the first three: a portfolio-level recap of SWOT, GAP analysis, and the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) growth-share matrix.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 SWOT at the portfolio level

SWOT (Topic 4) is normally run per business unit, but at the corporate level managers also look across units: do units share strengths that could be transferred (an argument for related diversification, Topic 3)? Do some units' weaknesses expose the whole corporation to a common threat? A corporate-level SWOT view feeds directly into decisions about which units to grow, hold, or divest.

2.2 GAP analysis (supplementary — not covered in Hill & Jones or Parnell)

GAP analysis compares where a firm (or business unit) currently is, or is projected to be if it continues on its present course, against where it wants to be (its objectives, from Unit I Topic 5). The difference is the "gap." Management then evaluates strategic alternatives — new products, market expansion, acquisitions, productivity improvements — specifically for their ability to close that gap. It is a simple but useful discipline: it forces objectives and current trajectory to be compared explicitly, rather than assumed to align.

2.3 The BCG Growth-Share Matrix (Parnell)

Developed by the Boston Consulting Group in 1967, this is one of the most widely recognized corporate portfolio frameworks for firms with multiple business units. Each business unit is plotted on two axes — the market's growth rate (vertical) and the unit's relative market share (horizontal) — with a circle sized to the unit's relative size within the corporation.

High Relative Market ShareLow Relative Market Share
High Market GrowthStar — profitable but cash-hungry to sustain growth and fend off rivalsQuestion Mark — needs investment to become a Star, or risks being divested
Low Market GrowthCash Cow — highly profitable, low investment needed, funds other unitsDog — marginal, often liquidated or divested
  • Star — large share (generally 10%+) of a high-growth market. Usually very profitable but needs considerable cash to sustain growth and fend off competitors attracted to the fast-growing market.
  • Question mark — small share of a fast-growing market, often a new entrant. If it can grow into a leader it becomes a Star; if not, it's typically divested or liquidated.
  • Cash cow — large share (generally 10%+) of a slow-growth market. Highly profitable, doesn't need heavy promotional spending since it's well established; its surplus cash funds Stars and Question Marks elsewhere in the portfolio.
  • Dog — small share of a slow-growth (or declining) market. Marginal — small profits or losses — and often liquidated.

A well-balanced corporate portfolio should have mostly Stars and Cash Cows, using Cash Cow surplus to fund promising Question Marks into Stars, while divesting persistent Dogs — directly informing the "combination strategy" idea from Topic 1 (grow some units, hold others, retrench others).

Limitations: the model heavily emphasizes market-share leadership as the route to profitability, which does not hold in every industry; and how a business unit is classified can shift markedly depending on how its market/industry is defined.

3. Key Terms

GAP analysis
Comparing a firm's current/projected trajectory against its objectives to identify the "gap" strategy must close. (Supplementary)
BCG Growth-Share Matrix
A portfolio framework plotting business units by market growth rate and relative market share, classifying each as Star, Question Mark, Cash Cow, or Dog.
Star
High market share in a high-growth market — profitable but cash-hungry.
Cash cow
High market share in a low-growth market — highly profitable, funds the rest of the portfolio.
Question mark
Low market share in a high-growth market — needs investment or divestment.
Dog
Low market share in a low-growth market — usually divested.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Portfolio-level SWOT informs which units to grow/hold/divest.
  • GAP analysis (supplementary): current/projected trajectory vs. objectives → the "gap" that strategy must close.
  • BCG Matrix: Market Growth Rate × Relative Market Share → Star / Question Mark / Cash Cow / Dog.
  • Ideal portfolio: mostly Stars and Cash Cows; Cash Cow surplus funds Question Marks into Stars; Dogs typically divested.
  • BCG limitations: overweights market-share leadership as the route to profit; classification is sensitive to how the market is defined.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain the four quadrants of the BCG growth-share matrix and the investment logic for each. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Star (high share/high growth) — profitable but needs heavy cash investment to sustain growth and fend off rivals. Question Mark (low share/high growth) — needs investment to become a Star, or risks divestment/liquidation. Cash Cow (high share/low growth) — highly profitable and low-investment, generating surplus cash to fund Stars and Question Marks. Dog (low share/low growth) — marginal, usually liquidated or divested. A balanced portfolio uses Cash Cow surplus to grow promising Question Marks into Stars while shedding persistent Dogs.
  2. What are the main limitations of the BCG matrix? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    It heavily emphasizes market-share leadership as the path to profitability, which does not hold true in every industry. It also assumes a clearly definable market/industry — a unit's classification (e.g. Star vs. Cash Cow) can change markedly depending on how broadly or narrowly its market is defined.
  3. Explain GAP analysis and how it differs from (or complements) the BCG matrix. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    GAP analysis compares a firm's current or projected trajectory against its stated objectives, identifying the gap that strategy must close. It is more general and objective-driven than the BCG matrix, which specifically classifies business units by market growth and relative share to guide portfolio investment decisions. The two can complement each other: GAP analysis identifies that a gap exists and needs closing; the BCG matrix helps decide which business units are best positioned to help close it.
  4. How does the BCG matrix support a "combination strategy" across a diversified corporation's business units? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    The BCG matrix classifies each business unit by its cash-generation and cash-need profile, directly suggesting a different grand strategy for each: grow/invest in Question Marks with potential, maintain and harvest Cash Cows, invest further in Stars, and retrench (divest or liquidate) Dogs. This is exactly the logic of a combination strategy — applying growth, stability, and retrenchment simultaneously across different units of the same corporation, based on each unit's portfolio position rather than a single uniform corporate posture.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. What is GAP analysis? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Comparing where a firm currently is, or is projected to be on its present course, against where it wants to be (its objectives) — the difference is the "gap" strategy must close.
  2. What is a "Cash Cow" in the BCG matrix? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A business unit with high relative market share in a low-growth market — highly profitable, needs little investment, and funds other units in the portfolio.
  3. What two axes define the BCG growth-share matrix? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Market growth rate (vertical axis) and the business unit's relative market share (horizontal axis).

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain the four quadrants of the BCG growth-share matrix and the investment logic for each. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Star (high share/high growth) — profitable but needs heavy cash to sustain growth. Question Mark (low share/high growth) — needs investment to become a Star, or risks divestment. Cash Cow (high share/low growth) — highly profitable, low investment, funds Stars and Question Marks. Dog (low share/low growth) — marginal, usually liquidated or divested. A balanced portfolio uses Cash Cow surplus to grow promising Question Marks while shedding persistent Dogs.
  2. What are the main limitations of the BCG matrix? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    It heavily emphasizes market-share leadership as the path to profitability, which does not hold in every industry. It also assumes a clearly definable market/industry — a unit's classification (Star vs. Cash Cow, etc.) can change markedly depending on how broadly or narrowly its market is defined, making the tool sensitive to a subjective boundary decision.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss portfolio-level SWOT, GAP analysis, and the BCG growth-share matrix as tools for allocating resources across a diversified corporation's business units. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Portfolio-level SWOT: run per business unit at the operational level, but at the corporate level managers also look across units — whether units share strengths that could be transferred (an argument for related diversification), or whether some units' weaknesses expose the whole corporation to a common threat — feeding directly into decisions on which units to grow, hold, or divest.

    GAP analysis (supplementary): compares where a firm currently is, or is projected to be on its present course, against its stated objectives; the difference is the "gap." Management then evaluates alternatives — new products, market expansion, acquisitions, productivity improvements — for their ability to close that gap, forcing objectives and trajectory to be compared explicitly rather than assumed aligned.

    BCG Growth-Share Matrix: developed by Boston Consulting Group in 1967, plots each business unit on market growth rate (vertical) and relative market share (horizontal), sized by relative importance to the corporation. Star (high share/high growth) is profitable but cash-hungry; Question Mark (low share/high growth) needs investment or divestment; Cash Cow (high share/low growth) is highly profitable and funds the rest of the portfolio; Dog (low share/low growth) is marginal and usually divested. A well-balanced portfolio has mostly Stars and Cash Cows, using Cash Cow surplus to fund promising Question Marks into Stars while divesting persistent Dogs — directly informing the combination-strategy idea (Topic 1). Limitations: it overweights market-share leadership as the route to profitability, and unit classification is sensitive to how the market/industry is defined.

Corporate Portfolio Analysis II: McKinsey's 7S, GE 9-Cell, Selection of Matrix and Balanced Scorecard

Unit III · Topic 7

Source note

McKinsey's 7S Framework and the GE 9-Cell Model are not covered in Hill & Jones or Parnell — like ETOP (Topic 5), they belong to the broader Indian strategic-management curriculum (e.g. Kazmi). They're explained accurately below for syllabus completeness, clearly marked as supplementary. "Selection of Matrix" and the Balanced Scorecard, by contrast, are grounded in the assigned texts (Parnell's SLSC matrix; both books' Balanced Scorecard, already covered in Unit I Topic 5).

1. Overview

This topic completes the corporate-portfolio toolkit: two more portfolio/organizational-fit frameworks (McKinsey's 7S, the GE 9-cell), a recap of distinctive competitiveness, the book-grounded question of how to choose among competing matrices, and the Balanced Scorecard as the tool that ties portfolio strategy back to measurable performance.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 McKinsey's 7S Framework (supplementary)

Developed by McKinsey & Company consultants, the 7S framework argues that successful strategy execution requires seven organizational elements to be aligned, not just a good strategy on paper:

ElementWhat it covers
StrategyThe plan for building competitive advantage
StructureHow the organization is divided and coordinated
SystemsDaily processes and procedures (IT, budgeting, control systems)
StaffThe people and how they are developed/motivated
SkillsThe organization's actual capabilities/competencies
StyleLeadership and management culture
Shared valuesThe core beliefs/culture at the center, connecting the other six

"Strategy" and "Structure" are considered "hard" elements (easier to define/change); "Staff," "Skills," "Style," and "Shared Values" are "soft" elements (harder to change but often decisive for successful implementation).

2.2 GE 9-Cell (Business Screen) Model (supplementary)

Developed by General Electric with McKinsey, this extends the BCG matrix's 2×2 logic into a more nuanced 3×3 grid, plotting each business unit on industry attractiveness (high/medium/low — considering factors like market size, growth rate, and competitive intensity, not just growth rate alone) against competitive/business strength (high/medium/low — considering market share, brand, profitability, and more, not just relative share alone). The resulting nine cells group into three broad zones: invest/grow (high attractiveness/strength), selectively invest/hold (medium combinations), and harvest/divest (low attractiveness/strength) — a richer, multi-factor alternative to BCG's single-dimension-per-axis simplicity.

2.3 Distinctive competitiveness — recap

Recall from Unit II (Topic 4) that distinctive competencies come from resources and capabilities, and produce advantage through the four building blocks. At the portfolio level, the question becomes: which business units' competencies are genuinely distinctive (valuable, rare, hard to imitate) versus merely adequate? Portfolio tools like BCG and GE 9-cell should be read alongside this — a "Star" or "invest" cell unit is a much safer growth bet if its position also rests on a genuinely distinctive (not easily copied) competency.

2.4 Selection of matrix — the SLSC matrix (Parnell)

With several matrices available (SW/OT, BCG, GE 9-cell, and more), how should a firm choose among the strategic alternatives they generate? Parnell's own answer is the Strategy Level–Strategy Complexity (SLSC) matrix: alternatives are plotted by (a) strategy level — corporate, business, or functional — and (b) strategy complexity — how difficult the alternative will be to execute. The more complex and higher-level a strategy is, the harder implementation tends to be, so the SLSC matrix warns against trying to implement multiple high-level, high-complexity strategies at once. It's a practical selection filter applied after the SW/OT matrix has generated a list of candidate alternatives.

2.5 Balanced Scorecard — recap

Recall from Unit I (Topic 5) that Kaplan & Norton's Balanced Scorecard tracks strategic objectives and measures across four perspectives — Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, and Learning & Growth. At the portfolio/corporate-strategy level, it plays a distinct role from BCG/GE 9-cell: those matrices help decide where to allocate resources across the portfolio, while the Balanced Scorecard tracks whether the resulting strategy is actually working once implemented — connecting Unit III's strategy-selection tools back to Unit I's objective-setting.

3. Key Terms

McKinsey's 7S Framework
A model of 7 aligned organizational elements (Strategy, Structure, Systems, Staff, Skills, Style, Shared Values) needed for successful strategy execution. (Supplementary)
GE 9-Cell Model
A 3×3 portfolio matrix plotting business units on industry attractiveness and competitive/business strength. (Supplementary)
SLSC matrix
Parnell's tool for evaluating strategic alternatives by strategy level (corporate/business/functional) and strategy complexity.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • McKinsey's 7S (supplementary): Strategy, Structure, Systems (hard) + Staff, Skills, Style, Shared Values (soft) — all must align for execution to succeed.
  • GE 9-Cell (supplementary): Industry Attractiveness × Competitive Strength (3×3) → Invest/Grow, Selective Hold, Harvest/Divest — a richer alternative to BCG's 2×2.
  • Distinctive competitiveness recap: a portfolio position is only as safe as the competency it rests on being genuinely hard to imitate.
  • Selection of matrix (Parnell): SLSC matrix — Strategy Level × Strategy Complexity — filters SW/OT-generated alternatives for what's actually executable.
  • Balanced Scorecard recap: tracks whether the chosen strategy is working (4 perspectives), distinct from BCG/GE 9-cell which decide where to invest.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain McKinsey's 7S Framework and the distinction between its "hard" and "soft" elements. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    The 7S framework argues successful strategy execution requires seven aligned elements: Strategy, Structure, Systems, Staff, Skills, Style, and Shared Values. Strategy and Structure are "hard" elements — relatively easy to define and change on paper. Staff, Skills, Style, and Shared Values are "soft" elements — harder to change but often decisive for whether execution actually succeeds, since a good strategy on paper fails if the people, culture, and capabilities aren't aligned with it.
  2. How does the GE 9-cell model improve on the BCG matrix? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    BCG plots units on just two single-factor axes: market growth rate and relative market share. GE 9-cell replaces each axis with a multi-factor composite — industry attractiveness (market size, growth, competitive intensity, and more) and competitive/business strength (market share, brand, profitability, and more) — each rated high/medium/low, producing a richer 3x3 grid rather than BCG's simpler 2x2. This captures more nuance than relying on a single metric per axis.
  3. Explain the SLSC matrix and how it is used after the SW/OT matrix in the strategy formulation process. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    The SW/OT matrix (Topic 4) generates a list of candidate strategic alternatives by combining strengths/weaknesses with opportunities/threats. The SLSC (Strategy Level-Strategy Complexity) matrix is then used to evaluate those alternatives by plotting each on its organizational level (corporate, business, or functional) and its complexity of execution. Since higher-level, more complex strategies are harder to implement, the SLSC matrix warns against attempting multiple high-level, high-complexity strategies simultaneously, helping managers select which generated alternatives are actually executable.
  4. How does the Balanced Scorecard's role differ from that of the BCG matrix or GE 9-cell model in corporate strategy? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The BCG matrix and GE 9-cell model help decide where to allocate resources across a portfolio of business units before or during strategy formulation. The Balanced Scorecard operates after a strategy is chosen and implemented, tracking whether it is actually working across financial, customer, internal process, and learning/growth perspectives — connecting resource-allocation decisions back to measurable performance.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Name the seven elements of McKinsey's 7S Framework. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Strategy, Structure, Systems, Staff, Skills, Style, and Shared Values.
  2. What two axes define the GE 9-cell model? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Industry attractiveness and competitive/business strength, each rated high/medium/low.
  3. What does the SLSC matrix stand for? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Strategy Level–Strategy Complexity matrix, Parnell's tool for evaluating strategic alternatives by organizational level and execution difficulty.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Distinguish the "hard" and "soft" elements of the 7S Framework. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Strategy and Structure are "hard" elements — relatively easy to define and change on paper. Staff, Skills, Style, and Shared Values are "soft" elements — harder to change but often decisive for whether execution actually succeeds, since a good strategy fails if the people, culture, and capabilities aren't aligned with it.
  2. How does the GE 9-cell model improve on the BCG matrix? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    BCG plots units on two single-factor axes — market growth rate and relative market share. The GE 9-cell replaces each with a multi-factor composite — industry attractiveness (market size, growth, competitive intensity) and competitive/business strength (market share, brand, profitability) — each rated high/medium/low, producing a richer 3×3 grid than BCG's simpler 2×2, capturing more nuance than a single metric per axis.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss McKinsey's 7S Framework, the GE 9-cell model, the SLSC matrix for selecting among strategic alternatives, and the role of the Balanced Scorecard in corporate strategy. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    McKinsey's 7S (supplementary): argues successful strategy execution requires seven aligned organizational elements — Strategy and Structure ("hard," easier to change) plus Systems, Staff, Skills, Style, and Shared Values ("soft," harder to change but often decisive for implementation success).

    GE 9-Cell (supplementary): extends the BCG matrix's 2×2 logic into a 3×3 grid, plotting business units on industry attractiveness (market size, growth, competitive intensity) against competitive/business strength (market share, brand, profitability), grouping into invest/grow, selectively invest/hold, and harvest/divest zones — a richer, multi-factor alternative to BCG.

    SLSC matrix (Parnell): used after the SW/OT matrix has generated candidate alternatives, plotting each by strategy level (corporate, business, or functional) and strategy complexity (difficulty of execution). Since higher-level, more complex strategies are harder to implement, it warns against attempting multiple high-level, high-complexity strategies simultaneously.

    Balanced Scorecard: tracks strategic objectives across Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, and Learning & Growth perspectives. At the portfolio level it plays a distinct role from BCG/GE 9-cell — those matrices decide where to allocate resources, while the Balanced Scorecard tracks whether the resulting strategy is actually working once implemented, connecting strategy-selection tools back to objective-setting.

Unit III — Assignments

Two assignments: a merger/acquisition case analysis, and a corporate portfolio exercise.

Assignment 1: Merger or Acquisition Case Analysis

Task: Choose a real merger or acquisition you are familiar with (or can research). Apply the five-step case-analysis framework from the Unit III case study to it:

  1. Identify the grand strategy behind the deal — growth, stability, retrenchment, or a combination.
  2. Classify the external growth move — horizontal integration, related/unrelated diversification, vertical integration, or alliance — and its stated rationale.
  3. Assess where the combined business(es) would sit on a BCG matrix.
  4. Check for strategic fit between the merging firms' competencies, customer groups, and generic strategies.
  5. Evaluate whether the deal's outcomes matched its original objectives.

Format: 900–1,300 words, or equivalent structured slide deck. Use publicly available facts and figures (news coverage, annual reports) to support your analysis.

Assignment 2: Corporate Portfolio Exercise

Task: Choose a diversified company with at least three distinct business units. Plot each unit on a BCG growth-share matrix (Topic 6), justifying its quadrant placement with real or reasonably estimated market-growth and market-share data. Then recommend a grand strategy (Topic 1) for each unit based on its quadrant.

Format: A labeled BCG matrix diagram plus 400–600 words of justification and recommendations.

Grading Rubric (applies to both assignments)

CriterionWeightWhat it looks for
Concept understanding25%Correct, precise use of Unit III terminology and frameworks.
Application to the chosen case30%Specific, evidence-based analysis grounded in real facts about the companies involved.
Critical analysis25%Evaluates strategic fit and outcomes, not just describes the deal/portfolio.
Structure & clarity10%Follows the framework's steps in order; clearly organized.
Use of course material10%Explicit references back to the relevant Unit III topics and frameworks used.

Unit III — Quiz

10 questions. Select an answer for each, then click Submit to see your score and which answers were correct.

1. Which of the following is NOT one of Parnell's three basic corporate-level alternatives?

Correct answer: D. Diversification is a sub-type of external growth, not one of the three top-level alternatives (growth, stability, retrenchment).

2. Which retrenchment strategy is described as the "strategy of last resort"?

Correct answer: C. Liquidation terminates the business entirely and should only be pursued when other options aren't viable.

3. A global strategy pursued under HIGH cost pressure and LOW local-responsiveness pressure is:

Correct answer: B. Global standardization fits high cost pressure/low local-responsiveness pressure — a standardized product from a few low-cost locations.

4. Acquiring one's own suppliers is called:

Correct answer: B. Backward integration expands "upstream" by acquiring suppliers.

5. Conglomerate (unrelated) diversification is primarily driven by:

Correct answer: B. Unrelated diversification is primarily a financially-driven move, unlike related diversification's strategic synergy rationale.

6. Which is a disadvantage of strategic alliances compared to mergers/acquisitions?

Correct answer: B. Alliances risk moral hazard — one partner may withhold its best resources while still sharing in the benefits.

7. ETOP stands for:

Correct answer: A. ETOP = Environmental Threat and Opportunity Profile, a sector-by-sector environmental scanning technique.

8. In the BCG matrix, a business unit with LOW market share in a HIGH-growth market is a:

Correct answer: C. Low share/high growth = Question Mark — needs investment to become a Star, or risks divestment.

9. Which tool does Parnell use to generate strategic alternatives by combining strengths/weaknesses with opportunities/threats?

Correct answer: B. The SW/OT matrix generates alternatives from strength/weakness × opportunity/threat combinations.

10. Which of McKinsey's 7S elements is considered central, connecting all the others?

Correct answer: C. Shared Values sits at the center of the 7S framework, connecting the other six elements.

Case Study — Applying Unit III

Unit III · Topic 8

Note for instructors

As in Units I and II, the syllabus lists "Case study" without naming one. This page gives (1) a case-analysis framework for corporate-level strategy and (2) a worked example using the 2004 Kmart–Sears merger (Parnell, Ch. 6), since it directly illustrates grand strategy, horizontal integration/diversification, and the limits of anticipated synergy. Swap in any preferred case using the same framework.

Seminar Discussion Agenda (~45–50 min session)

  1. Framing (5 min) — presenter sets up the Kmart/Sears background (section 2.1) and today's guiding question: why does a deal that looks sound on a portfolio matrix still fail?
  2. Walk the framework (15 min) — presenter works through case-analysis steps 1–5 in order (section 1), pausing after each step for class agreement.
  3. Open discussion — Question 1 (8 min) — classify the merger using the grand-strategy/external-growth vocabulary.
  4. Open discussion — Question 2 (10 min) — why combining two struggling firms often fails to fix either firm's underlying problem.
  5. Open discussion — Question 3 (7 min) — what evidence in the case shows the anticipated synergy never materialized.
  6. Wrap-up (5 min) — class collectively picks a familiar merger/acquisition and sketches steps 1–5 for it.

1. Case Analysis Framework

  1. Identify the current grand strategy for each business unit or the corporation as a whole — growth, stability, or retrenchment (or a combination).
  2. Classify any external growth moves — horizontal integration, related/unrelated diversification, vertical integration, or strategic alliance — and identify the stated rationale (strategic synergy vs. financial).
  3. Run a portfolio-level assessment — where would each business unit sit on a BCG matrix (or GE 9-cell), and does the overall portfolio look balanced?
  4. Check for strategic fit — do the combined units' competencies, customer groups, and generic strategies actually reinforce each other, or is there a mismatch (Unit II, Topic 5–6)?
  5. Evaluate outcomes against objectives — did the anticipated synergy/value materialize? Use the Balanced Scorecard's four perspectives if performance data allows.

2. Worked Example: The Kmart–Sears Merger

2.1 Background

In November 2004, Kmart acquired Sears in an $11.5 billion deal, forming Sears Holding Corporation — placing the combined firm third in U.S. retailing behind Walmart and Home Depot. Both were century-old retailers that had each struggled for the preceding decade.

2.2 Grand strategy and classification

This was an external growth move via acquisition, combining two firms in the same line of business (general merchandise retailing) — best classified as horizontal integration, with elements of horizontal (related) diversification given each retailer's differing store-brand portfolio (Sears: Craftsman, DieHard, Kenmore, Lands' End; Kmart: Martha Stewart, Jaclyn Smith, Joe Boxer). Management's stated rationale was strategic — combined efficiencies and cross-selling each other's strong brands through the other's stores.

2.3 Strategic fit and outcome

Pre-merger, Sears was viewed as the stronger brand but was less profitable (a $61 million loss over nine months of 2004) than Kmart (an $801 million profit over the same period, following its own earlier turnaround) — itself a sign the two firms were in quite different competitive positions going in. Following the merger, both chains saw sales decline every year from 2005–2011, roughly 1,200 store closures were announced by 2012, and analysts pointed to under-investment in store maintenance (Sears spent under $2/sq ft annually vs. an industry norm of $6–8) as a symptom of the strain. The anticipated synergy from combining the two brand portfolios failed to materialize in a way that reversed either chain's decline.

2.4 Diagnosis using the framework

Using the framework above: the grand strategy was growth via horizontal integration/diversification: on paper, a reasonable portfolio move (in BCG terms, attempting to combine two struggling "question mark" or "dog"-trending units hoping scale would create a stronger competitor). But strategic fit was weak — the retailers had different target customer positioning (Sears skewing more premium, Kmart more discount), and integration didn't resolve the underlying competitive threat from Walmart and Home Depot's core cost/scale advantages. The case illustrates Parnell's general warning (Topic 1) that anticipated M&A synergy frequently fails to materialize, especially when the underlying competitive problem the merger was meant to solve isn't actually addressed by combining two weakened firms.

3. Discussion / Practice Questions

  1. Classify the Kmart–Sears merger using the grand-strategy and external-growth vocabulary from Topics 1 and 3. (Applied)
    Show model answer
    It was an external growth strategy via acquisition, primarily horizontal integration (both firms in the same general-merchandise retail industry), with elements of horizontal (related) diversification given their differing store-brand portfolios. The stated rationale was strategic (combined efficiencies and cross-brand selling) rather than purely financial.
  2. Why might combining two struggling retailers fail to produce a stronger combined competitor, even if their brand portfolios are complementary? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Combining two weakened firms does not, by itself, fix the underlying competitive disadvantage each faced independently — in this case, both Sears and Kmart were losing ground to Walmart's and Home Depot's cost/scale advantages before the merger. Complementary brands can create cross-selling opportunities on paper, but if the combined firm still lacks a coherent, reinforcing generic strategy (Unit II, Topic 5) and the resources to invest in stores and operations, the merger mainly combines two problems rather than solving either.
  3. What evidence in the case suggests the anticipated synergy did not materialize? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Sales declined every year from 2005 to 2011 at both retail brands, roughly 1,200 stores were slated for closure by 2012, and store-maintenance spending fell well below the industry norm — all signs that the combined firm was retrenching rather than realizing the growth/efficiency synergy that was the original strategic rationale for the deal.
  4. Choose a merger or acquisition you are familiar with and repeat steps 1–5 of the case-analysis framework for it. (Applied / open-ended)
    Show model answer
    Open-ended — no single correct answer. A strong response identifies the grand strategy involved, classifies the type of external growth and its stated rationale, positions the combined business(es) on a portfolio matrix, checks whether competencies/customer groups/generic strategies actually reinforce each other post-combination, and evaluates whether the deal's original objectives were actually achieved.

The Implementation Process and Resource Allocation

Unit IV · Topic 1

1. Overview

Units I–III covered how a strategy is chosen. Unit IV turns to implementation — the process of translating a chosen strategy into organizational structure, systems, resource commitments, and day-to-day action. A brilliant strategy poorly implemented delivers no advantage; this unit is about the machinery that turns intent into results.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Structure follows strategy (Chandler)

Alfred Chandler's foundational study of large U.S. corporations (DuPont, GM) in the early 20th century established two enduring principles: (1) organizational structure follows the range and variety of tasks an organization chooses to pursue, and (2) a company's structure changes as its strategy changes, in a predictable way over time. This is the starting premise of the whole implementation process — structure, systems, and resource allocation are not independent choices; they are chosen to fit whatever strategy has already been decided.

2.2 The implementation process, in outline

Putting a strategy into action generally requires managers to work through several interlocking decisions, each covered in more depth in the topics that follow this one:

  1. Design an organizational structure that groups people/tasks appropriately (Topic 2).
  2. Design control systems to monitor whether the strategy is working (Topic 3).
  3. Match structure and control specifically to the chosen strategy (Topic 4) — since different strategies require different implementation choices.
  4. Manage the transition — implementing strategic change itself is a distinct challenge (Topic 5), often complicated by organizational politics (Topic 6).
  5. Evaluate results and feed them back into the next planning cycle (Topic 7).

2.3 Resource allocation

A central, recurring mechanism for implementation is the operating budget — a blueprint stating how managers intend to use organizational resources to achieve their goals (Hill & Jones). Typically, managers at one level allocate a specific amount of resources to managers at the level below, who then decide how to divide that budget across activities (e.g. R&D, engineering, sales) to best support the strategy. Large firms commonly treat each division as a stand-alone profit center, evaluating it by its contribution to corporate profitability. Resource allocation is therefore not a one-time event but an ongoing control mechanism — how a corporation allocates capital across its business units (via budgets, and via the portfolio-analysis tools from Unit III such as the BCG matrix) directly shapes how well strategy gets executed.

Because resource allocation and control are so tightly linked, the boundary between "implementing" a strategy and "controlling" it is blurry by design — budgets are simultaneously a resource-allocation tool and a behavior-control tool (see Topic 3).

3. Key Terms

Implementation
The process of translating a chosen strategy into organizational structure, systems, resource commitments, and action.
Structure follows strategy
Chandler's principle that organizational structure is (and should be) shaped by the strategy an organization pursues, changing predictably as strategy changes.
Operating budget
A blueprint stating how managers intend to allocate organizational resources to achieve their goals.
Profit center
A well-defined organizational unit (often a division) headed by a manager accountable for its own revenues and expenditures.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Chandler: structure follows strategy — structure is chosen/changed to fit the firm's chosen tasks and strategy, not the reverse.
  • Implementation process (this unit's roadmap): design structure → design control systems → match both to strategy → manage change & politics → evaluate results.
  • Resource allocation mainly happens through operating budgets, cascading from higher to lower levels of management.
  • Divisions are often treated as profit centers, evaluated on their contribution to corporate profitability.
  • Budgets are dual-purpose: they allocate resources AND function as a behavior-control mechanism (Topic 3).

Practice Questions

  1. Explain Chandler's "structure follows strategy" principle and its significance for implementation. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Chandler found, from studying large U.S. corporations like DuPont and GM, that organizational structure follows the range and variety of tasks a firm chooses to pursue, and that structure changes predictably as strategy changes. Its significance is that implementation choices (structure, systems, resource allocation) should not be made independently of strategy — they must be designed specifically to fit whatever strategy has already been chosen, or the strategy will be poorly executed regardless of how sound it is.
  2. Describe how operating budgets function as a resource-allocation mechanism. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    An operating budget is a blueprint for how managers intend to use organizational resources to achieve their goals. Typically, higher-level managers allocate a specific amount of resources to managers at the level below, who then decide how to divide that budget across activities such as R&D, engineering, and sales to best support the strategy. Many firms treat each division as a stand-alone profit center, evaluating managers on their division's contribution to corporate profitability, which ties resource allocation directly to performance accountability.
  3. Why is the line between "resource allocation" and "control" blurry in practice? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Because the same mechanism — the operating budget — serves both purposes at once: it allocates resources to managers to carry out the strategy, and it simultaneously constrains and standardizes their behavior (a form of behavior control, covered in Topic 3) by defining what they are and are not authorized to spend. Managers are then evaluated on their ability to stay within budget and use it effectively, which is itself a control function.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. State Chandler's "structure follows strategy" principle. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Organizational structure follows the range and variety of tasks an organization chooses to pursue, and changes predictably as its strategy changes.
  2. What is an operating budget? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A blueprint stating how managers intend to use organizational resources to achieve their goals.
  3. What is a profit center? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A well-defined organizational unit, often a division, headed by a manager accountable for its own revenues and expenditures.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Describe how operating budgets function as a resource-allocation mechanism. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Higher-level managers allocate a specific amount of resources to managers at the level below, who then decide how to divide that budget across activities such as R&D, engineering, and sales to best support the strategy. Many firms treat each division as a stand-alone profit center, evaluating managers on their division's contribution to corporate profitability, tying resource allocation directly to performance accountability.
  2. Outline the five interlocking decisions in the strategy implementation process. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    (1) Design an organizational structure grouping people/tasks appropriately; (2) design control systems to monitor whether the strategy is working; (3) match structure and control specifically to the chosen strategy; (4) manage the transition of implementing strategic change, often complicated by organizational politics; (5) evaluate results and feed them back into the next planning cycle.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss Chandler's "structure follows strategy" principle, the overall implementation process, and the role of resource allocation through operating budgets. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Structure follows strategy: Chandler's study of large U.S. corporations (DuPont, GM) established that organizational structure follows the range and variety of tasks an organization pursues, and changes predictably as strategy changes. This is the starting premise of implementation — structure, systems, and resource allocation are chosen to fit whatever strategy has already been decided, not the reverse.

    Implementation process: putting strategy into action requires several interlocking decisions — designing an organizational structure (Topic 2), designing control systems (Topic 3), matching structure and control to the chosen strategy (Topic 4), managing the transition of implementing change, often complicated by organizational politics (Topics 5–6), and evaluating results to feed back into the next planning cycle (Topic 7).

    Resource allocation: operates mainly through the operating budget, a blueprint for how managers intend to use resources to achieve goals. Higher-level managers allocate resources to managers below, who divide the budget across activities. Large firms commonly treat divisions as stand-alone profit centers, evaluated by contribution to corporate profitability. Resource allocation is an ongoing control mechanism, not a one-time event — budgets are simultaneously a resource-allocation tool and a behavior-control tool, which is why the boundary between "implementing" and "controlling" a strategy is blurry by design.

Designing Organisational Structure

Unit IV · Topic 2

1. Overview

Organizational structure is the formal system of task and reporting relationships that coordinates and motivates employees to work toward a firm's goals. This topic covers how structure is built up — from grouping tasks, to setting the hierarchy, to choosing an overall structural form — before Topic 4 connects each choice back to strategy.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Grouping tasks: functions and divisions (Hill & Jones)

Most companies first group people and tasks into functions (people who perform similar tasks — e.g. all salespeople form the sales function) and then group functions into divisions (a way of combining functions to better produce and deliver goods/services, e.g. a company with five product lines organizing five divisions, each with its own marketing/sales/accounting). As organizations grow, the volume and complexity of handoffs — work exchanges between people, functions, and subunits — increases, driving up bureaucratic costs (the costs of monitoring and managing these exchanges). Grouping into functions and divisions is fundamentally a way of managing these costs.

2.2 Hierarchy of authority

As organizations grow, managers need a clear chain of command defining each manager's relative authority, and a defined span of control (the number of subordinates reporting directly to a manager). Structures range from tall (many levels relative to company size) to flat (few levels). Tall structures create three problems: (1) communication delays — decisions take longer to reach lower levels, and feedback takes longer to reach the top; (2) message distortion — accidental (different functional perspectives) or intentional (self-interested reinterpretation); (3) high cost — more managers means more salaries, benefits, and overhead.

The principle of minimum chain of command: a company should use the fewest hierarchical levels necessary to use its resources efficiently and effectively (illustrated by Bob Iger dismantling Disney's strategic-planning bureaucracy to speed up innovation, and Southwest Airlines deliberately keeping middle management minimal).

2.3 Centralization vs. decentralization

CentralizationDecentralization
DefinitionTop managers retain authority for important decisionsAuthority is delegated to divisions, functions, and lower-level employees
AdvantagesEasier coordination; decisions fit broad organizational objectives; enables fast, unified response in a crisisReduces information overload on top managers; increases lower-level motivation/accountability; flattens hierarchy since fewer overseeing managers are needed
ExampleMerrill Lynch centralizing branch oversight when branches got "out of hand"; HP centralizing R&D for a more directed strategySouthwest Airlines empowering employees to act without waiting for managerial sign-off

2.4 Integrating mechanisms

As structure grows more complex, hierarchy alone is not enough to coordinate people, functions, and divisions — organizations add integrating mechanisms to increase communication and cooperation. These include direct contact between managers of equal authority (limited because disagreements have no resolution mechanism short of appealing to the CEO), and more complex mechanisms like liaison roles and cross-functional teams as complexity increases.

2.5 Four structural forms (Parnell)

StructureDescriptionAdvantagesDisadvantages
FunctionalSubunits organized by function (marketing, HR, finance, production)Specialization, productivity, economies of scale from centralizing functional activityHard to pinpoint profit/loss responsibility; prone to interdepartmental conflict and narrow functional perspectives
Product DivisionalSelf-contained divisions, each responsible for its own product line (own R&D, marketing, finance)Clear product focus and customer orientation; each division is a profit center; good management training groundDuplicated functional staff raises cost; harder corporate-level coordination; divisions may compete for resources
Geographic DivisionalActivities/personnel grouped by geographic location (local, national, or international)Products/services tailored to regional legal/social/climatic differences; can exploit location-based cost or skill advantagesDuplicated functional staff per region; harder company-wide coordination; regional managers may lose the company-wide view
MatrixCombination of functional and product divisional; personnel report to both a "functional boss" and a "project boss"Combines benefits of both forms; flexible staff reassignment; develops lower-level employees through project exposure; frees top management for strategic focusHeavy coordination/meeting burden raises bureaucratic cost; conflict between project and functional managers over resources; dual-reporting can create role conflict

Functional and divisional structures sit at opposite ends of a continuum — quality/price pressures pull toward functional; service/speed pressures pull toward divisional — with the matrix structure as a deliberate attempt to sit between the two extremes.

2.6 Organizational culture as a structural element

Beyond the formal chart, organizational culture — the shared values and norms of an organization — functions as an informal but powerful coordination and control mechanism (Hill & Jones). Founders imprint values on a company (e.g. Bill Gates' entrepreneurship/ownership/creativity values at Microsoft; Sam Walton's customer-first culture at Walmart); through organizational socialization, members internalize these values so thoroughly that culture substitutes for some of the direct supervision and rules a taller, more centralized structure would otherwise require.

3. Key Terms

Function
A collection of people performing similar tasks within an organization.
Division
A grouping of functions that lets an organization better produce and deliver its goods/services.
Bureaucratic costs
The costs of monitoring and managing handoffs/exchanges among people, functions, and divisions.
Span of control
The number of subordinates who report directly to a manager.
Minimum chain of command
The principle that a firm should use the fewest hierarchical levels necessary to use resources efficiently.
Matrix structure
A structure combining functional and product-divisional reporting lines, giving employees two supervisors.
Organizational culture
The shared values and norms of an organization, functioning as an informal control mechanism.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Grouping: tasks → functions → divisions, done to manage rising bureaucratic costs as firms grow.
  • Tall structures: communication delay, message distortion, high cost. Fix: minimum chain of command.
  • Centralization: easier coordination, unified crisis response. Decentralization: less info overload on top, more lower-level motivation, flatter hierarchy.
  • Integrating mechanisms (direct contact, liaison roles, teams) coordinate across functions/divisions as hierarchy alone becomes insufficient.
  • 4 structural forms (Parnell): Functional (specialization, but siloed), Product Divisional (product focus/profit centers, but duplicated staff), Geographic Divisional (regional fit, but coordination cost), Matrix (dual-boss flexibility, but conflict/complexity).
  • Organizational culture (values/norms, transmitted via socialization) acts as an informal, powerful control/coordination mechanism alongside formal structure.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain the difference between a function and a division, and why bureaucratic costs rise as firms grow. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    A function is a group of people performing similar tasks (e.g. all salespeople). A division groups several functions together to produce and deliver a specific set of goods/services (e.g. a product line with its own marketing, sales, and finance). Bureaucratic costs rise as firms grow because the volume and complexity of handoffs — work exchanges between people, functions, and subunits — increases, raising the cost of monitoring and coordinating those exchanges.
  2. List the three problems associated with "tall" organizational structures. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) Communication delays — decisions and feedback take longer to travel up and down the hierarchy; (2) message distortion — either accidental (different functional interpretations) or intentional (self-interested reinterpretation by lower-level managers); (3) high cost — more management levels mean more salaries, benefits, and overhead.
  3. Compare the advantages and disadvantages of centralization and decentralization. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Centralization keeps decision authority at the top, enabling easier coordination, ensuring decisions fit broad organizational objectives, and allowing fast unified action in a crisis (e.g. Merrill Lynch centralizing branch oversight). Decentralization delegates authority downward, reducing information overload on top managers, increasing lower-level managers' motivation and accountability, and flattening the hierarchy since fewer overseeing managers are needed (e.g. Southwest Airlines empowering employees). The right choice depends on the firm's need for coordinated control versus local responsiveness and speed.
  4. Describe the four structural forms and identify one advantage and one disadvantage of each. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Functional: organized by department (marketing, HR, etc.) — advantage: specialization and economies of scale; disadvantage: hard to assign profit/loss responsibility and prone to interdepartmental conflict. Product Divisional: self-contained divisions per product line — advantage: clear profit-center accountability; disadvantage: duplicated functional staff raises costs. Geographic Divisional: grouped by region — advantage: products tailored to local conditions; disadvantage: harder company-wide coordination. Matrix: dual functional/project reporting — advantage: flexible, combines both forms' benefits; disadvantage: conflict between functional and project managers and role confusion from dual reporting.
  5. How does organizational culture function as a control mechanism alongside formal structure? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Organizational culture consists of shared values and norms that guide how members should behave and what goals they should pursue. Through organizational socialization, members internalize these values so deeply that they follow them without needing direct supervision or explicit rules — substituting, in effect, for some of the hierarchy and behavior control a more formally structured organization would otherwise need. Founders like Bill Gates (Microsoft) or Sam Walton (Walmart) deliberately cultivate values suited to their strategy, and as culture strengthens, coordination and cooperation improve because members share a common language and set of expectations.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Define span of control. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The number of subordinates who report directly to a manager.
  2. State the principle of minimum chain of command. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A company should use the fewest hierarchical levels necessary to use its resources efficiently and effectively.
  3. What is a matrix structure? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    A structure combining functional and product-divisional reporting lines, where personnel report to both a functional boss and a project boss.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. List the three problems associated with "tall" organizational structures. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    (1) Communication delays — decisions and feedback take longer to travel up and down the hierarchy; (2) message distortion — accidental (differing functional perspectives) or intentional (self-interested reinterpretation); (3) high cost — more management levels mean more salaries, benefits, and overhead. The principle of minimum chain of command addresses these by using the fewest levels necessary.
  2. Compare centralization and decentralization with examples. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Centralization keeps decision authority at the top, enabling easier coordination and fast, unified action in a crisis (e.g. Merrill Lynch centralizing branch oversight). Decentralization delegates authority downward, reducing information overload on top managers and increasing lower-level motivation and accountability while flattening the hierarchy (e.g. Southwest Airlines empowering employees to act without sign-off).

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the four structural forms — functional, product divisional, geographic divisional, and matrix — with their advantages and disadvantages, and explain the role of organizational culture as an informal control mechanism. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Functional: subunits organized by function (marketing, HR, finance, production). Advantages: specialization, productivity, economies of scale. Disadvantages: hard to pinpoint profit/loss responsibility, prone to interdepartmental conflict and narrow functional perspectives.

    Product Divisional: self-contained divisions, each responsible for its own product line. Advantages: clear product focus, each division is a profit center, good management training ground. Disadvantages: duplicated functional staff raises cost, harder corporate-level coordination, divisions may compete for resources.

    Geographic Divisional: activities/personnel grouped by location. Advantages: products tailored to regional differences, can exploit location-based advantages. Disadvantages: duplicated staff per region, harder company-wide coordination.

    Matrix: combination of functional and product divisional, with dual reporting. Advantages: combines benefits of both forms, flexible staff reassignment, frees top management for strategic focus. Disadvantages: heavy coordination burden, conflict between project and functional managers, role conflict from dual reporting.

    Organizational culture: the shared values and norms of an organization function as an informal but powerful coordination and control mechanism alongside the formal structure. Founders imprint values on a company (Bill Gates at Microsoft, Sam Walton at Walmart); through organizational socialization, members internalize these values so thoroughly that culture substitutes for some of the direct supervision and rules a taller, more centralized structure would otherwise require.

Designing Strategic Control Systems

Unit IV · Topic 3

1. Overview

Structure (Topic 2) creates the framework for action, but managers still need to know whether the strategy is actually working. Strategic control systems are the formal target-setting, measurement, and feedback tools that answer this — and, just as importantly, motivate employees to keep working toward the strategy's goals.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Why control matters — link to the four building blocks

Hill & Jones tie strategic control directly back to the four building blocks of competitive advantage (Unit II, Topic 4):

  • Control and efficiency — a control system supplies the input/output measures needed to know how efficiently resources are being used.
  • Control and quality — feedback (e.g. customer complaints, return rates) tells managers how much quality is actually built into the product.
  • Control and innovation — the right control design can empower employees to experiment and take risks rather than discouraging it.
  • Control and customer responsiveness — monitoring customer-facing employee performance reveals training needs and improves consistency.

2.2 Three characteristics of an effective control system

It should be flexible (adaptable to unexpected events), accurate (gives a true picture of performance), and timely (delivers information before it goes stale — decisions on outdated information are "a recipe for failure").

2.3 Four steps in designing a control system (Hill & Jones)

Establish Standards & Targets
→
Create Measuring & Monitoring Systems
→
Compare Performance vs. Targets
→
Evaluate Result & Take Action

2.4 Four levels of strategic control

Control systems operate at corporate, divisional, functional, and individual levels. Controls at each level should provide the context within which the level below designs its own controls (Board → corporate managers → divisional managers → functional managers → first-line managers). Measures at every level should tie back to the four building blocks, and — echoing the Balanced Scorecard (Unit I, Topic 5) — care must be taken that a division's attempt to hit its own targets doesn't damage corporate-level performance.

2.5 Three types of control systems

TypeMechanismRisk
Personal controlShaping behavior through face-to-face interaction — direct supervision, or peer control within teams.Doesn't scale well in large, dispersed organizations.
Output controlSetting performance goals (divisional → functional → individual) and measuring actual results against them; often tied to rewards.Inappropriate targets (e.g. across-the-board ROIC targets) can cause divisions to maximize their own numbers at the expense of corporate performance, or even manipulate figures.
Behavior controlStandardizing the means of reaching goals via operating budgets, and standardizing inputs/conversion activities/outputs (e.g. McDonald's standardizing all restaurant operations).Rules are easier to add than remove — over time an organization can become over-bureaucratized and slow to adapt.

Information technology reinforces all three: it's a form of behavior control (standardizing processes via shared software), output control (real-time, codified performance data), and an integrating mechanism (cross-functional information sharing) — letting even flat, decentralized organizations (e.g. Cypress Semiconductor's CEO monitoring 2,000 employees via a lightweight IT system rather than a tall management hierarchy) maintain control without adding bureaucracy.

2.6 Strategic reward systems

Control and reward systems are deliberately linked: based on the firm's strategy (e.g. cost leadership vs. differentiation), managers decide which behaviors to reward, build a control system to measure those behaviors, and tie the reward structure to the resulting measures — so that what gets measured and rewarded actually reinforces the chosen strategy rather than working against it.

3. Key Terms

Strategic control system
Formal target-setting, measurement, and feedback systems used to evaluate whether a strategy is being implemented successfully.
Personal control
Shaping behavior through direct, face-to-face supervision or peer interaction.
Output control
Setting performance goals and measuring actual results against them, often linked to rewards.
Behavior control
Standardizing the means (rules, procedures, budgets) by which goals are reached, rather than the goals themselves.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Control links to all 4 building blocks: efficiency (measurement), quality (feedback), innovation (safe-to-experiment design), responsiveness (monitoring customer-facing performance).
  • Effective control = flexible + accurate + timely.
  • 4 design steps: establish standards → create measuring/monitoring → compare vs. targets → evaluate/act.
  • 4 levels: corporate, divisional, functional, individual — each level's controls provide context for the level below.
  • 3 types: Personal (face-to-face), Output (goals + measurement, reward-linked, risk of gaming/conflict), Behavior (standardize the means — budgets, rules; risk of over-bureaucratization).
  • IT amplifies all 3 control types and can substitute for a taller hierarchy.
  • Reward systems should be explicitly linked to the behaviors that support the chosen strategy.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain how strategic control connects to each of the four building blocks of competitive advantage. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Control and efficiency: measurement systems tell managers how many input units are used per unit of output, enabling efficiency improvements to be tracked. Control and quality: feedback like customer complaints or return rates reveals how much quality is actually being delivered. Control and innovation: a well-designed control system can empower employees to experiment and take risks rather than discouraging it. Control and customer responsiveness: monitoring customer-facing employees' performance reveals training needs and improves service consistency.
  2. List the three characteristics of an effective control system and the four steps in designing one. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Characteristics: flexible (adapts to unexpected events), accurate (gives a true picture of performance), timely (delivered before it's outdated). Design steps: establish standards and targets, create measuring and monitoring systems, compare actual performance against targets, evaluate the result and take action if necessary.
  3. Compare personal, output, and behavior control, including a risk associated with each. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Personal control shapes behavior through direct, face-to-face supervision or peer interaction — its risk is that it doesn't scale well in large, dispersed organizations. Output control sets performance goals and measures results against them, often tied to rewards — its risk is that inappropriate targets (like uniform ROIC targets) can cause divisions to maximize their own numbers at the expense of corporate performance, or even manipulate figures. Behavior control standardizes the means of reaching goals via rules, budgets, and standardized inputs/processes/outputs — its risk is that rules accumulate over time and are rarely removed, leading to over-bureaucratization and slower adaptation.
  4. How does information technology function as all three types of control simultaneously? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    IT is a form of behavior control because a shared software platform standardizes how work is done across functions. It is a form of output control because it provides real-time, codified data on performance against goals. It is also an integrating mechanism, since it gives people across levels and functions the shared information they need to coordinate effectively. This combination lets even flat, decentralized organizations maintain rigorous control without needing a tall management hierarchy — as with Cypress Semiconductor's CEO managing 2,000 employees' weekly goal progress through an IT system rather than layers of middle management.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. Name the three characteristics of an effective control system. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Flexible (adaptable to unexpected events), accurate (gives a true picture of performance), and timely (delivers information before it goes stale).
  2. What is personal control? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Shaping behavior through face-to-face interaction — direct supervision or peer control within teams.
  3. Name the four levels at which strategic control operates. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Corporate, divisional, functional, and individual.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Describe the four steps in designing a control system. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    (1) Establish standards and targets; (2) create measuring and monitoring systems; (3) compare actual performance against targets; (4) evaluate the result and take action. This sequence, per Hill & Jones, ensures control is tied to concrete, comparable measures rather than informal impression.
  2. Compare output control and behavior control, including a risk of each. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Output control sets performance goals and measures results against them, often tied to rewards — risk: inappropriate targets (e.g. uniform ROIC targets) can cause divisions to maximize their own numbers at corporate expense, or manipulate figures. Behavior control standardizes the means of reaching goals via budgets and standardized procedures — risk: rules are easier to add than remove, leading to over-bureaucratization over time.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss how strategic control connects to the four building blocks of competitive advantage, and explain the three types of control systems in detail. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Link to building blocks: control and efficiency — supplies input/output measures needed to know how efficiently resources are used; control and quality — feedback like customer complaints or return rates tells managers how much quality is built into the product; control and innovation — the right control design can empower employees to experiment rather than discouraging it; control and customer responsiveness — monitoring customer-facing performance reveals training needs and improves consistency.

    Three types of control: Personal control shapes behavior through direct face-to-face supervision or peer interaction — doesn't scale well in large, dispersed organizations. Output control sets performance goals and measures results against them, often reward-linked — risks divisions gaming or manipulating figures if targets are poorly designed. Behavior control standardizes the means of reaching goals via operating budgets and standardized inputs/processes/outputs (e.g. McDonald's standardizing restaurant operations) — risks over-bureaucratization since rules are easier to add than remove.

    Information technology reinforces all three simultaneously: it standardizes processes (behavior control), provides real-time codified performance data (output control), and enables cross-functional information sharing (an integrating mechanism) — letting even flat, decentralized organizations like Cypress Semiconductor maintain rigorous control without a tall hierarchy. Reward systems, finally, must be deliberately tied to whichever behaviors the chosen strategy needs, so what gets measured and rewarded reinforces rather than undermines the strategy.
