New Business Models and Strategies for the Internet Economy

Unit V · Topic 3

1. Overview

The internet is not just another sales channel — Parnell treats it as a distinct force that changes how strategic managers must analyze their environment and structure their business models. This topic covers its five strategic dimensions, the resulting forms of e-commerce, and two competing trends it has created.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Five strategic dimensions of the internet (Parnell)

  1. Movement toward information symmetry — information symmetry exists when all parties to a transaction share the same information; information asymmetry (one party knows more than the other) is a major reason many markets are less competitive than pure-competition theory predicts. Businesses often deliberately maintain information asymmetry to their advantage (e.g. car dealers not posting bottom-line prices) — but the internet has systematically eroded this advantage, letting buyers instantly compare prices (e.g. "showrooming" with smartphone apps in-store), forcing even offline retailers to compete more transparently.
  2. The internet as a distribution channel — for intangible goods/services (music, software, insurance, stock trades), the internet can replace physical distribution entirely, speeding transactions and lowering costs; even for physical goods, the intangible parts (product info, warranty terms) can move online.
  3. Speed — 24-hour access, immediate order processing, and follow-the-sun global work handoffs (e.g. US and Indian software teams working in relay) have raised the pace of business and consumer expectations alike.
  4. Interactivity — customers can discuss products in forums/reviews, firms can engage directly with customers and industry groups — but this cuts both ways, since negative information (rumors, bad reviews) also spreads rapidly.
  5. Potential for cost reduction and cost shifting — distributing information to millions of recipients online avoids print/postage costs, and "virtual storefronts" can reduce (though not always eliminate) the overhead of a physical retail presence.

2.2 Forms of electronic commerce

E-commerce activities are classified by who initiates and who receives the offer:

FormDescriptionNote
B2B (Business-to-Business)Businesses transact with other businessesThe largest e-commerce segment by far (~$6.8 trillion globally in 2007) — reduces search/negotiation transaction costs, though consumers rarely notice it.
B2C (Business-to-Consumer)Businesses sell directly to consumers ("e-tailing")Second-largest and fastest-growing segment; success depends on site "stickiness" (getting visitors to stay and complete a purchase) and fulfilling orders reliably — failures here contributed to the 2000–01 "dot-com" bust.
B2G (Business-to-Government)Businesses sell to government entities onlineGrew as agencies recognized efficiency gains from online procurement.
C2C (Consumer-to-Consumer)Consumers transact directly with other consumersRequires intermediaries (eBay for listings, PayPal for payment) due to high transaction costs; small relative to B2B/B2C.
C2B (Consumer-to-Business)Consumers generate an offer; businesses accept/declineLeast developed form — e.g. Priceline's "reverse auction," where price discrimination is possible because no buyer knows what others are paying.

Firms increasingly blend "clicks and bricks" — combining online and physical retail (e.g. Walmart.com offering free delivery to physical stores, an option pure online retailers like Amazon can't match).

2.3 Commoditization and mass customization — two competing trends

  • Commoditization — as technology gives firms more ways to differentiate products, buyers can become overwhelmed by too many features to evaluate, and respond by reducing their decision to a few simple factors (price, one headline feature) — effectively treating genuinely different products as interchangeable commodities. Ironically, firms investing heavily in differentiation can still lose to price-based competition if buyers can't parse the differences (e.g. early digital cameras' feature-overload confusing buyers relative to simple film cameras).
  • Mass customization — the ability to individualize offerings for each buyer (e.g. Amazon's personalized recommendations) while still capturing the economies of scale that come from producing at volume — normally an inverse trade-off, but internet-enabled technology lets some firms achieve both simultaneously.

The two trends interact: firms can use mass-customization technology to fight back against commoditization — cutting through buyer confusion with personalized, relevant offers rather than competing purely on price.

3. Key Terms

Information asymmetry
A situation where one party to a transaction has information the other lacks, historically a source of competitive advantage that the internet has eroded.
Showrooming
Consumers evaluating a product in a physical store, then price-comparing and purchasing online.
Commoditization
The tendency for buyers, overwhelmed by product differentiation, to treat differentiated products as interchangeable and decide mainly on price.
Mass customization
Individualizing product/service offerings for each customer while still capturing production-scale economies.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • 5 strategic dimensions of the internet: information symmetry, distribution channel, speed, interactivity, cost reduction/shifting.
  • 5 e-commerce forms: B2B (largest), B2C (fastest-growing, "e-tailing"), B2G, C2C (needs intermediaries), C2B (least developed, e.g. reverse auctions).
  • "Clicks and bricks" blends online and physical retail for advantages neither channel alone can match.
  • Commoditization: too much differentiation overwhelms buyers, who default to price-based decisions.
  • Mass customization: individualizes offerings while keeping scale economies — can be used to fight commoditization.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain how the internet has shifted the balance of information asymmetry between buyers and sellers, with an example. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Before the internet, sellers like car dealers could maintain an information advantage by not disclosing bottom-line prices, forcing buyers to haggle without knowing true wholesale costs. The internet has eroded this advantage: buyers can now compare prices instantly online or via smartphone apps in-store ("showrooming"), forcing even offline retailers to compete more transparently on price, since consumers who research online — even if they don't purchase online — negotiate more aggressively as a result.
  2. Describe the five forms of electronic commerce and give an example of each. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    B2B (business-to-business) — the largest segment, e.g. wholesale supplier platforms. B2C (business-to-consumer/"e-tailing") — e.g. Amazon selling directly to consumers. B2G (business-to-government) — e.g. a firm bidding for a government procurement contract online. C2C (consumer-to-consumer) — e.g. eBay listings between individuals, facilitated by PayPal for payment. C2B (consumer-to-business) — e.g. Priceline's reverse auction, where consumers name a price and businesses accept or decline.
  3. What is commoditization, and why can it hurt firms that are actually investing heavily in genuine product differentiation? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Commoditization occurs when buyers, faced with more product differentiation than they can realistically evaluate, simplify their decision down to a few factors (often price) and treat genuinely different products as interchangeable. This hurts firms investing in differentiation because the extra features and quality that cost money to develop go unrecognized by confused buyers, who end up choosing based on price anyway — meaning the firm bears the cost of differentiation without capturing the pricing power differentiation is supposed to provide, as seen when early digital cameras' feature-heavy complexity confused buyers relative to simple film cameras.
  4. How can mass customization help a firm counteract commoditization? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Mass customization lets a firm personalize its offering to each individual buyer (e.g. personalized recommendations) while still producing at scale, cutting through the confusion that drives commoditization by making the product feel distinctly relevant to that specific buyer rather than one option among many indistinguishable choices — shifting the buyer's decision away from pure price comparison.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. What is showrooming? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Consumers evaluating a product in a physical store, then price-comparing and purchasing online.
  2. Define B2B e-commerce. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Business-to-Business — businesses transacting with other businesses; the largest e-commerce segment by far.
  3. What is commoditization? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The tendency for buyers, overwhelmed by product differentiation, to treat differentiated products as interchangeable and decide mainly on price.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain how the internet has shifted the balance of information asymmetry between buyers and sellers. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Before the internet, sellers like car dealers maintained an information advantage by not disclosing bottom-line prices. The internet has eroded this: buyers can compare prices instantly online or via smartphone apps in-store (showrooming), forcing even offline retailers to compete more transparently, since consumers who research online negotiate more aggressively as a result.
  2. Describe the five forms of electronic commerce with an example of each. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    B2B (business-to-business, largest segment); B2C (business-to-consumer/"e-tailing," e.g. Amazon); B2G (business-to-government, e.g. online procurement bids); C2C (consumer-to-consumer, e.g. eBay listings via PayPal); C2B (consumer-to-business, e.g. Priceline's reverse auction, the least developed form).

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the five strategic dimensions of the internet economy and the two competing trends of commoditization and mass customization. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Five strategic dimensions (Parnell): (1) Movement toward information symmetry — the internet has eroded sellers' historical information advantage, letting buyers instantly compare prices (showrooming). (2) The internet as a distribution channel — for intangible goods (music, software, insurance), it can replace physical distribution entirely. (3) Speed — 24-hour access, immediate order processing, and follow-the-sun global work handoffs. (4) Interactivity — customers can discuss products in forums/reviews, but negative information also spreads rapidly. (5) Potential for cost reduction and cost shifting — distributing information online avoids print/postage costs, and virtual storefronts can reduce physical overhead.

    Commoditization vs. mass customization: commoditization occurs when buyers, overwhelmed by too many product features to evaluate, reduce their decision to a few simple factors like price — meaning firms investing heavily in differentiation can still lose to price-based competition if buyers can't parse the differences (early digital cameras vs. simple film cameras). Mass customization is the ability to individualize offerings for each buyer (e.g. Amazon's recommendations) while still capturing economies of scale — normally an inverse trade-off, but internet-enabled technology lets some firms achieve both simultaneously, and firms can use mass customization to fight back against commoditization by cutting through buyer confusion with personalized, relevant offers.

Recent Trends I: Strategic Thinking and Organisational Culture

Unit V · Topic 4

1. Overview

This is the first of two "recent trends" topics closing out the course. Rather than introducing entirely new frameworks, it draws together how two ideas already covered — strategic thinking and organizational culture — are evolving, and why they increasingly sit at the center of strategic management rather than at its margins.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Strategic thinking — recap and trend

Recall Parnell's distinction (Unit III, Topic 2) between the scientific perspective (systematic, analytical planning) and the artistic perspective (Mintzberg's "craftsman" — intuition and creativity). The trend across recent strategic management practice has been toward valuing "strategic thinking" as a distinct skill from "strategic planning": planning produces a document, but thinking is an ongoing cognitive habit — continuously questioning assumptions, spotting weak signals of change, and synthesizing patterns (much like Mintzberg's emergent-strategy insight from Unit I, Topic 2, where organizations often discover successful strategies through action and feedback rather than prior planning alone). As environments become less predictable (a theme carried through Units II–V), the ability to think strategically in real time has become at least as valuable as the ability to produce a five-year plan.

2.2 Organizational culture — recap and trend

Recall from Unit IV (Topic 2) that organizational culture — shared values and norms, transmitted through socialization — functions as an informal control mechanism, letting founders like Bill Gates or Sam Walton shape behavior without needing exhaustive rules or supervision. The trend here is that culture has moved from being treated as a "soft," secondary implementation detail to being recognized as a first-order strategic asset in its own right (echoed in McKinsey's 7S framework from Unit III, Topic 7, where "Shared Values" sits at the center connecting all other organizational elements).

Two culture-related shifts stand out in recent practice:

  • Culture as a source of competitive advantage, not just an implementation aid — a strong, adaptive culture is increasingly treated as a distinctive competency in its own right (Unit II, Topic 4), since culture built over years is hard for rivals to imitate — much harder than copying a visible resource or process.
  • Culture and strategic leadership are inseparable — the transformational leadership style (Unit IV, Topic 5) depends on a leader's ability to shape and communicate culture, not just direct tasks; emotional intelligence (also Unit IV, Topic 5) is what makes a leader credible enough to shift culture rather than simply issue new rules that culture quietly resists.

2.3 Why these two trends reinforce each other

Strategic thinking (recognizing when the environment demands a change in direction) and organizational culture (the shared capacity to actually act on that recognition, and to accept significant change) reinforce each other: a firm with excellent strategic thinking but a rigid culture will identify problems it cannot act on; a firm with an adaptable culture but weak strategic thinking will change readily but not necessarily in the right direction. Sustained strategic success increasingly depends on cultivating both together, rather than treating "strategy" and "culture" as sequential steps (choose the strategy, then adjust the culture to fit it).

3. Key Terms

Strategic thinking
The ongoing cognitive habit of questioning assumptions and synthesizing patterns in real time, distinct from formal strategic planning.
Culture as distinctive competency
Treating an organization's culture itself as a hard-to-imitate source of competitive advantage, not merely an implementation tool.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Strategic thinking (ongoing, real-time) is increasingly valued alongside strategic planning (periodic, document-based) — echoes Mintzberg's emergent-strategy and Parnell's scientific/artistic distinction.
  • Culture has shifted from "soft implementation detail" to first-order strategic asset — a genuine distinctive competency because it's hard to imitate.
  • Transformational leadership + emotional intelligence are what let leaders actually shift culture, not just issue new directives.
  • Strategic thinking and adaptive culture reinforce each other — recognizing the need for change (thinking) is only useful alongside the organizational capacity to actually change (culture).

Practice Questions

  1. Distinguish strategic thinking from strategic planning, and explain why the former has grown in importance. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Strategic planning produces a periodic, formal document mapping out a course of action. Strategic thinking is an ongoing cognitive habit of questioning assumptions, spotting early signals of change, and synthesizing patterns in real time. It has grown in importance because environments have become less predictable, making a static plan alone insufficient — organizations increasingly need the continuous sense-making that strategic thinking provides, echoing Mintzberg's insight that successful strategy often emerges through action and learning rather than upfront planning alone.
  2. Why is organizational culture increasingly treated as a distinctive competency rather than just an implementation tool? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    A distinctive competency (Unit II) must be valuable, rare, and hard for rivals to imitate. Organizational culture — built over years through founder influence and socialization — is extremely difficult for a competitor to copy, unlike a visible process or resource. This makes a strong, adaptive culture a genuine source of competitive advantage in its own right, not merely a mechanism for executing a strategy decided elsewhere — a shift reflected in frameworks like McKinsey's 7S, which places Shared Values at the center connecting all other organizational elements.
  3. Explain why strategic thinking and organizational culture need to be developed together rather than sequentially. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Strategic thinking is the capacity to recognize when the environment demands a change in direction; organizational culture is the shared capacity to actually accept and act on that change. A firm strong in one but not the other fails in different ways: excellent strategic thinking paired with a rigid culture identifies the right problems but cannot execute a response, while an adaptable culture paired with weak strategic thinking changes readily but not necessarily in a useful direction. Because the two capabilities address different halves of the same challenge — knowing what to change and being able to change it — sustained strategic success requires developing them together, not treating culture as something to adjust only after a strategy has already been chosen.

University Exam Pattern Questions

  1. Distinguish strategic thinking from strategic planning in one line. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Strategic planning produces a periodic, formal document; strategic thinking is an ongoing cognitive habit of questioning assumptions and synthesizing patterns in real time.
  2. What is "culture as a distinctive competency"? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Treating an organization's culture itself as a hard-to-imitate source of competitive advantage, not merely an implementation tool.
  3. Which framework places "Shared Values" at its center? (2 Marks)
    Show answer

    Show answer

Organizational culture, built over years through founder influence and socialization, is extremely difficult for a competitor to copy, unlike a visible process or resource — making a strong, adaptive culture a genuine source of competitive advantage in its own right, not merely a mechanism for executing a strategy decided elsewhere.
  2. Why has strategic thinking grown in importance relative to strategic planning? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Environments have become less predictable, making a static periodic plan alone insufficient — organizations increasingly need the continuous sense-making that strategic thinking provides: questioning assumptions, spotting weak signals of change, and synthesizing patterns in real time, echoing Mintzberg's insight that successful strategy often emerges through action and learning rather than upfront planning alone.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the trends in strategic thinking and organizational culture, and explain why the two need to be developed together. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Strategic thinking: recent practice increasingly values "strategic thinking" as a distinct skill from "strategic planning" — planning produces a document, but thinking is an ongoing cognitive habit of questioning assumptions, spotting weak signals of change, and synthesizing patterns, echoing Mintzberg's emergent-strategy insight. As environments become less predictable, the ability to think strategically in real time has become at least as valuable as producing a five-year plan.

    Organizational culture: culture has shifted from a "soft," secondary implementation detail to a first-order strategic asset — a strong, adaptive culture is increasingly treated as a distinctive competency in its own right, since culture built over years is hard for rivals to imitate. Culture and strategic leadership are inseparable: transformational leadership depends on a leader's ability to shape and communicate culture, and emotional intelligence is what makes a leader credible enough to shift culture rather than simply issue new rules that culture quietly resists.

    Why they reinforce each other: strategic thinking recognizes when the environment demands a change in direction; organizational culture is the shared capacity to actually act on that recognition. A firm with excellent strategic thinking but a rigid culture identifies problems it cannot act on; a firm with an adaptable culture but weak strategic thinking changes readily but not necessarily in the right direction. Sustained strategic success increasingly depends on cultivating both together, not treating "strategy" and "culture" as sequential steps.

Recent Trends II: Change Management and Strategic Management in a Globalised Economy

Unit V · Topic 5

1. Overview

This topic covers Parnell's own explicit list of trends reshaping the strategic management field, plus a recap of how change management (Unit IV) applies at the macro, industry-wide level rather than just within a single firm.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Five trends in strategic management (Parnell)

  1. An increasingly global strategic environment. With the "flattening" of the world and the rise of the BRIC nations (Brazil, Russia, India, China), global partnerships are becoming more common and more necessary for strategic success — firms must be willing and able to work with counterparts anywhere in the world to produce higher-quality products at lower cost. (This directly extends Unit III, Topic 2's global strategy postures and Unit II, Topic 3's Porter's Diamond.)
  2. The internet's continuing influence. Social media, the shift toward "real-time" over archived/print information, and internet portability (smartphones, tablets) mean organizations must respond to consumer demands with ever-greater precision and speed — organizations that keep pace with this technology are rewarded with customer loyalty (extends Topic 3 of this unit).
  3. The permanence of sustainability. Whatever one's view of the underlying debates, firms must meet consumer expectations for cleaner, more efficient production — organizations seen as wasteful or ecologically indifferent risk real marketplace harm (extends Unit I, Topic 6's CSR/triple-bottom-line material).
  4. The blurring of the low-cost/differentiation dichotomy. Businesses increasingly try to transcend the traditional cost-vs-differentiation trade-off (Unit II, Topic 5) and sail into "blue oceans" — new, uncontested market space rather than competing head-on within an existing one. Firms competing "in the middle" (e.g. Hyundai in autos, Hampton Inn in hotels, Panera Bread in fast-casual dining) are proving less likely to be "stuck in the middle" (Unit II, Topic 6) than Porter's classic theory suggested, instead exerting real pressure on pure cost leaders and pure differentiators alike by delivering reasonable quality at accessible prices.
  5. The growing importance of crisis management. Rising globalization, technology, and speed of business all increase the likelihood of organizational crises — crises are no longer rare events that "only happen to other companies." Firms that prepare for them systematically are more likely to thrive; those that don't risk catastrophic downturns or even dissolution.

2.2 Change management at the macro level

Unit IV, Topic 5 covered how an individual firm executes strategic change (recognize the need → create a shared vision → institutionalize the change). These five trends show the same logic operating at industry and economy-wide scale: firms and even entire industries must recognize when global, technological, or sustainability-driven shifts require a response, build organizational buy-in for adapting to them, and institutionalize new ways of operating — the same three-step pattern, just applied well beyond a single organization's four walls.

2.3 Strategic management in a globalised economy

Trend #1 above is effectively a standalone theme: as global partnerships deepen and BRIC economies grow in strategic weight, national-context analysis (Porter's Diamond, Unit II Topic 3) and global-strategy posture choice (Unit III, Topic 2) become permanent, first-order strategic questions for almost any firm of meaningful scale — not a specialized concern reserved for multinationals alone.

3. Key Terms

BRIC nations
Brazil, Russia, India, and China — economies whose growing strategic weight symbolizes the deepening of global partnerships.
Blue ocean
New, uncontested market space a firm creates rather than competing head-on within an existing (bloodied, "red ocean") market.
Crisis management
The ongoing process of planning for and responding to a wide range of negative events that could severely affect an organization.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • 5 trends (Parnell): (1) growing globalization/BRIC partnerships, (2) continuing internet influence (social/real-time/mobile), (3) permanence of sustainability expectations, (4) blurring of cost-leadership/differentiation ("blue ocean," mid-market players like Hyundai/Hampton Inn/Panera), (5) growing importance of crisis management.
  • Mid-market "in the middle" competitors are increasingly viable, not automatically "stuck," pressuring both pure cost leaders and pure differentiators.
  • Crises are now a normal risk for any firm, not a rare event — preparation is a strategic necessity.
  • Change management logic (recognize → vision → institutionalize, Unit IV) scales up from single-firm change to industry/economy-wide adaptation.

Practice Questions

  1. List Parnell's five trends in strategic management. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) An increasingly global strategic environment, driven partly by the rise of BRIC nations; (2) the internet's continuing and deepening influence via social media, real-time information, and mobile access; (3) the permanence of sustainability as a consumer and strategic expectation; (4) the blurring of the low-cost/differentiation dichotomy as firms pursue "blue ocean" middle-ground positions; (5) the growing importance of crisis management as globalization, technology, and speed increase organizational risk.
  2. Explain the "blue ocean" trend and why it challenges the classical "stuck in the middle" warning from generic strategy theory. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Classical generic strategy theory (Porter) warned that firms straddling cost leadership and differentiation without committing fully to either become "stuck in the middle," achieving neither advantage. The blue ocean trend challenges this: firms like Hyundai, Hampton Inn, and Panera Bread have found durable, profitable middle-ground positions — delivering reasonable quality at accessible prices — that pressure both pure cost leaders and pure differentiators, rather than failing between them. This suggests the traditional either/or framing of generic strategy is becoming less strict in practice, as firms find ways to transcend the trade-off rather than being punished for straddling it.
  3. Why has crisis management become a growing priority for strategic managers in recent years? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Increases in globalization, technology, and the speed of business have raised both the likelihood and the potential severity of organizational crises. Crises are no longer rare events limited to unlucky "other companies" — any firm can be affected, whether the crisis originates internally or externally. Firms that prepare systematically for crises are more likely to survive and thrive; those that don't risk catastrophic downturns or even dissolution.
  4. How does the three-step change-management process from Unit IV apply at the level of an entire industry adapting to globalization or sustainability pressures? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    The same recognize-vision-institutionalize logic that applies within a single firm scales up to industry-wide change: firms and industries must first recognize that a shift (e.g. rising BRIC competitiveness, or consumer demand for sustainability) genuinely requires a response rather than being a passing trend; they must build shared buy-in — within firms and often across industry associations or partnerships — for how to respond; and they must institutionalize new practices (new global partnership structures, new production processes) so the response sticks rather than reverting once initial pressure eases. The scale is different, but the underlying pattern of recognition, shared commitment, and institutionalization is the same.

  2. What is a "blue ocean"? (2 Marks)
    Show answer

  3. Name any two of Parnell's five trends in strategic management. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Any two of: an increasingly global strategic environment, the internet's continuing influence, the permanence of sustainability, the blurring of the low-cost/differentiation dichotomy, and the growing importance of crisis management.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. Explain the "blue ocean" trend and why it challenges the classical "stuck in the middle" warning. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Classical generic strategy theory warned that firms straddling cost leadership and differentiation without committing fully to either become "stuck in the middle." The blue ocean trend challenges this: firms like Hyundai, Hampton Inn, and Panera Bread have found durable, profitable middle-ground positions — reasonable quality at accessible prices — that pressure both pure cost leaders and pure differentiators, rather than failing between them.
  2. Why has crisis management become a growing priority for strategic managers? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Increases in globalization, technology, and the speed of business have raised both the likelihood and potential severity of organizational crises. Crises are no longer rare events limited to unlucky "other companies" — any firm can be affected. Firms that prepare systematically for crises are more likely to survive and thrive; those that don't risk catastrophic downturns or dissolution.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss Parnell's five trends reshaping strategic management, and explain how the change-management logic from Unit IV scales up to the industry/economy level. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    Five trends: (1) An increasingly global strategic environment, driven by the "flattening" of the world and the rise of BRIC nations, making global partnerships more common and necessary. (2) The internet's continuing influence — social media, real-time information, and mobile portability demanding ever-greater precision and speed from organizations. (3) The permanence of sustainability — firms must meet consumer expectations for cleaner, more efficient production or risk real marketplace harm. (4) The blurring of the low-cost/differentiation dichotomy — firms increasingly pursue "blue ocean" middle-ground positions (Hyundai, Hampton Inn, Panera Bread), proving less likely to be "stuck in the middle" than classical theory suggested. (5) The growing importance of crisis management, as globalization, technology, and speed all increase the likelihood of organizational crises.

    Change management at the macro level: Unit IV's three-step process for a single firm (recognize the need for change → create a shared vision → institutionalize the change) operates at industry and economy-wide scale too — firms and even entire industries must recognize when global, technological, or sustainability-driven shifts require a response, build organizational (and often cross-firm) buy-in for adapting, and institutionalize new ways of operating. The same three-step pattern applies well beyond a single organization's four walls, and as global partnerships deepen and BRIC economies grow in weight, national-context analysis and global-strategy posture choice become permanent, first-order strategic questions for almost any firm of meaningful scale.

Challenges in Strategic Management

Unit V · Topic 6

1. Overview

This closing topic is a synthesis rather than new material: a deliberate look back across all five units at the recurring patterns behind why strategy so often fails in practice, even when individual frameworks are applied correctly. Recognizing these patterns is itself a strategic skill — many of them recur across very different companies and industries.

2. Detailed Notes — Six Recurring Challenges

2.1 The agency and governance challenge (Unit I)

Strategy is chosen and executed by managers who are agents of shareholders and other stakeholders, not perfectly aligned interests. Moral hazard and adverse selection (Unit I, Topic 6) mean even well-designed governance structures — boards, compensation committees, audit committees — must be actively maintained, not assumed to work automatically. CEO duality and weak boards remain a persistent source of strategic drift.

2.2 The imitation and durability challenge (Unit II)

Competitive advantage is inherently temporary unless actively defended — barriers to imitation erode, industry dynamism accelerates, and "stuck in the middle" or overexpansion (People Express vs. Southwest, Unit II Topic 6) can destroy an advantage a firm spent years building. The challenge is not just building an advantage but continuously re-earning it.

2.3 The synergy challenge (Unit III)

Anticipated M&A and diversification synergy fails to materialize far more often than strategy textbooks' idealized frameworks suggest — AOL–Time Warner, Kmart–Sears, and Daimler–Chrysler all appeared logical on paper. The gap between a portfolio decision that looks sound on a BCG matrix and one that actually works operationally and culturally is one of the most consistent failure points in corporate strategy.

2.4 The implementation and politics challenge (Unit IV)

A sound strategy executed through the wrong structure, control system, or organizational politics fails just as surely as a poor strategy. Structural fit (Unit IV, Topic 4) is easy to describe and hard to achieve in a real organization full of competing power bases (Unit IV, Topic 6) — implementation failure, not flawed strategy formulation, is a leading explanation for why good strategies underperform.

2.5 The disruption and unpredictability challenge (Unit V)

Even firms executing everything correctly by prior standards can be destroyed by disruptive technology (Unit V, Topic 1) precisely because they rationally listened to their existing customers. The strategic thinking vs. strategic planning tension (Unit V, Topic 4) exists because environments increasingly change faster than formal planning cycles can track — making adaptability itself a scarce strategic resource.

2.6 The measurement challenge (running throughout)

From the Balanced Scorecard (Unit I) through strategic control systems (Unit IV) to nonprofit performance measurement (Unit V), a persistent challenge is that the things easiest to measure (short-term financial results) are not always the things that matter most for long-term competitive advantage (innovation, culture, customer relationships). Firms that over-index on what's measurable at the expense of what's strategically important are a recurring failure pattern across every unit of this course.

3. Key Terms

Implementation gap
The difference between a strategy's theoretical soundness and its actual execution results, often the real cause of strategic failure.
Strategic drift
The gradual, often unnoticed divergence between an organization's strategy and its changing environment, frequently linked to weak governance or measurement.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • 6 recurring challenges across the course: (1) agency/governance, (2) imitation/durability of advantage, (3) M&A/diversification synergy failure, (4) implementation/politics, (5) disruption/unpredictability, (6) measurement (over-indexing on the measurable at the expense of the strategically important).
  • These are not independent — weak governance (1) often causes poor measurement (6); poor implementation (4) often destroys advantage built under (2); disruption (5) exploits firms that listened correctly to existing customers.
  • Recognizing these patterns is itself a strategic skill, useful across nearly any case-study analysis.

Practice Questions

  1. List and briefly explain the six recurring challenges in strategic management covered across this course. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) Agency/governance — managers' interests may diverge from shareholders', requiring active governance maintenance. (2) Imitation/durability — competitive advantage erodes over time and must be continuously re-earned. (3) Synergy failure — anticipated M&A/diversification benefits frequently fail to materialize in practice. (4) Implementation/politics — sound strategies fail when structure, control, or organizational politics don't support them. (5) Disruption/unpredictability — even well-run firms can be destroyed by disruptive technology or unpredictable environmental shifts. (6) Measurement — organizations often over-focus on easily measurable short-term results at the expense of harder-to-measure long-term strategic factors.
  2. Using examples from earlier units, explain why "the strategy looked sound on paper" is not a sufficient defense against strategic failure. (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Several cases covered in this course looked entirely sound using standard frameworks yet failed: the Kmart-Sears merger made sense as horizontal integration/diversification but failed due to weak strategic fit and unresolved competitive disadvantages; AOL-Time Warner's anticipated synergy never materialized due to cultural and coordination problems; excavator-industry incumbents rationally declined to invest in hydraulics based on real customer feedback, yet were still destroyed by disruptive technology. In each case, the formal analysis (portfolio logic, synergy rationale, customer research) was reasonable — the failure came from implementation, cultural fit, or unpredictable technological change that the framework alone couldn't capture. This illustrates why strategic management is a practice of continuous judgment and execution, not a one-time analytical exercise.
  3. How does weak corporate governance (Unit I) contribute to the measurement challenge (Unit V)? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Weak governance — for example, a board that doesn't rigorously scrutinize management's reported numbers — makes it easier for managers to emphasize easily measurable, favorable short-term metrics (like quarterly profit) while under-reporting or ignoring harder-to-measure but strategically important factors (like eroding innovation capacity or customer relationships). Strong governance mechanisms, like an independent audit committee, are partly what force organizations to confront the full, more balanced picture that measurement frameworks like the Balanced Scorecard are designed to capture.

University Exam Pattern Questions

Part A — 2 Mark Questions

  1. What is strategic drift? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The gradual, often unnoticed divergence between an organization's strategy and its changing environment, frequently linked to weak governance or measurement.
  2. What is the implementation gap? (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    The difference between a strategy's theoretical soundness and its actual execution results, often the real cause of strategic failure.
  3. Name any two of the six recurring challenges in strategic management covered in this course. (2 Marks)
    Show answer
    Any two of: agency/governance, imitation/durability of advantage, synergy failure, implementation/politics, disruption/unpredictability, and measurement.

Part B — 5 Mark Questions

  1. How does weak corporate governance contribute to the measurement challenge? (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Weak governance — e.g. a board that doesn't rigorously scrutinize management's reported numbers — makes it easier for managers to emphasize easily measurable, favorable short-term metrics (like quarterly profit) while under-reporting harder-to-measure but strategically important factors (like eroding innovation capacity or customer relationships). Strong governance mechanisms, like an independent audit committee, are partly what force organizations to confront a fuller, more balanced picture.
  2. Explain the synergy challenge with reference to well-known M&A cases. (5 Marks)
    Show answer
    Anticipated M&A and diversification synergy fails to materialize far more often than idealized frameworks suggest — AOL–Time Warner, Kmart–Sears, and Daimler–Chrysler all appeared logical on paper (e.g. sound on a BCG matrix) but failed operationally and culturally. The gap between a portfolio decision that looks sound analytically and one that actually works in practice is one of the most consistent failure points in corporate strategy.

Part C — 12 Mark Questions

  1. Discuss the six recurring challenges in strategic management identified across this course, explaining how they connect to concepts from earlier units. (12 Marks)
    Show answer
    (1) Agency and governance (Unit I): strategy is chosen and executed by managers who are agents of shareholders, not perfectly aligned interests — moral hazard and adverse selection mean governance structures (boards, compensation/audit committees) must be actively maintained, not assumed to work automatically; CEO duality and weak boards remain a persistent source of strategic drift.

    (2) Imitation and durability (Unit II): competitive advantage is inherently temporary unless actively defended — barriers to imitation erode, industry dynamism accelerates, and "stuck in the middle" or overexpansion can destroy an advantage a firm spent years building.

    (3) Synergy failure (Unit III): anticipated M&A and diversification synergy fails to materialize far more often than idealized frameworks suggest (AOL–Time Warner, Kmart–Sears, Daimler–Chrysler) — the gap between a decision that looks sound on paper and one that works operationally/culturally is a consistent failure point.

    (4) Implementation and politics (Unit IV): a sound strategy executed through the wrong structure, control system, or organizational politics fails just as surely as a poor strategy — structural fit is easy to describe and hard to achieve amid competing power bases.

    (5) Disruption and unpredictability (Unit V): even firms executing everything correctly by prior standards can be destroyed by disruptive technology precisely because they rationally listened to existing customers; environments increasingly change faster than formal planning cycles can track.

    (6) Measurement (running throughout): the things easiest to measure (short-term financial results) are not always what matters most for long-term advantage (innovation, culture, customer relationships) — firms that over-index on the measurable at the expense of the strategically important are a recurring failure pattern.

    These challenges are not independent — weak governance (1) often causes poor measurement (6); poor implementation (4) often destroys advantage built under (2); disruption (5) exploits firms that listened correctly to existing customers. Recognizing these patterns is itself a strategic skill.

Unit V — Assignments

A capstone case analysis using tools from across the whole course, plus a nonprofit strategy exercise.

Assignment 1: Whole-Course Capstone Analysis

Task: Choose a real company that was significantly disrupted by a competitor's new technology or business model. Apply the whole-course, six-step framework from the Unit V case study to it:

  1. Mission and stakeholders (Unit I).
  2. Industry and competitive position (Unit II) — Five Forces, life-cycle stage, competencies.
  3. Strategic choices made (Unit III) — grand strategy, corporate strategy, portfolio positioning.
  4. Implementation (Unit IV) — structure, control, and how strategic change was (or wasn't) managed.
  5. The specific "other strategic issue" driving the disruption (Unit V) — technology, internet economy, or another theme.
  6. Which of the six recurring challenges (Topic 6) best explains the outcome.

Format: 1,200–1,800 words, or equivalent structured slide deck — this is the semester's largest single assignment and should draw explicitly on material from all five units.

Assignment 2: Nonprofit Strategy Brief

Task: Choose a nonprofit organization (charity, NGO, university department, government agency). Identify its central performance goal (Topic 2), map who pays for its work versus who benefits from it, and assess its exposure to "mission drift" — is there evidence its programs have shifted toward what funders want rather than its stated mission?

Format: 500–700 words.

Application to the chosen case30%Specific, evidence-based analysis grounded in real facts.
Critical analysis25%Synthesizes across units rather than treating each step as an isolated checklist item.
Structure & clarity10%Follows the framework's steps in order; clearly organized.
Use of course material10%Explicit references back to relevant topics and frameworks across multiple units.

Unit V — Quiz

10 questions. Select an answer for each, then click Submit to see your score and which answers were correct.

1. Christensen's theory of disruptive technology explains why:

Correct answer: B. Even rational, well-managed incumbents can be disrupted by an emerging technology they correctly declined based on current customer feedback.

2. According to Christensen, established firms should ask customers:

Correct answer: B. The forward-looking question accounts for the technology's S-curve improvement, avoiding a myopic "no."

3. HP's separate inkjet division illustrates which strategic response to disruptive technology?

Correct answer: B. HP gave inkjet its own division with separate manufacturing/marketing, avoiding suffocation by the laser-jet business model.

4. A key structural difference between nonprofit and for-profit strategy is:

Correct answer: B. This payer/beneficiary split complicates stakeholder analysis compared to a typical business transaction.

5. Which e-commerce form is the largest by transaction volume?

Correct answer: C. B2B is by far the largest e-commerce segment, even though consumers rarely notice it.

6. "Commoditization" refers to:

Correct answer: B. Commoditization occurs when too much differentiation confuses buyers into treating products as interchangeable.

7. Which of Parnell's five recent trends refers to firms occupying profitable middle-ground positions like Hyundai or Panera Bread?

Correct answer: B. Mid-market players are increasingly viable, pressuring both pure cost leaders and pure differentiators.

8. BRIC refers to:

Correct answer: B. BRIC nations symbolize the deepening of global partnerships in Parnell's trends discussion.

9. Which recurring "challenge" in strategic management is best illustrated by the Kmart–Sears merger?

Correct answer: B. Kmart-Sears illustrates how anticipated M&A synergy frequently fails to materialize in practice.

10. In the Blockbuster case, what does the failed 2010 turnaround illustrate?

Correct answer: B. Blockbuster recognized the threat (hence the turnaround attempt) but couldn't execute a response fast or fundamentally enough to survive.

Case Study — Applying Unit V

Unit V · Topic 7

Note for instructors

As in previous units, the syllabus lists "Case study" without naming one. This page gives (1) a synthesis framework pulling together tools from across the whole course and (2) a worked example using Blockbuster's disruption by Netflix and Redbox (Parnell, Ch. 6), since it directly combines disruptive technology, the internet economy, and failed strategic change. Swap in any preferred case using the same framework — this is a good place to use a case that spans the entire semester's material.

Seminar Discussion Agenda (~50–55 min session — capstone format)

  1. Framing (5 min) — presenter sets up Blockbuster's rise and the three-pronged disruption (section 2.1) and today's guiding question: what does it take to survive a technology that makes your core strength irrelevant?
  2. Walk the whole-course framework (20 min) — presenter works through all 6 steps (section 1), explicitly naming which earlier unit each step draws from — this is the semester's synthesis exercise, not just a Unit V topic.
  3. Open discussion — Question 1 (8 min) — why Blockbuster's core competency became a liability rather than an asset.
  4. Open discussion — Question 2 (10 min) — recognizing a threat vs. successfully responding to it (Blockbuster's failed turnaround).
  5. Wrap-up / capstone task (10 min) — in groups, apply all 6 framework steps to a company of the class's choosing; each group reports one finding before the session ends.

1. Whole-Course Case Analysis Framework

Because this is the final unit, this framework deliberately pulls in tools from every prior unit rather than introducing new ones:

  1. Mission and stakeholders (Unit I) — what was the firm's stated direction, and whose interests were at stake?
  2. Industry and competitive position (Unit II) — Five Forces, life-cycle stage, and the firm's distinctive competencies (or lack of them).
  3. Strategic choices made (Unit III) — grand strategy, corporate strategy, and portfolio positioning.
  4. Implementation (Unit IV) — structure, control systems, and whether strategic change was managed well or poorly.
  5. Special strategic context (Unit V) — was technology, the internet economy, or another "other strategic issue" a decisive factor?
  6. Which of the six recurring challenges (Topic 6) were at play, and what would a better strategic response have looked like?

2. Worked Example: Blockbuster's Disruption

2.1 Background

Blockbuster dominated the video-rental industry for over a decade, built on a network of physical stores. By the mid-to-late 2000s, its business model was under sustained attack from three directions: Netflix's mail-order and (later) online streaming rental service, Redbox's $1-a-night vending machines in grocery/convenience stores, and the expansion of pay-per-view movies via cable/satellite.

2.2 Applying the framework

  • Industry/competitive position (Unit II): Blockbuster's distinctive competency — store location density and physical inventory scale — was precisely the asset that Netflix and Redbox's business models made irrelevant. This mirrors Unit V, Topic 1's disruptive-technology pattern: the new entrants' technology (mail/online distribution, vending automation) initially looked like a niche play (mail-order DVDs seemed slower and less convenient than an in-store rental) but improved rapidly.
  • Strategic response and implementation (Units III–IV): Blockbuster attempted a turnaround (Unit III, Topic 1) in 2010 — but the case notes this turnaround was unsuccessful, and the firm entered bankruptcy and was acquired by Dish Network in 2011. Applying Unit IV's change-management framework (Topic 5): the need for change was arguably recognized too late relative to Netflix's growth curve, and whatever vision/institutionalization efforts followed weren't sufficient to overcome a business model built entirely around physical retail.
  • Special strategic context (Unit V, Topics 1 & 3): This is a textbook disruptive-technology case combined with new internet-economy business models — Netflix's subscription/streaming model and Redbox's automated micro-footprint distribution both exploited exactly the strategic dimensions of technology change (cost reduction, distribution-channel disruption, speed) that make incumbents vulnerable.
  • Recurring challenges (Unit V, Topic 6): This case centrally illustrates challenge #5 (disruption/unpredictability) and challenge #4 (implementation) — Blockbuster's turnaround attempt shows that recognizing a threat is not the same as successfully restructuring a business model fast enough to survive it.

3. Discussion / Practice Questions

  1. Using Unit V, Topic 1's disruptive-technology framework, explain why Blockbuster's core competency became a liability rather than an asset. (Applied)
    Show model answer
    Blockbuster's distinctive competency was its dense network of physical retail stores and large in-store inventory — an asset perfectly suited to a rental model built around customers physically browsing and returning videos. Netflix and Redbox's disruptive models (mail/streaming distribution, automated kiosks) didn't need this asset at all, and in fact benefited from lower fixed costs than a store network required. As their technology improved and reached mainstream convenience, Blockbuster's core competency stopped being a source of advantage and became a costly legacy structure it couldn't easily unwind — the same trap Christensen describes for incumbents facing disruptive technology.
  2. What does Blockbuster's failed 2010 turnaround suggest about the difference between recognizing a strategic threat and successfully responding to it? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Blockbuster clearly recognized the threat by 2010 — the turnaround attempt itself proves awareness. But recognition (step 1 of Unit IV's change process) is not the same as successful execution of steps 2 and 3: building genuine organizational commitment to a fundamentally different business model, and institutionalizing that change fast enough to matter. A turnaround built on cutting costs within the existing store-based model could not resolve the more fundamental disruptive-technology problem — the core business model itself needed replacing, not just optimizing, and by the time this was attempted, Netflix's head start on distribution technology and cost structure had become insurmountable. This illustrates that late recognition plus a merely incremental response is often equivalent, in outcome, to no response at all.
  3. Choose a company you are familiar with that was disrupted by a competitor's new technology or business model, and repeat the whole-course framework (steps 1–6) for it. (Applied / open-ended)
    Show model answer
    Open-ended — no single correct answer. A strong response works through all six steps: state the firm's mission and key stakeholders, analyze its industry position and competencies, identify the strategic choices it made (or failed to make) in response to the threat, assess how well (or poorly) it implemented any response, identify the specific "other strategic issue" driving the disruption (technology, internet economy, or another Unit V theme), and name which of the six recurring challenges from Topic 6 best explains the outcome.

Continuous Internal Assessment Test I

Strategic Management (24MTPCBA301) · Units I & II · Time: 90 minutes · Total: 50 marks

Instructions

Answer any 5 questions from Part A and any 3 questions from Part B. All questions carry equal marks within their part. Part A: 4 marks each (20 total). Part B: 10 marks each (30 total).

Part A — Short Answer (Answer any 5 of 7)

  1. Define strategic management and explain how it differs from operational management. [Unit I]
  2. Compare Chandler's and Porter's definitions of strategy. [Unit I]
  3. Define "stakeholder" and distinguish between internal and external stakeholders with examples. [Unit I]
  4. Differentiate between goals and objectives as defined by Parnell, with an example of each. [Unit I]
  5. Why are stockholders usually treated as a distinct class of stakeholder? [Unit I]
  6. Explain why it is important to define an industry from the customer's need rather than the product itself. [Unit II]
  7. Distinguish between quality as excellence and quality as reliability, with an example of each. [Unit II]

Part B — Long Answer / Essay (Answer any 3 of 5)

  1. Describe the strategic management process as a continuous cycle, using a diagram. [Unit I]
  2. What is the agency problem? Explain how moral hazard and adverse selection contribute to it. [Unit I]
  3. Explain Carroll's CSR Pyramid with an example for each layer. [Unit I]
  4. Explain Porter's Five Forces model and how it helps identify opportunities and threats. [Unit II]
  5. List and explain the four generic building blocks of competitive advantage. [Unit II]

Model Answer Key (for instructor use — do not display to students during the test)

Part A

  1. Strategic vs. operational management: Strategic management is the set of analyses, decisions, and actions an organization undertakes to create and sustain competitive advantage — it addresses "are we doing the right things" at the level of mission, goals, and long-term direction. Operational management focuses on "how do we do this task well" — day-to-day execution within a chosen strategy.
  2. Chandler vs. Porter: Chandler defined strategy as the determination of long-term goals plus the courses of action and resource allocation to carry them out. Porter defined strategy as deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique value mix, with "fit" among activities creating a hard-to-imitate system.
  3. Stakeholder definition: Any group or individual who can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organization's objectives (Freeman). Internal: shareholders, board, managers, employees. External: customers, suppliers, government, community.
  4. Goals vs. objectives: Goals are general, usually unquantified desired ends (e.g. "be known as the innovation leader"). Objectives are specific, verifiable, often quantified versions of a goal (e.g. "30% of sales from products launched in the last 4 years").
  5. Stockholders as distinct class: Stockholders provide risk capital with no guarantee of being recouped, so managers prioritize strategies maximizing long-run profitability/growth for them, alongside other key stakeholders.
  6. Customer-need industry definition: A product-based definition can blind a firm to competitors serving the same need through a different product — e.g. Coca-Cola narrowly defining itself as "soda," missing the rise of bottled water and juices.
  7. Quality as excellence vs. reliability: Excellence = design, styling, features, aesthetic appeal (e.g. a Rolex). Reliability = consistently performing without failure (e.g. Toyota's reliability ratings). A product can rate high on one and low on the other.

Part B

  1. Strategic management process cycle: Mission, Vision & Goals → External Analysis (O/T) → Internal Analysis (S/W) → Strategy Formulation (SWOT-based) → Strategy Implementation → Evaluation & Control, feeding back into mission/goals. Continuous because performance and environmental change constantly prompt reconsideration.
  2. Agency problem: Managers (agents) may fail to act in shareholders' (principals') best interest. Moral hazard: owners bear capital risk while managers capture disproportionate benefits. Adverse selection: shareholders can't fully verify a manager's true competence/intent before hiring.
  3. Carroll's CSR Pyramid: Economic (be profitable — foundation), Legal (obey the law), Ethical (do what's right beyond legal minimums), Philanthropic (be a good corporate citizen). Balanced together, not pursued strictly in sequence.
  4. Five Forces: Risk of entry, rivalry among incumbents, buyer power, supplier power, threat of substitutes. A strong force limits pricing power (threat); a weak force allows greater profit (opportunity).
  5. Four building blocks: Efficiency (lowers cost via productivity), Quality (excellence raises willingness to pay; reliability lowers cost via less waste), Innovation (creates temporary uniqueness), Customer Responsiveness (meeting needs better/faster). Feed into low-cost and/or differentiation advantage.

Continuous Internal Assessment Test II

Strategic Management (24MTPCBA301) · Unit III, cumulative with Units I–II · Time: 90 minutes · Total: 50 marks

Instructions

Answer any 5 questions from Part A and any 3 questions from Part B. Part A: 4 marks each (20 total). Part B: 10 marks each (30 total). Part B includes one cumulative question drawing on Units I–III together.

Part A — Short Answer (Answer any 5 of 7)

  1. What is a combination strategy, and why might a diversified corporation adopt one? [Unit III]
  2. Explain the two competitive pressures that shape global strategy, and why they conflict. [Unit III]
  3. Why is the transnational strategy considered the most difficult to implement? [Unit III]
  4. Distinguish between backward and forward vertical integration, with an example of each. [Unit III]
  5. Explain the concept of moral hazard in the context of strategic alliances, with an example. [Unit III]
  6. Describe the ETOP technique and how it relates to a standard SWOT analysis. [Unit III]
  7. What are the main limitations of the BCG matrix? [Unit III]

Part B — Long Answer / Essay (Answer any 3 of 5)

  1. Distinguish between internal and external growth, and list the five forms of external growth. [Unit III]
  2. Explain the three forms of retrenchment strategy, in order of severity. [Unit III]
  3. Explain the four quadrants of the BCG growth-share matrix and the investment logic for each. [Unit III]
  4. Explain how the SW/OT matrix extends a basic SWOT analysis into a tool for generating strategic alternatives. [Unit III]
  5. Cumulative: Using concepts from Units I–III, explain how a company's mission and stakeholders (Unit I), competitive positioning (Unit II), and corporate-level strategy (Unit III) should reinforce each other. Illustrate with a real or hypothetical example. [Units I–III]

Model Answer Key (for instructor use — do not display to students during the test)

Part A

  1. Combination strategy: Applies different grand strategies — growth, stability, retrenchment — to different business units of the same corporation at once. Adopted because business units rarely share identical performance/market conditions; a portfolio approach usually creates more value than one uniform posture.
  2. Two global pressures: Cost reduction (push toward low-cost locations, standardized product) and local responsiveness (push toward customization per market). They conflict because customization raises costs through duplication/shorter runs, undermining the cost-reduction goal.
  3. Transnational difficulty: Requires simultaneous global cost efficiency AND local responsiveness — two pressures pulling in opposite directions — typically requiring sophisticated coordination (e.g. leveraging subsidiary-level innovation globally).
  4. Backward/forward integration: Backward = acquiring suppliers (upstream), e.g. a carmaker acquiring a tire maker. Forward = acquiring buyers/distribution (downstream), e.g. a manufacturer acquiring its own retail outlets.
  5. Moral hazard in alliances: Parties don't share risk/benefit equally, so each partner has an incentive to withhold its best resources or shift cost/risk to the other — weakening the alliance's performance.
  6. ETOP: Divides the environment into sectors, rates factors as opportunities/threats, and summarizes into an overall environmental profile — a structured, sector-by-sector cousin of SWOT's Opportunities/Threats half.
  7. BCG limitations: Overweights market-share leadership as the route to profitability (not true in every industry); classification is sensitive to how the market/industry is defined.

Part B

  1. Internal/external growth: Internal growth expands revenue/capacity/workforce organically, preserving culture and control. External growth occurs via merger or acquisition. Five forms of external growth: horizontal integration, horizontal (related) diversification, conglomerate (unrelated) diversification, vertical integration, strategic alliances.
  2. Retrenchment forms: Turnaround (least severe — leaner, more effective operation without exiting any business), Divestment (selling a specific underperforming/non-synergistic unit), Liquidation (most severe, last resort — terminating the business by selling all assets).
  3. BCG quadrants: Star (high share/high growth — profitable but cash-hungry), Question Mark (low share/high growth — invest or divest), Cash Cow (high share/low growth — highly profitable, funds other units), Dog (low share/low growth — usually divested).
  4. SW/OT matrix: Places strengths/weaknesses on one axis and opportunities/threats on the other; each combination (S+O, S+T, W+O, W+T) suggests a specific type of strategic alternative — systematically generating options rather than relying on ad hoc brainstorming.
  5. Cumulative synthesis: A strong answer shows the mission/stakeholders from Unit I set the direction and boundaries a firm's competitive positioning (Unit II — cost leadership/differentiation, distinctive competencies) should serve, and that corporate-level strategy (Unit III — grand strategy, diversification, portfolio choices) should in turn support that competitive positioning rather than undermine it (e.g. an unrelated diversification move that ignores the firm's stated distinctive competencies breaks this chain). Reward answers that trace a coherent thread across all three units with a concrete example, not just a list of definitions.

Continuous Internal Assessment Test III

Strategic Management (24MTPCBA301) · Units IV & V, cumulative with the whole course · Time: 90 minutes · Total: 50 marks

Instructions

Answer any 5 questions from Part A and any 3 questions from Part B. Part A: 4 marks each (20 total). Part B: 10 marks each (30 total). Part B includes one whole-course synthesis question.

Part A — Short Answer (Answer any 5 of 7)

  1. Explain Chandler's "structure follows strategy" principle and its significance for implementation. [Unit IV]
  2. Why is the line between "resource allocation" and "control" blurry in practice? [Unit IV]
  3. Explain the difference between a function and a division, and why bureaucratic costs rise as firms grow. [Unit IV]
  4. List the three problems associated with "tall" organizational structures. [Unit IV]
  5. Explain CEO duality and why separating the CEO and chairman roles is considered a governance cornerstone. [Unit IV]
  6. Why is the best time to initiate strategic change often when an organization is performing well, and why is this difficult in practice? [Unit IV]
  7. What question should established companies ask about an emerging technology, according to Christensen, and why does the more obvious question lead them astray? [Unit V]

Part B — Long Answer / Essay (Answer any 3 of 5)

  1. Explain why a cost-leadership strategy fits best with a functional structure, while a differentiation strategy across multiple product lines fits best with a product divisional structure. [Unit IV]
  2. How does the choice between related and unrelated diversification affect the centralization decision? [Unit IV]
  3. Describe Parnell's five-step strategic control process. [Unit IV]
  4. Using the mechanical excavator example, explain why rational, well-managed incumbents can still be destroyed by disruptive technology. [Unit V]
  5. Whole-course synthesis: List and briefly explain the six recurring challenges in strategic management covered across this course. Which of these are most directly illustrated by Units IV and V specifically? [Whole course]

Model Answer Key (for instructor use — do not display to students during the test)

Part A

  1. Structure follows strategy: Chandler found organizational structure follows the range/variety of tasks a firm pursues, and changes predictably as strategy changes. Significance: implementation choices (structure, systems, resources) must be designed to fit the chosen strategy, or execution suffers regardless of strategy quality.
  2. Resource allocation/control overlap: Operating budgets serve both purposes at once — they allocate resources to carry out strategy AND simultaneously constrain/standardize behavior (a form of behavior control) by defining what managers are authorized to spend.
  3. Function/division and bureaucratic costs: A function groups people performing similar tasks; a division groups functions to deliver a product/service line. Bureaucratic costs rise with firm growth because the volume/complexity of handoffs between people, functions, and subunits increases.
  4. Tall structure problems: (1) Communication delays, (2) message distortion (accidental or intentional), (3) high cost (more managers = more salaries/overhead).
  5. CEO duality: When one person holds both CEO and chairman roles, weakening independent board oversight since insiders' career prospects depend on the CEO, making a "rubber-stamp" board more likely and letting the CEO control the board's agenda.
  6. Timing of change: Change is easier to execute from a position of strength, but the need is hardest to see when things are going well — organizations naturally keep allocating resources to what drove past success rather than what future success requires.
  7. Christensen's question: Ask "would you be interested once it improves over time?" rather than "are you interested today?" — the obvious question gets a truthful "no" on an early, underpowered version, ignoring the technology's likely S-curve improvement.

Part B

  1. Structure-strategy fit: Functional structure centralizes activity by function, fostering the economies of scale and tight cost/quality control a cost leader needs. Product divisional structure gives each product line dedicated resources and profit-center accountability, letting each division pursue distinct positioning — what a multi-line differentiator needs.
  2. Diversification and centralization: Unrelated diversification typically leads to decentralization (corporate managers lack expertise across unrelated businesses; rely on output/financial controls). Related diversification often centralizes shared functions (R&D, purchasing) to capture the cross-unit synergy that justified staying related.
  3. Five-step control process: Identify the focus of control (aligned with strategy) → develop standards/benchmarks → measure actual performance → compare against standards → take corrective action as needed.
  4. Excavator disruption example: Incumbents asked existing large-bucket customers about early hydraulics and correctly got "no" — a rational decision not to invest. New entrants served the small niche hydraulics could handle, improved the technology, and eventually invaded the large-bucket market — only 4 of ~30 cable-equipment makers survived.
  5. Six recurring challenges: (1) agency/governance, (2) imitation/durability of advantage, (3) M&A/diversification synergy failure, (4) implementation/politics, (5) disruption/unpredictability, (6) measurement. Units IV and V most directly illustrate (4) implementation/politics (Unit IV's whole focus) and (5) disruption/unpredictability (Unit V's technology and trends topics) — reward answers that explicitly connect specific Unit IV/V content to these two challenges, not just list all six generically.

Banking and Financial Services

Unit-wise teaching notes and exam-preparation material, for classroom use and student revision.

Reference books

Padmalatha Suresh & Justin Paul, Management of Banking and Financial Services, Pearson, Delhi, 2017
Peter S. Rose & Sylvia C. Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Tata McGraw Hill, New Delhi, 2017

Units

  • I
    Introduction to Indian Banking System

    Overview, structure and functions of Indian banking — key regulations (RBI Act, Banking Regulation Act, Negotiable Instruments Act) — CRR/SLR provisions — provisions for NPAs — bank financial statements — CAMEL(S) rating framework.

  • II
    Products & Risk Management

    Capital adequacy, deposit and non-deposit sources, designing/pricing deposit schemes, loan management, investment management, asset-liability management, financial distress, predictive models, risk management (interest rate/forex/credit/market/operational/solvency), NPAs, M&A of banks into securities market.

  • III
    Developments in Banking Technology

    Payment systems in India (paper-based, e-payment, electronic banking), plastic & e-money, forecasting cash demand at ATMs, IT Act 2000, RBI's Financial Sector Technology Vision, security threats in e-banking.

  • IV
    Asset-Based Financial Services

    NBFCs (RBI framework), leasing and hire purchase, venture capital and private equity, housing finance, IPO and underwriting, mutual funds.

  • V
    Insurance and Financial Services

    Insurance contract principles, IRDA regulations, insurance products, bill discounting, factoring, merchant banking, role of SEBI.

Unit I — Introduction to Indian Banking System

Six topics covering how Indian banking is structured, the laws that govern it, how NPAs are recognized and provisioned, how banks report their finances, and how regulators rate bank soundness.

  1. 1
    Overview of the Indian Banking System: Structure and Functions

    The financial institutional structure in India, who owns commercial banks, and the newer niche banks (Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks).

  2. 2
    Key Regulations I: The RBI Act and Banking Regulation Act

    RBI's establishment, objectives, and functions; the Banking Regulation Act's core provisions on what "banking" is, reserves, and disclosure.

  3. 3
    Key Regulations II: The Negotiable Instruments Act and CRR/SLR Provisions

    Promissory notes, bills, and cheques under the NI Act, 1881; the Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio.

  4. 4
    Provisions for Non-Performing Assets (NPAs)

    What makes a loan an NPA, income recognition rules, asset classification (sub-standard/doubtful/loss), and RBI's provisioning norms.

  5. 5
    Bank Financial Statements: Balance Sheet and Income Statement

    The 12-schedule balance sheet structure, the income statement, net interest income, burden, and the efficiency ratio.

  6. 6
    The CAMELS Rating Framework

    Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, Sensitivity to market risk — and how RBI applies it to Indian banks.

  7. 7
    Assignments

    Two graded assignment briefs with rubrics, built from this unit's applied analysis tasks.

  8. 8
    Quiz

    10-question auto-graded multiple-choice quiz covering all six topics.

  9. 9
    Case Study

    Applied case analysis, worked example, and seminar discussion agenda tying together Unit I concepts.
