Overview of the Indian Banking System: Structure and Functions

Unit I · Topic 1

1. Overview

What sets Indian banking apart from many other countries' systems is the sheer variety of institution types built to serve different segments of the economy — from large public-sector banks down to tiny credit cooperatives serving marginal farmers. This topic maps that structure before the following topics dig into the laws, statements, and ratings that govern it.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The financial institutional structure in India (Padmalatha & Paul)

India's financial institutional structure is broadly classified into four groups: (a) commercial banks, (b) financial institutions, (c) non-banking finance companies (NBFCs), and (d) co-operative credit institutions. Within "banks," the structure further splits into commercial banks (including Regional Rural Banks), co-operative banks, and the newer "niche banks" — Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks.

The commercial banking sector alone holds roughly 60% of the total assets of all financial intermediaries in India (commercial banks, urban co-operative banks, rural financial institutions, NBFCs, housing finance companies, development financial institutions, mutual funds, and insurance combined) — despite the capital market's growth since liberalization, India's financial system is still dominated by intermediaries rather than direct market financing.

2.2 The commercial banking system: who owns the banks?

CategoryOwnership / Regulation
Public Sector BanksState Bank of India (regulated by the SBI Act, 1955) and Nationalized Banks (regulated by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970/1980). The central government must hold a minimum of 51% in nationalized banks and 55% in SBI; foreign investment is capped at 20% of paid-up capital.
Private Sector BanksMust maintain a minimum net worth of ₹500 crore. Licensing rules (since 2013) permit business/industrial houses to promote banks and NBFCs to convert into banks, via a Non-Operative Financial Holding Company (NOFHC) structure.
Foreign BanksOperate branches or subsidiaries in India under RBI licensing.
Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)Created to combine the strengths of credit cooperatives and commercial banks, specifically to serve credit needs of backward rural sections.

2.3 The newer "niche" banks

  • Small Finance Banks (SFBs) — authorized by RBI (November 2014) to advance financial inclusion by providing savings vehicles and credit to small businesses, marginal farmers, and unorganized-sector entities via high-technology, low-cost operations. Minimum paid-up equity capital: ₹100 crore, with promoters required to contribute at least 40%. SFBs must follow all prudential norms applicable to commercial banks, including CRR and SLR. Several were converted from existing Microfinance Institutions (MFIs), since converting lets an MFI access public deposits and participate in the payment system.
  • Payments Banks — essentially "narrow banks": they do not lend, investing deposits instead in safe instruments like government securities. Permitted to accept demand deposits (capped at ₹1,00,000 per customer initially), issue ATM/debit cards (but not credit cards), and handle payments/remittances — aimed at financial inclusion for migrant workers, low-income households, and small businesses. Their deposits must be held as CRR with RBI, a minimum 75% as SLR in government securities, and a maximum 25% in deposits with other commercial banks.

2.4 Key functions of the banking system

Across all these institution types, the core functions of banking remain: accepting deposits, extending credit, facilitating payments and settlements, and — increasingly — cross-selling fee-based financial products (mutual funds, insurance, wealth management). The variety of institutional forms exists precisely because a single business model cannot efficiently serve everyone from a large corporate borrower to a marginal farmer needing a small working-capital loan.

3. Key Terms

Non-Operative Financial Holding Company (NOFHC)
A structure permitted since 2013 through which business/industrial houses and public-sector entities can promote new private banks.
Small Finance Bank (SFB)
A licensed bank category focused on financial inclusion — savings and small-value credit for underserved segments — with lower minimum capital than a universal bank.
Payments Bank
A "narrow bank" permitted to accept deposits and handle payments/remittances but prohibited from lending.
Regional Rural Bank (RRB)
A bank combining features of credit cooperatives and commercial banks, created to serve rural credit needs.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • 4-part financial institutional structure: commercial banks, financial institutions, NBFCs, co-operative credit institutions.
  • Commercial banks hold ~60% of all financial intermediary assets in India.
  • Public sector banks: govt. must hold ≥51% (nationalized banks) / ≥55% (SBI); foreign investment capped at 20%.
  • Private sector banks: minimum net worth ₹500 crore; NOFHC structure permits new entrants since 2013.
  • Small Finance Banks: financial-inclusion focused, min. capital ₹100 crore, must follow CRR/SLR like commercial banks.
  • Payments Banks: narrow banks — can't lend; must hold CRR + min. 75% SLR + max. 25% in other bank deposits.

Practice Questions

  1. Describe the four-part classification of India's financial institutional structure. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    India's financial institutional structure is classified into: (a) commercial banks (including RRBs, co-operative banks, and niche banks like Payments/Small Finance Banks), (b) financial institutions, (c) non-banking finance companies (NBFCs), and (d) co-operative credit institutions.
  2. What ownership rules apply to public sector banks in India? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The central government must hold a minimum shareholding of 51% in nationalized banks and 55% in the State Bank of India. Foreign investment in public sector banks is capped at 20% of paid-up capital. SBI must in turn hold at least 51% of the shareholding in its own subsidiaries.
  3. Explain what a Payments Bank is and why it is described as a "narrow bank." (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    A Payments Bank accepts deposits and handles payments/remittances but is prohibited from lending — it invests the bulk of its deposits in safe instruments like government securities instead, which is what makes it "narrow." It can accept demand deposits, issue ATM/debit cards (not credit cards), and act as a business correspondent for other banks. Its deposits must be held as CRR with RBI, a minimum 75% invested as SLR in eligible government securities, and a maximum 25% held as deposits with other commercial banks. The goal is financial inclusion — serving migrant workers, low-income households, and small businesses with basic savings and payment services.
  4. Why were Small Finance Banks created, and what capital requirements apply to them? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Small Finance Banks were authorized by RBI in November 2014 to advance financial inclusion — providing savings vehicles and credit to small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries, and other unorganized-sector entities, through high-technology, low-cost operations that universal banks aren't well-suited to deliver. They require a minimum paid-up equity capital of ₹100 crore, with promoters contributing at least 40% of that capital, and must follow all prudential norms applicable to commercial banks, including CRR and SLR.
  5. Why do Regional Rural Banks exist alongside ordinary commercial banks? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    RRBs were created to combine the positive features of credit cooperatives and commercial banks, specifically to address the credit needs of backward sections in rural areas — a segment that neither pure credit cooperatives nor mainstream commercial banks were fully serving on their own.

Key Regulations I: The RBI Act and Banking Regulation Act

Unit I · Topic 2

1. Overview

Two Acts form the legal backbone of Indian banking regulation: the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, which creates and empowers the regulator itself, and the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which governs how banking companies must actually operate.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 under this Act, with its central office in Mumbai since inception. The Act's preamble frames RBI's objective as: "to regulate the issue of bank notes and keeping of reserves with a view to securing monetary stability in India and generally to operate the currency and credit system of the country to its advantage."

The Act defines RBI's main functions as:

  1. Monetary authority — formulating and implementing monetary policy.
  2. Regulator and supervisor of the financial system — prescribing broad parameters of banking operations to protect depositors' interests and maintain public confidence.
  3. Manager of exchange control — facilitating external trade and payments, and promoting orderly development of the foreign exchange market.
  4. Developmental role — supporting national objectives (e.g. promoting priority-sector lending, financial inclusion).
  5. Related functions — including banker to the government and banker to banks.

The Act was significantly amended in 1997 (and later in 2006) to bring in a more comprehensive legislative framework for banking regulation — reflected in the syllabus's reference to "RBI Act, 1934/2006."

2.2 The Banking Regulation Act, 1949

Originally passed as the Banking Companies Act, 1949 (effective 16 March 1949), it was renamed the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 with effect from 1 March 1966. Some of its most important provisions:

SectionProvision
5(1)(b)Defines "banking" as accepting deposits of money from the public, for the purpose of lending or investment, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order, or otherwise.
5(1)(c)Defines a "banking company" as any company which transacts the business of banking.
5(1)(f)Distinguishes demand liabilities (must be met on demand) from time liabilities (all others).
6(1)Lists permitted business activities beyond core banking — borrowing, lockers, letters of credit, traveller's cheques, mortgages, and more.
17(1)Requires every banking company incorporated in India to transfer at least 20% of annual profit to a statutory reserve fund before declaring any dividend.
18/24Cash Reserve and Statutory Liquidity Ratio requirements (covered in full in Topic 3).
29Requires every bank to publish its balance sheet as of 31 March, prepared per the Act's Third Schedule format.
30(1)Requires the balance sheet to be audited by qualified auditors.
31Published balance sheet and auditor's report must be available to the public within 3 months of the period end (extendable by RBI by a further 3 months).
51Applies specific provisions of the Act to public sector banks.

Public sector banks are additionally regulated by their own dedicated statutes: the SBI Act, 1955 (for the State Bank of India), the SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959, and the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980 (for nationalized banks) — layered on top of the Banking Regulation Act's general framework.

2.3 Why two separate Acts?

The division of labor is deliberate: the RBI Act creates and empowers the regulator (what RBI is and can do), while the Banking Regulation Act governs the regulated (what a banking company must and cannot do). Understanding this split helps in correctly attributing which provision comes from which Act — a common source of confusion in exam answers.

3. Key Terms

Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Act that established RBI and defines its functions as monetary authority, regulator/supervisor, exchange-control manager, and developmental institution.
Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The principal Act governing how banking companies in India must operate — definitions of banking, reserve requirements, disclosure, and more. Originally the Banking Companies Act, 1949.
Statutory reserve
A reserve fund every Indian banking company must build from at least 20% of annual profit, before any dividend is paid, under Section 17(1) of the Banking Regulation Act.
Demand liabilities / Time liabilities
Demand liabilities must be met on demand (e.g. current account balances); time liabilities are all other liabilities (e.g. fixed deposits).

Exam-Prep Summary

  • RBI Act, 1934: established RBI (1 April 1935); preamble = monetary stability + currency/credit system management. Functions: monetary authority, regulator/supervisor, exchange-control manager, developmental role, related functions (amended 1997, 2006).
  • Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (originally the Banking Companies Act, 1949; renamed 1966): defines banking (S.5(1)(b)), banking company (S.5(1)(c)), demand/time liabilities (S.5(1)(f)); statutory reserve ≥20% of profit before dividend (S.17(1)); balance sheet publication/audit (S.29–31).
  • Public sector banks also carry their own statutes (SBI Act 1955, SBI Subsidiary Banks Act 1959, Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts 1970/1980) on top of the Banking Regulation Act.
  • RBI Act = regulator's powers; Banking Regulation Act = rules for the regulated banking companies.

Practice Questions

  1. State the preamble objective of the RBI Act, 1934, and list RBI's five main functions under the Act. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The preamble's objective: "to regulate the issue of bank notes and keeping of reserves with a view to securing monetary stability in India and generally to operate the currency and credit system of the country to its advantage." RBI's five main functions: monetary authority, regulator and supervisor of the financial system, manager of exchange control, developmental role, and related functions (e.g. banker to government/banks).
  2. How does the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 define "banking" and a "banking company"? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Under Section 5(1)(b), "banking" means accepting deposits of money from the public, for the purpose of lending or investment, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order, or otherwise. Under Section 5(1)(c), a "banking company" is any company which transacts the business of banking.
  3. Explain the statutory reserve requirement under Section 17(1) of the Banking Regulation Act. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Every banking company incorporated in India must transfer at least 20% of its annual profit (as disclosed in the profit and loss account) to a statutory reserve fund, and this transfer must happen before any dividend is declared for that year.
  4. Distinguish between the roles of the RBI Act and the Banking Regulation Act. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    The RBI Act, 1934 creates and empowers the regulator itself — it establishes the Reserve Bank of India and defines its functions as monetary authority, financial system regulator/supervisor, exchange-control manager, and developmental institution. The Banking Regulation Act, 1949, by contrast, governs the entities being regulated — banking companies — covering what counts as "banking," reserve and disclosure requirements, permitted business activities, and balance sheet publication rules. In short: the RBI Act is about the regulator's powers; the Banking Regulation Act is about the regulated banks' obligations. Public sector banks are additionally governed by their own dedicated statutes layered on top of the Banking Regulation Act.
  5. What balance sheet publication and audit requirements does the Banking Regulation Act impose on banks? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Under Section 29, every bank must publish its balance sheet as of 31 March, prepared per the Act's Third Schedule format. Under Section 30(1), the balance sheet must be audited by qualified auditors. Under Section 31, the published balance sheet and auditor's report must be made available to the public within 3 months of the period's end, a deadline RBI may extend by a further 3 months.

Key Regulations II: The Negotiable Instruments Act and CRR/SLR Provisions

Unit I · Topic 3

1. Overview

This topic covers the oldest of the three Acts in the syllabus — governing the everyday instruments (cheques, bills, promissory notes) banking runs on — and the two reserve ratios that give RBI direct control over how much of a bank's deposits it must keep safe versus lend out.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881

This Act defines the law relating to promissory notes, bills of exchange, and cheques — the paper instruments that predate (and still underlie much of) modern banking. Its drafting history stretched over 15 years: originally drafted by the Law Commission of India in 1866, redrafted in 1877 after objections, referred to a new law commission in 1880, and finally passed into law in 1881 as the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Act 26 of 1881).

Section 13 of the Act defines a negotiable instrument as "a promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque" payable either to order or to bearer. The Act's protections matter directly to bankers: for example, a banker collecting a cheque on a customer's behalf is protected under the Act provided the cheque is crossed before deposit and the banker acts as an agent of the customer whose account is credited.

2.2 Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)

Under the Banking Regulation Act (Section 18) — and separately under the RBI Act's reserve provisions (Section 42) — scheduled banks in India must maintain a minimum cash reserve, expressed as a percentage of their demand and time liabilities, either as cash with themselves or as a balance in a current account with RBI. This is the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR).

  • CRR is calculated against a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) — broadly, its deposit base.
  • Because CRR balances earn no or minimal interest, raising CRR directly tightens the money a bank has available to lend, making it one of RBI's primary tools for controlling money supply and inflation.
  • Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks (Topic 1) must also maintain CRR, just like full commercial banks.

2.3 Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)

Under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, every bank must additionally maintain a percentage of its demand and time liabilities in the form of cash, gold, or unencumbered approved securities — historically specified as a range of roughly 25–40% — measured as of the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight. This is the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).

Unlike CRR (held with RBI, earning nothing), SLR assets are held by the bank itself and typically do earn some return (e.g. government securities) — so SLR primarily serves a liquidity/prudential purpose (ensuring banks hold a buffer of safe, liquid assets), while CRR primarily serves a monetary-policy purpose (controlling the money supply).

2.4 CRR and SLR compared

Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
Legal basisBanking Regulation Act, S.18 (and RBI Act, S.42)Banking Regulation Act, S.24
Where heldWith RBI (cash or current account balance)With the bank itself (cash, gold, approved securities)
Return earnedNone / minimalYes (e.g. interest on government securities)
Primary purposeMonetary policy — controlling money supply/credit creationPrudential liquidity — ensuring a safe, liquid asset buffer

Both ratios are calculated against Net Demand and Time Liabilities and are among RBI's most direct levers over how much of a bank's deposit base can actually be lent out to the economy versus held back in reserve.

3. Key Terms

Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
The Act defining the law relating to promissory notes, bills of exchange, and cheques in India.
Negotiable instrument
Per Section 13 of the NI Act: a promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque, payable to order or to bearer.
Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)
The base (broadly, a bank's total deposits) against which CRR and SLR are calculated.
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
The minimum percentage of NDTL a bank must hold as cash with itself or as a balance with RBI, earning no return — a monetary-policy tool.
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
The minimum percentage of NDTL a bank must hold in cash, gold, or approved securities, held by the bank itself — a prudential-liquidity requirement.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • NI Act, 1881: governs promissory notes, bills of exchange, cheques. Section 13 defines "negotiable instrument." Long drafting history (1866 → 1881).
  • CRR: cash reserve held WITH RBI, no return, monetary-policy tool, calculated on NDTL (Banking Regulation Act S.18 / RBI Act S.42).
  • SLR: liquid assets held BY THE BANK (cash/gold/approved securities), can earn return, prudential-liquidity tool, historically ~25-40% range (Banking Regulation Act S.24).
  • Both calculated against Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL); both apply to SFBs and Payments Banks too.
  • Key distinction to remember: CRR = with RBI, no interest, controls money supply. SLR = with the bank, some interest, ensures liquidity buffer.

Practice Questions

  1. What does the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 govern, and how does Section 13 define a negotiable instrument? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The Act defines the law relating to promissory notes, bills of exchange, and cheques. Section 13 defines a negotiable instrument as a promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque, payable either to order or to bearer.
  2. Define CRR and explain why it is described as a monetary-policy tool. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) is the minimum percentage of a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities that must be held as cash with itself or as a balance with RBI, earning no or minimal return. It is a monetary-policy tool because raising or lowering CRR directly changes how much money banks have available to lend, letting RBI tighten or loosen overall credit and money supply in the economy.
  3. Distinguish between CRR and SLR on at least three dimensions. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) Where held: CRR is held with RBI; SLR is held by the bank itself. (2) Return: CRR earns no/minimal return; SLR assets (like government securities) typically earn interest. (3) Purpose: CRR primarily serves monetary policy (controlling money supply); SLR primarily serves prudential liquidity (ensuring the bank has a buffer of safe, liquid assets). (4) Legal basis: CRR arises under Banking Regulation Act S.18 and RBI Act S.42; SLR arises under Banking Regulation Act S.24. Both are calculated against Net Demand and Time Liabilities.
  4. Why do Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks also have to maintain CRR and SLR, even though their business models differ from full commercial banks? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    RBI requires SFBs and Payments Banks to follow all prudential norms applicable to commercial banks, including CRR and SLR, because they too accept public deposits and must be held to the same safety and monetary-policy discipline as any deposit-taking institution — regardless of how narrow or specialized their permitted activities are.

Provisions for Non-Performing Assets (NPAs)

Unit I · Topic 4

1. Overview

A loan a bank made is only worth what the borrower actually pays back. When repayment stops, RBI's Income Recognition and Asset Classification (IRAC) norms dictate exactly when a bank must stop counting that loan as healthy income, how to categorize it, and how much profit to set aside as a cushion against the loss — rules that directly shape a bank's reported profitability.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 What is an NPA?

An asset, including a leased asset, becomes non-performing when it stops generating income for the bank. Per RBI's Master Circular on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning, a loan or advance is an NPA when:

  • Interest and/or principal installment remains overdue for more than 90 days on a term loan.
  • An overdraft/cash credit account remains "out of order" (irregular drawings against sanctioned limits).
  • A purchased/discounted bill remains overdue for more than 90 days.
  • A short-duration crop loan's installment remains overdue for two crop seasons; a long-duration crop loan's installment remains overdue for one crop season.
  • A securitization-related liquidity facility remains outstanding more than 90 days, or a derivative contract's positive mark-to-market receivable remains unpaid 90 days past due.

Important nuance: asset classification is borrower-wise, not facility-wise — if even one credit facility among several granted to a borrower becomes NPA, the entire borrowing relationship with that borrower must be classified as NPA.

2.2 Income recognition rules

In line with international best practice, income from an NPA is not recognized on an accrual basis — it is booked as income only when actually received (cash basis). If an advance becomes an NPA, any unrealized interest, fees, or commission already credited to income in past periods must be reversed. This applies even to government-guaranteed advances.

2.3 Asset classification: the three NPA categories

Standard Asset
→
Sub-standard
(NPA ≤ 12 months)
→
Doubtful
(>12 months in sub-standard)
→
Loss Asset
(uncollectible)
  • Sub-standard asset — has remained an NPA for 12 months or less. Shows well-defined credit weaknesses that jeopardize recovery, but the bank is likely to sustain only some loss if the deficiencies aren't corrected.
  • Doubtful asset — has remained in the sub-standard category for more than 12 months. Carries all sub-standard weaknesses, plus collection/liquidation in full is now highly questionable and improbable.
  • Loss asset — considered uncollectible, of such little value that continuing to carry it as a bankable asset isn't warranted, even though some salvage value may exist. Identified as such by the bank, its auditors, or RBI inspection.

Special situations worth noting: where security value has eroded to below 50% of assessed value, the account should be classified straight to "doubtful" (skipping sub-standard); where realizable security value is below 10% of the outstanding balance, security should be ignored entirely and the asset classified straight to "loss." Loans with an interest moratorium are not treated as overdue during the moratorium period.

2.4 Provisioning norms

CategoryProvisioning requirement
Standard assetsGeneral provision of 0.25%–1% on the global loan portfolio (varies by sector — e.g. 0.25% for agriculture/SME; 1% for commercial real estate).
Sub-standard assets15% general provision on total outstanding; unsecured sub-standard exposures attract an additional 10% (25% total). Infrastructure loans with escrowed cash flows get a reduced 20%.
Doubtful assets100% provision on the unsecured portion, plus a tiered provision on the secured portion: 25% (up to 1 year in doubtful), 40% (1–3 years), 100% (more than 3 years).
Loss assetsWritten off, or 100% provided for.

An "unsecured" exposure, per RBI, is one where the realizable security value is not more than 10% of the outstanding exposure — and "security" here means tangible security only (guarantees and comfort letters don't count).

3. Key Terms

Non-Performing Asset (NPA)
A loan or advance that has ceased to generate income for the bank, per RBI's overdue-period criteria.
Out of order
The condition of an overdraft/cash credit account showing irregular drawings against its sanctioned limit, triggering NPA classification.
Sub-standard asset
An NPA that has remained non-performing for 12 months or less.
Doubtful asset
An NPA that has remained in the sub-standard category for more than 12 months.
Loss asset
An NPA considered uncollectible and of such little value that carrying it as a bankable asset isn't warranted.
IRAC norms
RBI's Income Recognition, Asset Classification, and Provisioning norms — the rule set covered in this topic.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • NPA trigger: >90 days overdue (term loans/bills), "out of order" (OD/CC), 1–2 crop seasons (agricultural loans).
  • Classification is borrower-wise: one bad facility taints the whole borrower relationship.
  • Income recognition on NPAs: cash basis only; unrealized past interest/fees must be reversed.
  • 3 asset categories: Sub-standard (≤12 months NPA) → Doubtful (>12 months) → Loss (uncollectible).
  • Provisioning: Standard 0.25–1%; Sub-standard 15% (+10% if unsecured); Doubtful 25/40/100% tiered by duration (secured portion) + 100% (unsecured portion); Loss 100%/write-off.
  • Security erosion rules: <50% of assessed value → straight to doubtful; <10% of outstanding → ignore security, straight to loss.

Practice Questions

  1. Define a Non-Performing Asset and list the key overdue-period triggers RBI uses for term loans and cash credit accounts. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    An asset becomes non-performing when it ceases to generate income for the bank. A term loan becomes an NPA when interest/principal remains overdue for more than 90 days; an overdraft/cash credit account becomes an NPA when the account remains "out of order" (irregular drawings against its sanctioned limit).
  2. Explain why asset classification is done borrower-wise rather than facility-wise. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Even if only one credit facility among several granted to a single borrower turns non-performing, the entire borrowing account/relationship with that borrower must be classified as NPA — RBI's logic is that financial distress affecting one facility reflects the borrower's overall creditworthiness, not just that isolated facility.
  3. Describe the three categories of NPAs and the criteria distinguishing them. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Sub-standard asset: has remained an NPA for 12 months or less, showing well-defined credit weaknesses but likely to result in only some loss if uncorrected. Doubtful asset: has remained in the sub-standard category for more than 12 months, with collection or liquidation now highly questionable. Loss asset: considered uncollectible and of such little value that carrying it as a bankable asset isn't warranted, though some salvage value may remain.
  4. Explain the provisioning requirements for doubtful assets, including the treatment of secured versus unsecured portions. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    For a doubtful asset, the unsecured portion (not covered by realizable security value) requires 100% provisioning. The secured portion is provisioned on a tiered basis depending on how long the advance has remained in the doubtful category: 25% if up to 1 year, 40% if 1–3 years, and 100% if more than 3 years. This tiering reflects the declining likelihood of recovery — and the declining reliability of the security's value — the longer an account stays doubtful.
  5. Why does RBI require income from NPAs to be recognized on a cash basis rather than an accrual basis, and what must a bank do when a performing loan turns into an NPA? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Recognizing NPA income only when actually received (cash basis), rather than as it accrues, prevents banks from overstating profitability on loans that are unlikely to be fully repaid — accrual-based recognition would let a bank keep booking "income" on interest it may never actually collect, misleading shareholders, regulators, and depositors about the bank's true financial health. This is why, when an advance turns into an NPA, RBI requires the bank to reverse any unrealized interest, fees, or commission that had already been credited to income in past periods (even for government-guaranteed advances) — correcting the income statement to reflect economic reality rather than an optimistic accrual assumption that has since been proven wrong.

Bank Financial Statements: Balance Sheet and Income Statement

Unit I · Topic 5

1. Overview

Because banks in India must all prepare financial statements per the same statutory format (the Banking Regulation Act's Third Schedule), every Indian bank's balance sheet and income statement look almost identically structured — making them unusually easy to compare across institutions once you know the schedule layout.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The 16-schedule format

Under Section 29 of the Banking Regulation Act (Third Schedule), a typical Indian bank's balance sheet has 12 schedules, with Schedules 13–16 allocated to the income statement:

Balance Sheet (Schedules 1–12)Income Statement (Schedules 13–16)
1. Capital
2. Reserves and Surplus
3. Deposits
4. Borrowings
5. Other Liabilities and Provisions
6. Cash and balances with RBI
7. Balances with banks / money at call and short notice
8. Investments
9. Advances
10. Fixed Assets
11. Other Assets
12. Contingent Liabilities		13. Interest Earned (income)
14. Other Income (income)
15. Interest Expended (expense)
16. Operating Expenses (expense)

Schedules 17 and 18 typically cover Notes to Accounts / provisions and contingencies, and Significant Accounting Policies.

2.2 Reading the balance sheet — liabilities

  • Capital — authorized, subscribed, and paid-up capital. Minimum capital to set up a new bank: ₹500 crore, maintained at that level thereafter.
  • Reserves and Surplus — includes statutory reserves (≥20% of profit, per S.17(1) — see Topic 2), capital reserves (e.g. profit on sale of permanent investments), share premium, revenue/other reserves, and the retained balance in the profit and loss account.
  • Deposits — split into demand deposits (current accounts, no interest), savings deposits (mainly for household savings), and term deposits (Fixed Deposits, Recurring Deposits, Certificates of Deposit, NRE/NRO/FCNR deposits, etc., ranging from 15 days to 10 years' maturity).

2.3 The income statement logic

A bank's income statement works differently from a typical non-financial firm's, but maps onto familiar concepts:

Interest Income
(like "revenue")
−
Interest Expended
(like "direct costs")
=
Net Interest Income (NII)
(like "gross profit")
  • Net Interest Income (NII) = interest income (from advances and investments) minus interest expended (on deposits and borrowings). NII is the core profitability measure banks use to calculate their "spread," roughly comparable to gross profit in a non-financial firm.
  • Burden = non-interest (fee-based) income minus non-interest expenses (overheads). Non-interest income is typically less than overhead costs, so "burden" is usually a negative figure that must be covered by NII.
  • From NII minus burden minus provisions for loan losses, you arrive at operating income; adjusting for profit/loss on sale of long-term securities or assets gives net operating income before taxes; deducting taxes gives net income.
  • Efficiency ratio = overhead expenses ÷ (NII + non-interest income). It measures how well a bank controls overhead relative to the income it's generating — a lower efficiency ratio is better (less overhead consumed per unit of income).

Banks are increasingly growing the non-interest income share of revenue (fund transfers, custodial services, letters of credit/guarantee, derivatives dealing) — reflecting the broader industry shift toward fee-based services described in Topic 1.

3. Key Terms

Net Interest Income (NII)
Interest income minus interest expended — a bank's core profitability measure, analogous to "gross profit."
Burden
Non-interest income minus non-interest (overhead) expenses — usually a negative figure that NII must cover.
Efficiency ratio
Overhead expenses divided by the sum of NII and non-interest income; lower is better.
Statutory reserve
The reserve fund (≥20% of annual profit) every Indian bank must build before declaring dividends (Banking Regulation Act, S.17(1)).

Exam-Prep Summary

  • 16-schedule format under the Banking Regulation Act's Third Schedule: 12 for balance sheet (Capital, Reserves, Deposits, Borrowings, Other Liabilities, Cash/RBI balances, Bank balances, Investments, Advances, Fixed Assets, Other Assets, Contingent Liabilities), 4 for income statement (Interest Earned, Other Income, Interest Expended, Operating Expenses).
  • Deposits split into demand (no interest), savings, and term deposits.
  • NII = Interest income − Interest expended (like "gross profit"). Burden = Non-interest income − overheads (usually negative).
  • Operating income = NII − burden − loan-loss provisions; adjust for securities gains/losses → net operating income before tax → net income after tax.
  • Efficiency ratio = overhead ÷ (NII + non-interest income); lower is better.

Practice Questions

  1. Describe the 16-schedule structure of an Indian bank's financial statements. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    The balance sheet uses Schedules 1–12: Capital, Reserves and Surplus, Deposits, Borrowings, and Other Liabilities and Provisions on the liabilities side; Cash and balances with RBI, Balances with banks/money at call, Investments, Advances, Fixed Assets, and Other Assets on the assets side; plus Contingent Liabilities (Schedule 12). The income statement uses Schedules 13–16: Interest Earned and Other Income (income), and Interest Expended and Operating Expenses (expenses). This uniform format, required under the Banking Regulation Act's Third Schedule, makes all Indian banks' statements directly comparable.
  2. Define Net Interest Income (NII) and explain why it is described as analogous to "gross profit." (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    NII is interest income (from advances and investments) minus interest expended (on deposits and borrowings). It's analogous to gross profit because, just as gross profit subtracts direct costs from revenue in a non-financial firm, NII subtracts the bank's most direct "cost" (interest paid to fund itself) from its most direct "revenue" (interest earned on what it lends/invests) — leaving the core spread the bank has to work with before overheads and provisions.
  3. What is "burden" in a bank's income statement, and why is it usually a negative figure? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Burden is non-interest (fee-based) income minus non-interest expenses (overheads). It is usually negative because non-interest income is typically smaller than overhead costs — meaning NII usually has to cover this shortfall for the bank to remain profitable overall.
  4. Explain the efficiency ratio and what a lower value indicates about a bank. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The efficiency ratio is overhead expenses divided by the sum of NII and non-interest income. A lower efficiency ratio indicates the bank is spending less on overhead relative to the income (both interest and fee-based) it generates — i.e. it is running its operations more cost-effectively.
  5. Trace the path from interest income down to net income on a bank's income statement. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Interest income minus interest expended gives Net Interest Income (NII). Non-interest income minus overhead expenses gives the "burden" (usually negative). NII minus burden minus provisions for loan and other losses gives operating income. Adjusting operating income for profit or loss on sale of long-term securities/assets gives net operating income before taxes. Deducting taxes and other adjustments gives net income (profit after tax).

The CAMELS Rating Framework

Unit I · Topic 6

1. Overview

The syllabus calls this "CAMEL," but both assigned textbooks — one India-focused, one US-focused — describe the modern version as CAMELS (six components, with "S" added for sensitivity to market risk). It's the standard framework regulators use to condense a bank's overall financial condition into a single, comparable supervisory rating.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The six CAMELS components

LetterComponentWhat it measures
CCapital adequacyThe bank's capacity to maintain capital commensurate with its risks, and management's ability to identify/measure/monitor/control those risks.
AAsset qualityThe credit risk embedded in the bank's loans, advances, investments, and off-balance-sheet activities.
MManagement qualityThe board and senior management's ability to identify/measure/monitor/control banking risks — assessed via risk-management policies and processes.
EEarningsThe amount and trend of earnings, and the robustness of expected future earnings growth.
LLiquidityThe adequacy of current and potential liquidity sources, including the strength of funds-management practices.
SSensitivity to market riskHow much changes in interest rates, exchange rates, commodity prices, and equity prices could affect earnings and capital.

This is the origin story worth remembering for exams: the "S" is a comparatively recent addition to what was originally a "CAMEL" framework — both books confirm this, and Rose & Hudgins even note that some US bank examiners further add an "I" (for Information technology), producing "CAMELS-I," reflecting the growing importance of IT to sound bank management, especially for online financial services.

2.2 Rating scale and interpretation

Each component is rated on a scale of 1 (best) to 5 (worst), and an overall composite rating is also assigned:

Rating rangeInterpretation
1.0–1.4Strong — sound in every respect; no supervisory response required.
1.6–2.4Satisfactory — fundamentally sound with modest, correctable weaknesses.
2.6–3.4Fair (watch category) — weaknesses that, if not addressed, will become severe; more than normal supervision required.
3.6–4.4Marginal — immoderate weaknesses that could impair future viability unless addressed; needs close supervision.
4.6–5.0Unsatisfactory — high risk of failure in the near term; under constant supervision or cease-and-desist order.

Banks rated 1 or 2 present few, if any, supervisory concerns; banks rated 3, 4, or 5 present moderate-to-extreme supervisory concern and are examined more frequently than highly-rated institutions.

2.3 CAMELS in India — application and weights

Since 1995, RBI's on-site inspections of domestic banks have been based on the CAMELS model, aiming to: evaluate safety and soundness, appraise board/management quality, ensure compliance with prudential regulations, identify areas needing corrective action, and review compliance with banking laws. Foreign banks operating in India, by contrast, are rated on a related but distinct CALCS model (Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Liquidity, Compliance, Systems and control) — reflecting that foreign bank branches don't have the same domestic "Management" and "Earnings" structure to assess in the same way.

ComponentCAMELS weight (domestic banks)CALCS weight (foreign banks)
Capital Adequacy1818
Asset Quality1818
Management18—
Earnings10—
Liquidity1818
Compliance—26
System and Control1820

2.4 Where CAMELS is heading in India

RBI itself has flagged that the CAMELS system is primarily a lag indicator — a "post-mortem" view of a bank's condition — rather than a lead indicator of the bank's ability to create value or absorb risk going forward. A 2012 high-level steering committee review concluded CAMELS lacked adequate forward-looking, risk-focused assessment, leading RBI to propose replacing it with INROADS (Indian Risk-Oriented and Dynamic Rating System), intended to better capture the risks that could cause a bank to fail, rather than merely documenting past performance.

3. Key Terms

CAMELS
A bank-rating framework covering Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, and Sensitivity to market risk.
CALCS
The related model (Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Liquidity, Compliance, Systems and control) used by RBI to rate foreign banks operating in India.
Lag indicator vs. lead indicator
A lag indicator reflects past/current performance (like CAMELS); a lead indicator would forecast future risk of failure — the gap RBI's proposed INROADS system aims to close.
INROADS
Indian Risk-Oriented and Dynamic Rating System — RBI's proposed forward-looking replacement for CAMELS.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • CAMELS = Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, Sensitivity to market risk. "S" is a later addition to the original "CAMEL."
  • Rating scale 1 (best) to 5 (worst); composite bands: 1.0–1.4 Strong, 1.6–2.4 Satisfactory, 2.6–3.4 Fair/Watch, 3.6–4.4 Marginal, 4.6–5.0 Unsatisfactory.
  • India: domestic banks rated on CAMELS since 1995; foreign banks rated on CALCS (Compliance and Systems substitute for Management and Earnings).
  • Criticism: CAMELS is a lag indicator (backward-looking); RBI has proposed INROADS as a forward-looking replacement.
  • Rose & Hudgins note some US examiners add "I" for Information Technology, making it "CAMELS-I."

Practice Questions

  1. List and briefly explain the six components of the CAMELS rating framework. (Long answer / diagram-based)
    Show model answer
    Capital adequacy (capacity to maintain risk-commensurate capital), Asset quality (credit risk in loans/investments/off-balance-sheet items), Management (board/senior management's risk-control ability), Earnings (amount, trend, and robustness of future earnings), Liquidity (adequacy of liquidity sources and funds-management strength), and Sensitivity to market risk (exposure of earnings/capital to interest rate, exchange rate, commodity, and equity price changes).
  2. How does RBI's rating approach differ between domestic banks and foreign banks operating in India? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Domestic banks are rated using the full CAMELS model (Capital, Asset quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, Sensitivity), used since 1995 for on-site inspections. Foreign banks are instead rated on the CALCS model — Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Liquidity, Compliance, and Systems and control — substituting Compliance and Systems for Management and Earnings, since foreign bank branches in India don't have the same standalone board/management or earnings structure that CAMELS' Management and Earnings components are designed to assess.
  3. Why has RBI proposed replacing CAMELS with INROADS? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    RBI's 2012 high-level steering committee review found that CAMELS was primarily a lag indicator — a backward-looking, "post-mortem" assessment of a bank's condition — rather than a forward-looking measure of the bank's ability to create value or its risk of future failure. INROADS (Indian Risk-Oriented and Dynamic Rating System) was proposed to better capture forward-looking risk rather than merely documenting past performance.
  4. Explain the CAMELS composite rating scale and what a rating of 4.0 would imply for a bank. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Ratings run from 1.0 (strongest) to 5.0 (weakest), in bands: 1.0–1.4 Strong, 1.6–2.4 Satisfactory, 2.6–3.4 Fair/Watch, 3.6–4.4 Marginal, 4.6–5.0 Unsatisfactory. A rating of 4.0 falls in the "Marginal" band, meaning the bank shows immoderate weaknesses that, unless properly addressed, could impair its future viability — it would require close supervisory attention.

Unit I — Assignments

Two assignments: a real-bank profile analysis, and an NPA classification/provisioning problem.

Assignment 1: Bank Profile Analysis

Task: Choose a real Indian bank (public sector, private sector, or a Small Finance/Payments Bank). Using its latest published annual report or RBI/bank website disclosures, write a profile covering:

  1. Its ownership category (Topic 1) and which statutes govern it besides the Banking Regulation Act.
  2. Its balance sheet, mapped to the 12-schedule structure (Topic 5) — note the three largest liability and asset line items.
  3. Its Net Interest Income and, if disclosed, its efficiency ratio — compare to one other bank of your choice.
  4. Any disclosed NPA figures (gross/net NPA ratio) and how they compare to the sector average.

Format: 800–1,200 words, or equivalent structured slide deck, with figures cited from your source.

Assignment 2: NPA Classification and Provisioning Problem

Task: Construct (or use a provided) loan scenario: a ₹50 lakh term loan, secured by property currently valued at ₹30 lakh, that stops receiving payments. Track it through the NPA lifecycle (Topic 4):

  1. At what point does it first become an NPA?
  2. Classify it as sub-standard, then doubtful (state the dates/durations that trigger each reclassification).
  3. Calculate the provisioning required at each stage, showing your secured/unsecured split and citing the applicable percentage.
  4. What happens to income already recognized on this loan once it turns NPA?

Format: A worked numerical answer with a short explanation for each step (400–600 words plus calculations).

Grading Rubric (applies to both assignments)

CriterionWeightWhat it looks for
Concept understanding25%Correct, precise use of Unit I terminology and regulatory provisions.
Application / accuracy30%Correct application of rules to real figures or the given scenario (especially for Assignment 2's calculations).
Critical analysis25%Goes beyond stating facts to interpreting what they mean for the bank's soundness.
Structure & clarity10%Clearly organized, easy to follow, each step justified.
Use of course material10%Explicit references back to the relevant Unit I topics and provisions used.

Unit I — Quiz

10 questions. Select an answer for each, then click Submit to see your score and which answers were correct.

1. What share of total financial intermediary assets in India does the commercial banking sector hold?

Correct answer: C. The commercial banking sector holds roughly 60% of total financial intermediary assets in India.

2. Which Act defines "banking" as accepting deposits for the purpose of lending or investment, repayable on demand?

Correct answer: B. Section 5(1)(b) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 defines "banking."

3. Under Section 17(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, what minimum share of profit must go to statutory reserves before any dividend is declared?

Correct answer: C. At least 20% of annual profit must go to the statutory reserve fund before any dividend.

4. A Payments Bank is best described as:

Correct answer: B. Payments Banks are "narrow banks" — they cannot lend, investing deposits in safe instruments instead.

5. An NPA classified as "sub-standard" has remained non-performing for:

Correct answer: B. Sub-standard = NPA for 12 months or less; beyond that it becomes "doubtful."

6. What is the provisioning requirement for the unsecured portion of a doubtful asset?

Correct answer: C. The unsecured portion of a doubtful asset requires 100% provisioning; only the secured portion gets the tiered 25/40/100% treatment.

7. Net Interest Income (NII) is calculated as:

Correct answer: B. NII = interest income (advances/investments) minus interest expended (deposits/borrowings).

8. Which schedules of an Indian bank's financial statements relate to the income statement?

Correct answer: C. Schedules 13–16 cover Interest Earned, Other Income, Interest Expended, and Operating Expenses.

9. Under the CAMELS framework, which component was added most recently to the original "CAMEL"?

Correct answer: C. "Sensitivity to market risk" is a comparatively recent addition to the original CAMEL framework.

10. Foreign banks operating in India are rated using which model instead of CAMELS?

Correct answer: B. Foreign banks are rated on CALCS (Capital, Asset quality, Liquidity, Compliance, Systems and control).

Case Study — Applying Unit I

Unit I · Topic 7

Note for instructors

This page uses the Kingfisher Airlines NPA episode as its worked example — it is directly referenced in Padmalatha & Paul's textbook (Chapter 8, Annexure III: "Case Study: Kingfisher Airlines – A High Profile NPA") and cleanly illustrates asset classification, provisioning, and the knock-on effect on lending banks' financial statements and CAMELS ratings. Swap in any preferred case using the same framework.

Seminar Discussion Agenda (~45–50 min session)

  1. Framing (5 min) — presenter introduces the Kingfisher Airlines background (section 2.1) and today's guiding question: how does one large corporate default ripple through a lending bank's entire balance sheet?
  2. Walk the framework (15 min) — presenter works through case-analysis steps 1–5 (section 1) in order, pausing after each step for class agreement.
  3. Open discussion — Question 1 (8 min) — classify the loan's likely progression through NPA categories and calculate indicative provisioning.
  4. Open discussion — Question 2 (8 min) — how a single large NPA affects a bank's CAMELS "Asset Quality" and "Earnings" components.
  5. Open discussion — Question 3 (7 min) — why consortium lending (multiple banks financing one borrower) complicates NPA classification.
  6. Wrap-up (5 min) — class collectively picks a recent large corporate NPA and sketches steps 1–5 for it.

1. Case Analysis Framework

  1. Identify the borrower and lending structure — single bank or consortium? What type(s) of bank were exposed (Topic 1)?
  2. Trace the NPA classification path — when did the account first turn NPA, and how did it move through sub-standard → doubtful → loss (Topic 4)?
  3. Calculate provisioning impact — using Topic 4's tiered provisioning rules, estimate the loss the lending banks had to absorb.
  4. Assess the financial statement impact — how would this show up in the lending banks' balance sheet and income statement (Topic 5)?
  5. Assess the CAMELS impact — which components (Topic 6) would be most affected, and why?

2. Worked Example: Kingfisher Airlines — A High-Profile NPA

2.1 Background

Kingfisher Airlines, once one of India's prominent private airlines, accumulated large debts from a consortium of Indian banks (led by State Bank of India) as its finances deteriorated through the early 2010s. The airline eventually ceased operations, and its loans became one of the most widely discussed NPA cases in Indian banking, referenced directly in Padmalatha & Paul's textbook as an illustrative high-profile NPA.

2.2 Lending structure

The exposure was spread across a consortium of public and private sector banks rather than concentrated in one lender. Per Topic 4's asset-classification rules, consortium lending is classified based on the record of recovery of each individual member bank — meaning different banks in the same consortium could, in principle, classify their exposure to the same borrower differently depending on their own collection experience, even though the underlying borrower is the same.

2.3 NPA classification path

As repayments stopped, the loan would have followed the standard progression: once interest/principal remained overdue beyond 90 days, the account became an NPA and was classified sub-standard. Once it remained in that category beyond 12 months without recovery, it moved to doubtful. Given the scale of the airline's financial distress and the erosion in value of pledged assets (including brand/trademark collateral, whose realizable value proved far lower than book value), portions of the exposure would likely have met the "erosion in security value" trigger from Topic 4 — pushing classification straight toward doubtful or loss treatment for the affected portion, rather than working through the full 12-month sub-standard window.

2.4 Financial statement and CAMELS impact

For each lending bank, this NPA would have required: reversing any previously-recognized accrued interest income (Topic 4's income-recognition rule), raising loan-loss provisions (hitting the income statement's "provisions" line before arriving at operating income — Topic 5), and reducing net advances on the balance sheet. At the CAMELS level (Topic 6), the exposure directly worsens Asset Quality (higher NPA ratio) and Earnings (higher provisioning expense reduces profitability) — and, if the exposure was large relative to the bank's capital base, could also pressure Capital Adequacy.

3. Discussion / Practice Questions

  1. Why might different banks in the same lending consortium classify their exposure to Kingfisher Airlines differently? (Applied)
    Show model answer
    RBI's asset classification norms state that for consortium lending, classification should be based on the record of recovery of the individual member bank, not a single consortium-wide determination. Since different banks may have different repayment/recovery experiences with the same borrower (e.g. different security interests, different negotiation outcomes, different timing of last payment received), each bank applies the 90-day/12-month rules to its own facility, which can legitimately produce different classifications across consortium members for what is nominally "the same" loan.
  2. How would a large NPA like this affect a lending bank's CAMELS rating? (Essay)
    Show model answer
    Asset Quality worsens directly, since the NPA raises the bank's proportion of impaired loans relative to total advances. Earnings worsens because the required provisioning (potentially 100% for the unsecured portion, tiered up to 100% for the secured portion over time) is charged against operating income, reducing profitability. If the exposure is large relative to the bank's capital base, Capital Adequacy can also come under pressure, since absorbing the loss erodes the bank's capital cushion. Depending on how the bank's management responded (recognition timing, workout strategy), Management quality could also be scrutinized by regulators.
  3. What must happen to previously-recognized interest income once a loan like this turns NPA? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Per RBI's income recognition rules (Topic 4), any interest, fees, or commission that had already been credited to the bank's income account in past periods on an accrual basis must be reversed once the account becomes an NPA — the bank cannot continue reporting income it recognized before the loan showed signs of impairment, since income from NPAs must be recognized only on a cash (actually received) basis going forward.
  4. Choose a large corporate NPA case you are familiar with and repeat steps 1–5 of the case-analysis framework for it. (Applied / open-ended)
    Show model answer
    Open-ended — no single correct answer. A strong response identifies the lending structure (single bank or consortium), traces the likely NPA classification path with approximate dates/durations, estimates provisioning using Topic 4's tiered rules, describes the balance sheet/income statement impact, and identifies which CAMELS components were most affected and why.

Capital Adequacy: The Basel Framework and CRAR

Unit II · Topic 1

1. Overview

How much capital should a bank be required to hold? Too little, and the bank can't absorb losses before failing; too much, and it can't lend profitably. The Basel Accords are the international regulator community's successive attempts to answer this question precisely, and every Indian bank's capital position is ultimately measured against them.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 The basic capital adequacy ratio

At its core, capital adequacy is simply: Regulatory Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets (RWAs). The numerator (capital) and denominator (RWAs) have each been the subject of increasingly sophisticated definition across three successive Accords:

  • Numerator (capital) — not just book equity; the Accords define "regulatory capital" as instruments genuinely capable of absorbing losses, split into tiers (Tier 1: shareholders' equity and retained earnings; Tier 2: supplementary capital).
  • Denominator (risk-weighted assets) — each asset is assigned a risk weight (by the regulator or the bank's own approved internal models) reflecting how risky it is; safer assets carry a lower weight, riskier ones higher. Off-balance-sheet items are converted to a credit-equivalent amount first, via "credit conversion factors," then risk-weighted the same way.

2.2 Basel I (1988)

Required internationally active banks to hold capital equal to at least 8% of risk-weighted assets, with at least half of that in Tier 1 form. Used a simple "bucket" approach — assets classified into four risk-weight buckets (0%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100%) based on asset type, not the borrower's actual risk. Adopted by 100+ countries in the 1990s, but criticized as "one-size-fits-all": a flat 8% charge regardless of the actual creditworthiness of the specific borrower encouraged banks to move high-quality assets off their books, and the framework ignored credit-risk-mitigation techniques and portfolio diversification benefits.

2.3 Basel II — three pillars

Pillar 1
Minimum Capital Requirements
(Credit + Market + Operational Risk)
Pillar 2
Supervisory Review Process
Pillar 3
Market Discipline & Disclosure

Basel II replaced the crude bucket system with a spectrum of approaches from simple to advanced, and — crucially — extended the minimum capital requirement to cover market risk and operational risk alongside credit risk:

  • Credit risk — Standardized approach (risk weight from external credit ratings; e.g. a BBB-rated corporate borrower attracts a 100% risk weight, so regulatory capital = 8% × 100% × exposure), or Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approaches (Foundation/Advanced) where banks use their own estimates of Probability of Default, Loss Given Default, and Exposure at Default.
  • Market risk — losses from movements in interest rates, equities, forex, and commodities; measured via standardized or internal-models approaches.
  • Operational risk — losses from failed internal processes, people, systems, or external events (e.g. fraud); measured via the Basic Indicator Approach (a flat 15% of average gross income), the Standardized Approach (business-line-specific percentages), or the Advanced Measurement Approach (statistical/internal models).

Overall minimum capital ratio under Basel II remained 8%, but the risk-weighting became far more risk-sensitive than Basel I's flat buckets. Pillar 2 requires banks to set internal capital targets aligned to their own risk profile, subject to supervisory review; Pillar 3 requires enhanced public disclosure of capital adequacy and risk-assessment methods to strengthen market discipline.

2.4 Basel III — response to the 2007–08 crisis

Basel II's risk-sensitivity, while an improvement, proved insufficient to prevent the 2007–08 global financial crisis. Basel III's central innovation is tightening the definition and quality of the numerator (capital) — most notably introducing Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) as the highest-quality capital component, alongside additional capital buffers and, separately, new global liquidity standards. Unlike Basel I/II (which focused mainly on the risk-weighting denominator), Basel III largely carries forward the existing RWA methodology while raising the bar on what counts as loss-absorbing capital.

2.5 CRAR in India

India adopted a minimum Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 9% from 2000 — a full percentage point above the 8% international Basel norm, reflecting RBI's deliberately conservative stance. India's roadmap for Basel III implementation was formalized in 2012, phasing in the higher-quality capital and additional buffers over subsequent years.

3. Key Terms

Risk-Weighted Assets (RWAs)
A bank's assets (and credit-equivalent off-balance-sheet exposures), each multiplied by a risk weight reflecting its riskiness — the denominator of the capital adequacy ratio.
Tier 1 / Tier 2 capital
Tier 1 = core capital (shareholders' equity, retained earnings); Tier 2 = supplementary capital of lower quality/permanence.
CRAR
Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio — India's term for the capital adequacy ratio; minimum 9% since 2000 (above the 8% Basel norm).
Pillar 1 / 2 / 3 (Basel II)
Minimum capital requirements / supervisory review / market discipline and disclosure — the three mutually reinforcing pillars of Basel II.
Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1)
The highest-quality capital component introduced under Basel III.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Capital adequacy ratio = Regulatory Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets.
  • Basel I (1988): flat 8% minimum, simple risk buckets, "one-size-fits-all," no borrower-specific risk sensitivity.
  • Basel II: 3 pillars (minimum capital / supervisory review / market discipline); extends capital requirement to credit + market + operational risk; Standardized vs. IRB approaches; still 8% minimum.
  • Basel III: tightens the definition of capital (introduces CET1), adds capital buffers and liquidity standards, in response to the 2007–08 crisis.
  • India's CRAR: minimum 9% since 2000 (above Basel's 8%); Basel III roadmap formalized 2012.

Practice Questions

  1. Define the capital adequacy ratio and explain what the numerator and denominator each represent. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The capital adequacy ratio is regulatory capital divided by risk-weighted assets. The numerator (capital) is defined by the Basel Accords as instruments genuinely able to absorb losses, split into Tier 1 (core equity/retained earnings) and Tier 2 (supplementary capital). The denominator (risk-weighted assets) is each asset's value multiplied by a risk weight reflecting how risky it is, including credit-equivalent amounts for off-balance-sheet exposures.
  2. What was the main criticism of Basel I, and how did Basel II address it? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Basel I used a simple "bucket" approach that assigned risk weights based on broad asset type rather than the actual risk of the specific borrower — a flat 8% capital charge regardless of creditworthiness, which encouraged banks to move high-quality assets off their balance sheets and ignored diversification benefits. Basel II addressed this through its three-pillar structure: Pillar 1 introduced more risk-sensitive measurement (Standardized approach using external credit ratings, or Internal Ratings-Based approaches using the bank's own risk estimates) and extended minimum capital requirements to cover market and operational risk, not just credit risk; Pillar 2 required supervisory review of each bank's internal capital targets; Pillar 3 required enhanced public disclosure to strengthen market discipline.
  3. What is CRAR, and how does India's minimum requirement compare to the international Basel norm? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    CRAR (Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio) is India's term for the capital adequacy ratio. India has required a minimum CRAR of 9% since 2000 — one percentage point higher than the 8% international Basel minimum — reflecting a deliberately more conservative regulatory stance.
  4. How did Basel III's approach differ from Basel I and II's focus? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Basel I and II focused primarily on refining the denominator — how risk-weighted assets are measured. Basel III, developed in response to the 2007–08 financial crisis, largely carried forward the existing risk-weighting methodology and instead focused on tightening the numerator — the definition and quality of capital itself — most notably introducing Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) as the highest-quality capital component, alongside new capital buffers and separate global liquidity standards.

Deposit and Non-Deposit Sources: Designing and Pricing Deposit Schemes

Unit II · Topic 2

1. Overview

Deposits are a bank's raw material — and, like any raw material, getting the price wrong (too high, and margins vanish; too low, and depositors leave) directly threatens profitability. This topic covers the main funding sources banks draw on, and the pricing techniques used to balance competitiveness against cost.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Deposit and non-deposit sources

Banks fund themselves primarily through deposits (demand, savings, term — Unit I, Topic 5) but also draw on non-deposit sources when the deposit base isn't enough to fund lending growth — interbank borrowings, refinance from institutions like NABARD/SIDBI, certificates of deposit, and market borrowings. The gap between what deposits can fund and what a bank wants to lend is its funding gap, which non-deposit sources exist to bridge.

2.2 Five approaches to deposit pricing

ApproachLogic
Cost-plus margin pricingPrice = operating expense per unit of deposit service + allocated overhead + planned profit margin. Ties pricing directly to the bank's own costs — the discipline behind fees for excess withdrawals, balance enquiries, returned cheques, etc.
Market penetration pricingOffer above-market interest rates or below-market fees to aggressively capture market share in high-growth segments, betting that the resulting volume of funds and cross-sell opportunities offsets thinner margins.
Conditional pricingInterest rates/fees are tiered by deposit size or account activity — larger balances get better rates/lower fees, encouraging customers to keep higher average balances. Lets the customer effectively select into the plan suited to them.
Upscale target pricingAggressive, carefully designed pricing/advertising aimed at high-income customers (business owners, professionals) who are price-sensitive and respond quickly to rate differentials.
Relationship pricingFees depend on the breadth and intensity of a customer's overall relationship with the bank (multiple products used), not just one product in isolation — aims to build "convenience" loyalty that makes the customer less price-sensitive.

2.3 The marginal cost of funds approach

Before matching a competitor's rate hike, banks should analyze the true marginal cost of protecting deposits, not just the headline rate.

Worked example

Bank J has ₹250 crore in rate-sensitive premium deposits, currently paying 5%. A rival offers 6%. If Bank J does nothing, it expects to lose ₹50 crore of that base. Two costs arise from matching the rate instead: (1) paying 6% on the ₹50 crore it would otherwise have lost (₹3 crore), and (2) paying the extra 1% on the ₹200 crore that would have stayed anyway (₹2 crore). Total additional cost: ₹5 crore — against just ₹50 crore of deposits actually at risk. That works out to a marginal cost of 10% (₹5 crore ÷ ₹50 crore) — double the nominal 5% rate — because the bank must pay the higher rate to loyal depositors who were never going to leave, not just to those it's trying to retain.

This is why headline rate-matching can be far more expensive than it first appears, and why banks model multiple scenarios (different rate increases × different assumed deposit-loss percentages) before deciding whether, and by how much, to raise rates.

2.4 Designing deposit schemes

Common deposit scheme designs include: Recurring Deposits (RD) (fixed periodic installments over a term), Reinvestment Deposit Schemes (interest is compounded and reinvested rather than paid out), Fixed Deposit Schemes (FD) (lump-sum, fixed tenure, fixed rate), and Cash Certificates (a discounted-issue instrument, similar in spirit to a zero-coupon deposit). Design choices interact directly with pricing strategy — e.g. a reinvestment scheme's compounding structure is itself a form of conditional/relationship pricing, rewarding depositors who commit funds for longer.

3. Key Terms

Funding gap
The difference between what a bank's deposit base can fund and what it wants to lend — bridged by non-deposit sources.
Marginal cost of funds
The true incremental cost of retaining a targeted deposit segment when raising rates, which includes the extra rate paid to depositors who wouldn't have left anyway — often much higher than the nominal rate increase suggests.
Conditional pricing
Tiering deposit rates/fees by balance size or activity level so customers effectively self-select into the plan suited to them.
Relationship pricing
Pricing based on the breadth/intensity of a customer's overall relationship with the bank, aimed at building loyalty beyond any single product's price.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • 5 deposit pricing approaches: Cost-plus margin, Market penetration, Conditional, Upscale target, Relationship.
  • Marginal cost of funds approach: true cost of matching a rate hike includes both the higher rate paid to at-risk depositors AND the higher rate paid to loyal depositors who wouldn't have left — often making the effective marginal cost far higher than the nominal rate change.
  • Deposit scheme types: Recurring Deposit, Reinvestment Deposit, Fixed Deposit, Cash Certificates.
  • Non-deposit sources (interbank borrowing, refinance, CDs, market borrowings) bridge the "funding gap" when deposits alone can't fund desired lending growth.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain cost-plus margin deposit pricing and give two examples of fees it has led banks to introduce. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Cost-plus margin pricing sets the deposit price to cover operating expense per unit of service, allocated overhead, and a planned profit margin — tying price directly to the bank's own costs. It has led banks to introduce fees for things like excessive withdrawals from transaction accounts and charges for cheques returned unpaid, since these activities have a real cost to the bank that flat, cost-unaware pricing would otherwise not recover.
  2. Using the Bank J example, explain why the "marginal cost" of protecting a deposit segment can be much higher than the nominal interest rate. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    When a bank raises its rate to retain deposits, it must pay the higher rate not only to the customers actually at risk of leaving, but also to all the other customers in that same rate-sensitive segment who would have stayed regardless. In the Bank J example, matching a 1% rate rise to protect ₹50 crore of at-risk deposits costs ₹3 crore on that ₹50 crore plus ₹2 crore paid unnecessarily to the ₹200 crore of loyal depositors — ₹5 crore total against ₹50 crore of deposits genuinely at risk, a 10% marginal cost, double the nominal 5% rate the deposits originally cost. This is why banks must model the true marginal cost, not just the headline rate, before deciding whether to match a competitor.
  3. Distinguish between market penetration pricing and relationship pricing. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Market penetration pricing offers above-market rates or below-market fees to aggressively capture market share, betting that the resulting volume of funds offsets thinner margins. Relationship pricing instead bases fees on the breadth and intensity of a customer's overall relationship with the bank across multiple products, aiming to build loyalty that makes the customer less sensitive to any single product's price — the two target different goals (rapid growth vs. long-term retention).
