Loan Management and Investment Management

Unit II · Topic 3

1. Overview

Loans and investments together make up the bulk of a bank's assets and its interest income. Loan management is about pricing credit correctly for its risk; investment management is about balancing safety, liquidity, and yield in the securities portfolio the bank holds alongside its loan book.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Loan pricing — the basic model

Loan pricing parallels product pricing (price must cover variable costs, a share of fixed costs, and a profit margin) but with two key differences: every loan carries a unique risk profile that must be quantified and priced individually, and price also depends on the customer's overall profitability to the bank (relationship pricing) — so two borrowers with identical risk can still be priced differently. At minimum:

Loan price = Cost of funds + Servicing costs + Risk premium + Desired profit margin

2.2 Building the model step by step

StepWhat it determines
1. Cost of fundsEither the bank's average cost of funds, or the cost of funds with matching maturity if it must source fresh funds for this specific loan — the choice depends on the bank's investment policy.
2. Servicing costsCost of all credit and non-credit services the customer uses (loan administration, transfers, custodial services etc.), usually expressed as a percentage of loan size for credit services.
3. Risk premiumDerived from the probability of default (PD) and loss given default, via credit scoring; the gap between the contracted rate and the statistically expected rate is the risk premium.
4. Profit marginOften set using the bank's target Return on Equity: since ROE = ROA × Equity Multiplier, desired minimum return on assets = target ROE × (Capital ÷ Assets).

Worked example — cost of funds (Illustration 5.1 style)

A bank's average cost of funds is 8.30%, and it wants a 3% profit margin: Loan price = 8.30 + 3.00 = 11.30%. But if the bank must instead borrow fresh 3-year funds at 12% to match the loan's maturity, Loan price = 12 + 3 = 15% — the same loan can be priced very differently depending on whether the bank uses its average cost of funds or the marginal, maturity-matched cost.

Worked example — risk premium

A bank wants to quote 14% on a loan, believes there's a 95% probability of full repayment, and expects to recover 85% of principal and interest in the event of default. The expected rate works out to about 13.27% — 0.73 percentage points below the contracted 14%. That 0.73% gap is the risk premium. Adding cost of funds (12%) + servicing costs (0.25%) + risk premium (0.73%) + desired profit (3%) gives a minimum price of about 15.98% for this borrower.

2.3 Objectives of the investment portfolio

Alongside loans, banks hold a securities investment portfolio to meet several objectives simultaneously: safety of capital (low-default-risk securities offset loan-book credit risk), liquidity (marketable securities can be sold to meet unanticipated deposit demands without market borrowing), yield (a risk-return tradeoff against the safer, more liquid holdings), diversification of credit risk (spreading exposure beyond the bank's loan-concentration sectors/geographies), managing interest rate risk exposure (a securities portfolio's duration can be adjusted far more quickly than a loan portfolio's), and meeting pledging requirements (marketable securities qualify as collateral for the bank's own borrowings). No single portfolio can maximize all of these at once — regulators resolve the tension by mandating how banks classify and account for their holdings.

2.4 The three regulatory investment categories

CategoryObjectiveAccounting treatment
Held to Maturity (HTM)Purchased to hold until maturity.Carried at amortized cost; unrealized gains/losses from market fluctuation do not hit the income statement while held. Capped at 25% of the bank's total investments in India, with SLR securities under HTM further capped (22.5%/22% under RBI norms).
Held for Trading (HFT)Purchased with intent to sell in the near term, profiting from price/rate movements.Carried at market value; unrealized gains/losses do impact the income statement. Marked to market monthly or more often.
Available for Sale (AFS)The residual category — securities not classified as HTM or HFT.Carried at market value like HFT. Marked to market quarterly or more often.

Banks may shift investments to/from HTM only once a year with Board approval, and from AFS to HFT with Board/ALCO approval — but shifting from HFT to AFS is generally not allowed except in exceptional circumstances. This asymmetry prevents banks from using reclassification to dodge mark-to-market losses.

2.5 The treasury function

A bank's treasury manages the investment/trading book and is a significant profit center in its own right. Core treasury functions include investment advice to customers, managing the bank's own liquidity and asset-liability position, trading in currencies and securities, and developing new treasury products — all while identifying and mitigating market risk (risk from movements in interest rates, exchange rates, and security/commodity values).

3. Key Terms

Relationship pricing
Pricing a loan based partly on the borrower's overall profitability/relationship to the bank, not just risk — so identical-risk borrowers can get different prices.
Risk premium
The gap between a loan's contracted interest rate and its statistically expected rate given probability of default and recovery — compensates the bank for credit risk.
HTM / HFT / AFS
The three RBI-mandated categories for classifying a bank's investment portfolio, based on holding intent, each with different accounting/mark-to-market treatment.
Treasury
The bank function responsible for investment, trading, and liquidity/interest-rate-risk management on the securities and currency books.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Loan price = cost of funds + servicing costs + risk premium + desired profit margin; every loan is individually risk-priced, unlike standard product pricing.
  • Cost of funds can be the bank's average cost, or the marginal/maturity-matched cost — choice depends on investment policy and materially changes the quoted rate.
  • Risk premium = gap between contracted rate and statistically expected rate (from PD and loss-given-default).
  • Profit margin can be set via ROE: target ROA = target ROE × (Capital ÷ Assets).
  • Investment portfolio objectives: safety, liquidity, yield, credit-risk diversification, interest-rate-risk flexibility, pledging/collateral.
  • Three RBI categories: HTM (amortized cost, capped ~25% of investments), HFT (market value, marked monthly), AFS (market value, marked quarterly) — reclassification from HFT to AFS is restricted.

Practice Questions

  1. State the basic loan pricing formula and explain the two key differences between loan pricing and pricing a physical product. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Loan price = cost of funds + servicing costs + risk premium + desired profit margin. Two differences from product pricing: (1) every loan has a unique risk profile that must be individually quantified and priced, so a single price cannot be applied uniformly across a loan "product line"; (2) price also depends on the borrower's overall profitability/relationship with the bank (relationship pricing), so two borrowers with identical risk profiles can still receive different prices.
  2. A bank's average cost of funds is 9%, but it must source fresh 5-year funds at 13% to fund a specific large loan request, matching maturity. If its desired profit margin is 2.5%, what rate should it quote under each cost-of-funds approach, and which is more realistic for this transaction? (Numerical / long answer)
    Show model answer
    Using average cost of funds: 9 + 2.5 = 11.5%. Using matched-maturity marginal cost of funds: 13 + 2.5 = 15.5%. Since the bank must actually raise fresh 5-year funds to fund this specific loan, the marginal/matched-maturity approach (15.5%) is the economically realistic price — using the average cost would understate the true cost of funding this transaction and could cause a loss, even though the bank may choose to quote lower to retain the customer.
  3. Distinguish between the Held to Maturity, Held for Trading, and Available for Sale investment categories in terms of purpose and accounting treatment. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    HTM securities are bought with the intent to hold until maturity; they are carried at amortized cost, so unrealized market-value gains/losses do not affect the income statement while held, and India caps HTM holdings at around 25% of total investments. HFT securities are bought to sell in the near term to profit from price movements; they are carried at market value with unrealized gains/losses hitting the income statement, marked to market monthly or more often. AFS is the residual category for securities not classified as HTM or HFT; like HFT, they are carried at market value, but marked to market only quarterly or more often. Reclassification rules are asymmetric: banks may shift into/out of HTM once a year and from AFS to HFT with Board approval, but shifting from HFT back to AFS is generally restricted, preventing banks from dodging mark-to-market losses through reclassification.
  4. List the six objectives banks pursue through their investment portfolio, and explain why no single portfolio can maximize all of them simultaneously. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The six objectives are: safety of capital, liquidity, yield, diversification of credit risk, managing interest rate risk exposure, and meeting pledging requirements. They conflict because, for example, the safest and most liquid securities typically yield the least (a risk-return tradeoff), while higher-yield securities carry more price risk — so a portfolio manager must balance these competing goals rather than optimize any single one, which is why regulators mandate a categorized (HTM/HFT/AFS) approach rather than leaving the mix entirely to the bank.

Asset and Liability Management (ALM)

Unit II · Topic 4

1. Overview

A bank's capital is small relative to its total assets and liabilities, so even small mismatches between how those assets and liabilities behave can translate into large swings in capital — an inherently "leveraged" risk. Asset-Liability Management (ALM) is the discipline of managing the whole balance sheet together, rather than assets and liabilities separately, to control this risk.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Why ALM emerged

Traditionally, banks used accrual (book-value) accounting for both sides of the balance sheet, which didn't recognize the risk arising from how assets and liabilities were structured or how markets were moving. ALM evolved in the 1980s as a way to manage this risk without fully switching to market-value accounting (which isn't suitable for all bank business lines — a bank can show mark-to-market profits yet fail from inadequate cash flow). ALM is concerned with strategic balance sheet management: monitoring and mitigating risks from interest rate and exchange rate movements, credit risk, and liquidity position together, rather than managing assets (credit, NPAs) and liabilities (deposits) as separate silos.

2.2 The ALCO

Banks run this function through an Asset Liability Management Committee (ALCO) — senior/top management tasked with balancing the bank's risk exposures to meet its operating objectives. The ALCO reviews reports spanning economic conditions, interest rate forecasts, current loan/deposit mix and concentrated exposures, projected cash inflows/outflows, current and projected liquidity position, and the potential effect of interest rate risk on income and capital. It works through scenario analysis — e.g. unexpectedly large deposit withdrawals, early/late/non-repayment of loans, sudden rate moves, or counterparties failing to honor commitments — assessing the probability of each and positioning the bank to handle the likely ones at minimum cost. Most ALCOs focus primarily on liquidity risk and interest rate risk; credit risk is typically handled by a separate committee.

Traditional ALMModern ALM
Focus on short-term earningsFocus on earnings and value
Subjective scenarios based on parallel rate shiftsObjective, statistical-model-based scenarios complemented by subjective ones
Focus on home-currency interest rate riskIncludes forex, basis, credit, commodity, and equity risk factors
Static, scenario-independent portfolio assumptionDynamic balance sheet evaluation incorporating growth forecasts, reinvestment, and hedging

2.3 Interest rate risk — the earnings perspective

Interest rate risk is exposure of the bank's financial condition to adverse rate movements. It can be assessed from two perspectives: the earnings perspective (short-term impact on Net Interest Income) and the economic value perspective (long-term impact on the bank's underlying value). The earnings perspective is the traditional and more commonly examined one.

2.4 GAP analysis

The standard tool for the earnings perspective is static GAP analysis. Assets and liabilities are sorted into maturity/repricing time buckets, and within each bucket:

GAP = Rate Sensitive Assets (RSA) − Rate Sensitive Liabilities (RSL)
GAP signBank is termedNII rises when rates...NII falls when rates...
Positive (RSA > RSL)Asset-sensitiveRiseFall
Negative (RSL > RSA)Liability-sensitiveFallRise
Zero (RSA = RSL)MatchedNo change either way — income and expense move by equal amounts

This is summarized by the formula:

ΔNII (expected) = GAP × Δr (expected)

The sign of the GAP indicates the direction of NII change for a given rate move, and its magnitude indicates how much interest rate risk the bank is carrying — allowing the ALCO to deliberately position GAP based on its rate-movement forecast.

Worked example — GAP ratio

Bank A and Bank B both hold ₹1,000 crore total assets. Bank A has RSAs of ₹40 crore and RSLs of ₹20 crore (GAP = ₹20 crore, GAP ratio = 2). Bank B has RSAs of ₹400 crore and RSLs of ₹200 crore (GAP = ₹200 crore, GAP ratio = 2). Both banks have the identical GAP ratio, but Bank B's absolute GAP (₹200 crore) is ten times Bank A's (₹20 crore) — meaning Bank B carries far more interest rate risk in absolute NII terms despite the ratio being the same. This shows why the GAP ratio and the absolute GAP amount must both be examined together.

2.5 Limitations of GAP analysis

  • Assumes everything within a time bucket reprices simultaneously (aggregation reduces precision).
  • Ignores basis risk — different instruments tied to different reference rates/indexes that don't move in lockstep.
  • Ignores the time value of money and within-bucket timing of cash flows — a "zero GAP" position can still create losses if overnight funding finances a slightly longer asset.
  • Short-term focus misses the long-term impact on fixed-rate assets/liabilities.
  • Rate sensitivity of non-interest-bearing liabilities (e.g. demand deposits) is hard to estimate but not truly zero.
  • Ignores embedded options — early withdrawal by depositors, prepayment/foreclosure by borrowers — which can alter the GAP when exercised.
  • Fails to capture rate-driven variability in non-interest revenue and expenses.

Despite these limitations, GAP analysis remains widely used for its simplicity and transparency — it identifies exactly which balance sheet items drive the risk, even though it only gives a rough approximation of the actual NII impact.

3. Key Terms

ALCO
Asset Liability Management Committee — senior management group responsible for managing a bank's liquidity and interest rate risk across the whole balance sheet.
Rate Sensitive Assets/Liabilities (RSA/RSL)
Assets or liabilities that reprice or mature within a given time bucket, and are therefore sensitive to interest rate changes in that period.
GAP
RSA minus RSL for a given time bucket; positive = asset-sensitive, negative = liability-sensitive, zero = matched.
Basis risk
The risk that different instruments tied to different reference rates/indexes do not move together, undermining the precision of GAP analysis.
Economic value perspective
An interest-rate-risk assessment approach focused on long-term impact on the bank's underlying value, as opposed to the earnings perspective's short-term NII focus.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • ALM = strategic, integrated management of the whole balance sheet, evolved in the 1980s as an alternative to full market-value accounting.
  • ALCO manages liquidity and interest rate risk primarily; credit risk usually sits with a separate committee.
  • GAP = RSA − RSL; positive GAP = asset-sensitive (benefits from rate rises); negative GAP = liability-sensitive (benefits from rate falls); zero GAP = matched.
  • ΔNII (expected) = GAP × Δr (expected).
  • GAP ratio = RSA/RSL — must be read alongside the absolute GAP amount, since two banks can share a ratio but differ hugely in absolute risk.
  • Key GAP limitations: ignores basis risk, timing within buckets, embedded options, and non-interest income/expense sensitivity.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is a bank's balance sheet risk described as a "leveraged" risk? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Because a bank's capital is small relative to its total assets and liabilities, small percentage changes in the value of assets or liabilities can translate into large percentage changes in capital — especially since asset and liability values do not always move together. This magnification effect is why asset-liability risk is called "leveraged."
  2. A bank has RSAs of ₹500 crore and RSLs of ₹700 crore in the 0–90 day bucket. If interest rates are expected to rise by 1%, what happens to NII, and is this bank asset-sensitive or liability-sensitive? (Numerical / short answer)
    Show model answer
    GAP = RSA − RSL = 500 − 700 = −₹200 crore (negative GAP), making the bank liability-sensitive. Using ΔNII = GAP × Δr = −200 × 1% = −₹2 crore, so NII is expected to decrease by about ₹2 crore if rates rise by 1%, because more liabilities than assets reprice upward, raising interest expense more than interest income.
  3. Explain any three limitations of static GAP analysis as a measure of interest rate risk. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    (1) It assumes all positions within a time bucket reprice simultaneously, which aggregates instruments with genuinely different repricing dates and reduces precision. (2) It ignores basis risk — instruments tied to different reference rates/indexes may not move together even when nominally in the same bucket. (3) It ignores the timing of cash flows within a bucket and the time value of money — a nominally "zero GAP" position (e.g. a 1-month T-bill funded by overnight borrowing) can still expose the bank to loss if overnight rates rise before the offsetting position matures. Other valid limitations: it misses long-term effects on fixed-rate items, underestimates the true rate sensitivity of non-interest-bearing liabilities like demand deposits, ignores embedded options (early withdrawal, prepayment), and fails to capture rate-driven variability in non-interest income/expense.
  4. Distinguish between the earnings perspective and the economic value perspective on interest rate risk. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The earnings perspective assesses the short-term impact of interest rate changes on Net Interest Income (interest earned minus interest paid) and is the traditional method of risk assessment. The economic value perspective instead looks at the long-term impact of rate changes on the underlying economic value of the bank's assets, liabilities, and off-balance-sheet instruments. Both are needed because a bank could look healthy on one measure while deteriorating on the other.

Financial Distress: Signals to Borrowers and Predictive Models

Unit II · Topic 5

1. Overview

Bank profitability depends heavily on catching borrower trouble early. This topic covers how a firm slides into financial distress, the early warning signals banks watch for, and the statistical models — chiefly Altman's Z-Score — used to predict bankruptcy before it happens.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 What is financial distress?

Financial failure occurs after a prolonged period of lack of profitability, most visibly through decaying cash inflows — even while the balance sheet still shows healthy current and fixed assets. Common disguises: receivables that look fine on paper but aren't realizable, inventory that is high in quantity but poor in quality and non-moving (not written off due to low profitability), and fixed assets whose book value hasn't been written down despite rapidly falling market value. If this continues, economic failure follows: the return on investments drops below the cost of capital, and the market value of liabilities exceeds the market value of assets — insolvency.

2.2 Three categories of borrower sickness

CategoryCause
Sickness at birthThe project itself was infeasible from the start — faulty assumptions or a changed environment.
Induced sicknessCaused by management incompetence or willful default.
Genuine sicknessCircumstances beyond the borrower's control, despite sincere efforts to avert it.

When a borrower turns "sick," the bank must investigate: the reasons for sickness and whether remedial measures can revive the firm; the rationale for the sick classification; the risks in rehabilitating the firm; and, if rehabilitation is chosen, what additional financing, government support, management inputs, or technology upgrades it needs.

2.3 Warning signals of incipient sickness

  • Continuous irregularities in cash credit/overdraft accounts — inability to maintain the stipulated margin, funds drawn repeatedly exceeding the sanctioned limit, or periodical interest remaining unrealized.
  • Outstanding balance in the cash credit account continuously at the maximum.
  • Failure to make timely payment of principal/interest installments on term loans.
  • Complaints from suppliers (raw materials, power, water) about non-payment of bills.
  • Danger of violating loan covenants — and how critical such violations would be for debt service and the long-term relationship.

2.4 Altman's Z-Score model

The most widely used and thoroughly tested model for predicting corporate bankruptcy, built via discriminant analysis:

Z = 1.2X1 + 1.4X2 + 3.3X3 + 0.6X4 + 1.0X5
VariableDefinition
X1Working capital ÷ Total assets
X2Retained earnings ÷ Total assets
X3EBIT ÷ Total assets
X4Market value of equity ÷ Book value of debt
X5Sales ÷ Total assets (times)

Classification: Z > 2.99 → financially sound; Z < 1.81 → financially distressed/bankrupt (the 1.81–2.99 band is a "grey zone"). Note that total assets is the denominator in four of the five ratios, tying the model closely to operating leverage and asset utilization: high operating leverage means a small sales decline drives a disproportionately large EBIT decline, which lowers retained earnings, which lowers working capital, which depresses the market's view of equity value relative to debt — a chain reaction that shows up as a falling Z-score.

Important limitations

The original Z-Score assumes the firm's equity is publicly traded and that it is a manufacturing firm — it doesn't directly apply to private or non-manufacturing/emerging-market firms.

2.5 Alternate and later models

ModelKey feature
ZETA scoreExtends prediction to non-manufacturing firms; gives warning 3–5 years before bankruptcy (vs. Z-Score's ~2 years). Uses ROA, earnings stability, debt service, cumulative profitability, current ratio, capitalization, and firm size.
Emerging Market Scoring (EMS) modelAltman, Hartzell & Peck (1995) adaptation for countries lacking enough local credit-history data to build a domestic model; applicable to both manufacturing/non-manufacturing and private/public firms; the raw EM score is then adjusted for currency-devaluation vulnerability, industry environment, and competitive position.
Gambler's ruin approachCombines net liquidation value (asset liquidation value minus liabilities) with net cash flows; lower liquidation value + smaller/more volatile cash flows → higher failure probability.
Logit / probit / neural networks / CARTLater statistical and machine-learning approaches developed to improve on discriminant analysis's accuracy.

2.6 Restructuring as a workout response

When a borrower shows genuine distress, banks may grant restructuring concessions they would not otherwise offer — modifying repayment period, repayable amount, installment size, or interest rate. RBI restructuring guidelines are grouped by borrower type: industrial units (including the Corporate Debt Restructuring/CDR mechanism), SMEs, and all other advances. This "workout function," what the Basel Committee terms forbearance, was revamped from 2003 after the earlier BIFR/Sick Industrial Companies Act framework failed to help banks actually recover their dues.

3. Key Terms

Economic failure
State where return on investment falls below cost of capital and market value of liabilities exceeds market value of assets — i.e. insolvency.
Z-Score
Altman's discriminant-analysis model predicting bankruptcy from five financial ratios; Z > 2.99 = sound, Z < 1.81 = distressed.
Operating leverage
The degree to which a small change in sales produces a disproportionately large change in net operating income — central to why the Z-Score behaves the way it does.
Restructuring
Bank-granted concessions on credit terms (repayment period, rate, installment) for a borrower in genuine financial difficulty; termed "forbearance" by the Basel Committee.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Financial distress = prolonged unprofitability → decaying cash inflows despite a balance sheet that still looks healthy → economic failure/insolvency if unaddressed.
  • 3 sickness categories: at birth, induced, genuine.
  • Warning signals: CC/OD account irregularities, maxed-out balances, late installment payments, supplier complaints, covenant-violation risk.
  • Altman's Z-Score: Z = 1.2X1 + 1.4X2 + 3.3X3 + 0.6X4 + 1.0X5; Z>2.99 sound, Z<1.81 distressed; assumes publicly traded, manufacturing firm.
  • Alternate models: ZETA (non-manufacturing, earlier warning), EMS (emerging markets), gambler's ruin, logit/probit/neural nets/CART.
  • Restructuring/forbearance: concessions on troubled advances, categorized by borrower type (industrial/CDR, SME, other).

Practice Questions

  1. Explain how a firm can appear healthy on its balance sheet while actually being in financial distress. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    A firm's balance sheet can show healthy current and fixed asset levels even while cash inflows are decaying — for example, receivables may be high but unrealizable, inventory may look substantial but be poor-quality and non-moving without being written off due to low profitability, or fixed assets may not be adequately depreciated during a period of continuous losses, keeping their book value inflated even as market value falls. The result is a firm whose reported assets are not all realizable, masking the underlying distress until cash flows and revenues make the shortfall undeniable.
  2. State Altman's Z-Score formula, define its five variables, and explain the classification thresholds. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Z = 1.2X1 + 1.4X2 + 3.3X3 + 0.6X4 + 1.0X5, where X1 = working capital/total assets, X2 = retained earnings/total assets, X3 = EBIT/total assets, X4 = market value of equity/book value of debt, and X5 = sales/total assets. A firm is classified as financially sound if Z is greater than 2.99, and as financially distressed or bankrupt if Z is less than 1.81 (values in between fall in an ambiguous "grey zone"). The model assumes the firm's equity is publicly traded and that it operates in manufacturing.
  3. Why does the Z-Score model use total assets as the denominator in four of its five variables, and how does this connect to operating leverage? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Using total assets as the common denominator ties the model to asset utilization and operating leverage. For a firm with high operating leverage, a decline in sales causes a disproportionately large fall in EBIT, which lowers retained earnings and, in turn, working capital — pulling down the X1, X2, and X3 ratios together. The market also reacts negatively to these declining fundamentals, reducing the market value of equity while book value of debt stays roughly constant, so X4 falls too. This chain reaction, amplified by high operating leverage, shows up as a falling Z-score, which is why the model is considered grounded in real corporate-finance mechanics rather than being a purely statistical fit.
  4. What is restructuring, and how does it relate to the Basel Committee's concept of "forbearance"? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Restructuring is when a bank grants concessions on credit terms — such as altering the repayment period, repayable amount, installment size, or interest rate — to a borrower facing genuine financial difficulty, concessions the bank would not otherwise extend. The Basel Committee refers to this workout process for troubled loans as "forbearance." In India, restructuring guidelines are grouped by borrower category: industrial units (including under the Corporate Debt Restructuring mechanism), SMEs, and all other advances.

Risk Management I: Interest Rate, Forex, and Credit Risk

Unit II · Topic 6

1. Overview

Banks are, at their core, professional risk-takers — the business model itself is built on managing risk profitably rather than avoiding it. This topic covers three of the core risk categories every bank must actively monitor: interest rate risk, foreign exchange (and sovereign) risk, and credit/default risk.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Interest rate risk

Interest rate risk is the impact of changing market interest rates on a bank's profit margin — it bites when interest expenses on borrowed funds rise faster than interest revenues on loans/investments (or vice versa). Widely used exposure measures include:

  • Interest-sensitive assets ÷ Interest-sensitive liabilities — when rate-sensitive assets exceed rate-sensitive liabilities in a maturity range, the bank is vulnerable to falling rates; when RSLs exceed RSAs, it's vulnerable to rising rates (see the GAP analysis in Topic 4).
  • Uninsured deposits ÷ Total deposits — uninsured deposits (large government/corporate deposits above the insured limit) are highly rate-sensitive and can flee quickly if competitors offer even slightly higher yields.

Modern hedging tools against interest rate risk include interest-rate swaps, options, financial futures contracts, GAP management, and duration analysis.

2.2 Foreign exchange and sovereign risk

The global expansion of international finance opens new service markets but also exposes banks to loss from volatile foreign markets, changing government rules, and political instability abroad.

RiskDefinition
Foreign exchange riskFluctuating currency prices can reduce the value of a bank's foreign-currency-denominated assets, forcing a balance-sheet write-down.
Sovereign riskForeign governments facing domestic instability or armed conflict may lose the ability (or willingness) to service debts owed to international lenders — a risk distinct from the borrowing firm's own creditworthiness.

Bank treasuries manage this exposure by hedging — for example, banks may permit customers to hedge the exchange-rate risk on a foreign-currency loan by locking in the rate at which principal and interest will be converted, rather than bearing that risk themselves.

2.3 Credit (default) risk

Credit risk is the risk that a borrower or security issuer will default on principal or interest owed. It applies both to a bank's loan book and to its investment securities — regulators restrict banks to investment-grade securities (rated at least Baa/BBB) specifically to protect depositors from excessive credit risk on the securities side of the balance sheet.

Credit qualityMoody'sS&PBank-eligible?
Best qualityAaaAAAInvestment grade — acceptable for banks and other regulated financial firms
High gradeAaAA
Upper medium gradeAA
Medium gradeBaaBBB
Medium grade, speculative elementsBaBBSpeculative / "junk" — not suitable for banks
Lower medium gradeBB
Poor standing, may defaultCaaCCC
Speculative, often in defaultCaCC
Lowest grade / defaultedC / not ratedC / D

A common credit-risk exposure indicator for the loan book is Total loans ÷ Total deposits — since loans are typically the riskiest bank asset, a rising ratio signals growing depositor risk, especially if bad loans increase or good loans' market value declines.

3. Key Terms

Interest rate risk
The impact of changing market interest rates on a bank's profit margin, arising from a mismatch between rate-sensitive assets and liabilities.
Sovereign risk
The risk that a foreign government's instability or conflict impairs its ability to service debts owed to international lenders.
Investment-grade securities
Securities rated at least Baa (Moody's) or BBB (S&P) — the minimum credit quality most regulated banks are permitted to hold.
Total loans/Total deposits ratio
A traditional credit-risk exposure measure; a rising ratio signals greater depositor risk since loans are typically the riskiest bank asset.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Interest rate risk measured via RSA/RSL and uninsured-deposits/total-deposits ratios; hedged with swaps, options, futures, GAP management, duration.
  • Forex risk = currency fluctuation reducing foreign-currency asset values; sovereign risk = foreign government's own inability/unwillingness to honor debt due to instability.
  • Credit/default risk applies to both loans and investment securities; banks restricted to investment-grade (Baa/BBB or better) securities.
  • Total loans/total deposits ratio is a classic credit-risk exposure indicator.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain the two ratios commonly used to measure a bank's interest rate risk exposure. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The first is interest-sensitive assets divided by interest-sensitive liabilities within a maturity range: if rate-sensitive assets exceed rate-sensitive liabilities, the bank is vulnerable to losses from falling rates, while the reverse makes it vulnerable to rising rates. The second is uninsured deposits divided by total deposits — uninsured deposits (typically large government/corporate deposits above the insured threshold) are highly rate-sensitive and prone to rapid withdrawal if competing yields rise even slightly, so a higher ratio signals greater exposure.
  2. Distinguish between foreign exchange risk and sovereign risk. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Foreign exchange risk arises from fluctuating currency prices, which can reduce the value of a bank's foreign-currency-denominated assets and force a write-down. Sovereign risk is distinct: it arises when a foreign government faces domestic instability or armed conflict that damages its ability to service debts owed to international lenders — a risk tied to the government's own capacity/willingness to pay, not currency movements.
  3. Why are banks restricted to investment-grade securities in their investment portfolios, and what rating threshold defines "investment grade"? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Because investment securities carry credit (default) risk just as loans do, regulators restrict banks to investment-grade securities — rated at least Baa by Moody's or BBB by Standard & Poor's — to protect depositors from excessive risk on the investment side of the balance sheet. Securities rated below this threshold (Ba/BB and lower) are considered speculative or "junk" and are not suitable holdings for banks and other closely regulated financial firms, since a default on these securities would directly threaten depositor funds.
  4. What does a rising Total Loans/Total Deposits ratio indicate about a bank's risk position? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Since loans are typically among the riskiest assets a depository institution holds, a rising loans-to-deposits ratio means a larger share of depositor funds is committed to relatively risky assets. If bad loans increase or the market value of otherwise-good loans declines, this creates greater risk exposure for depositors, which is why bank examiners and regulators watch this ratio as a traditional credit-risk indicator.

Risk Management II: Market, Operational, and Solvency Risk; Current Issues on NPAs

Unit II · Topic 7

1. Overview

Continuing from Topic 6, this topic covers market risk, operational risk (plus its close relatives — legal/compliance, reputation, and strategic risk), solvency (capital) risk, and closes with where India's non-performing assets problem stands today, including the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code framework.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Market risk

Market risk arises because the market values of a bank's assets, liabilities, and net worth constantly fluctuate with market rates and prices. It has two components:

  • Price risk — bond portfolios and shareholders' equity can drop suddenly as market prices move adversely. Indicators include book-value assets/market value of those assets, book-value equity/market value of equity, and market value of bonds relative to their book value.
  • Interest rate risk — covered in Topic 6, also a component of market risk since it affects the market value of fixed-income holdings.

2.2 Operational risk and its relatives

RiskDefinition
Operational riskUncertainty in earnings from failures in computer systems, employee errors/misconduct, natural disasters, or similar events — broadly, loss from anything other than credit or market risk.
Legal riskVariability in earnings from unenforceable contracts, lawsuits, or adverse judgments.
Compliance riskBroader than legal risk — includes violations of rules/regulations, e.g. failing to hold adequate regulatory capital, triggering costly corrective action.
Reputation riskUncertainty from public opinion — negative publicity (true or not) can drive customers away.
Strategic riskEarnings variation from adverse business decisions, poor implementation, or failure to respond to industry change — the "human element" of bad long-range management.

Technology dependence, financial fraud, and disasters (natural or man-made, including terrorism) are recurring sources of operational risk in modern banking.

2.3 Solvency (capital) risk

Capital risk is the summary risk of a bank's long-run survival — the risk that losses from any of the other risk categories (bad loans, declining securities values, etc.) overwhelm the equity capital meant to absorb them. If depositors and investors sense this and withdraw funds, regulators may have no choice but to declare the institution insolvent. Because capital risk is a consequence of other risks rather than an independent source, it is often not tracked separately by regulators — but it captures the ultimate stakes: failure of the institution itself. This is why capital adequacy (Topic 1's CRAR/Basel framework) exists — it is the primary regulatory tool for keeping solvency risk within acceptable bounds.

2.4 NPA classification and provisioning coverage

India's regulatory NPA reporting distinguishes:

Gross NPAs (% of Gross Advances) = Gross NPAs ÷ Gross Advances
Net NPAs = Gross NPAs − Provisions (specific + floating + other deductions)
Net NPAs (% of Net Advances) = Net NPAs ÷ Net Advances

The Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR) = Provisions (specific + floating) ÷ Gross NPAs — it indicates how much of the bank's bad-loan exposure is already cushioned by provisions, i.e. how much capacity the bank has to absorb loan losses without further capital erosion.

2.5 Current issues on NPAs — the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016)

Rising NPAs after the mid-2010s prompted major legal reform. In 2016–17, India strengthened its resolution framework through: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016; amendments to the SARFAESI Act, 2002 and the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions (RDDBFI) Act, 1993; and the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Ordinance, 2017 (giving RBI more direct power to order stressed-asset resolution).

The IBC consolidates and amends insolvency law for corporates, partnership firms, and individuals in a time-bound manner, aiming to maximize asset value, promote entrepreneurship and credit availability, and balance stakeholder interests. Key institutional players:

  • Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) — apex regulator for transparency and governance under the Code.
  • Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs) — enroll and regulate Insolvency Professionals.
  • Insolvency Professionals (IPs) — conduct the actual resolution process.
  • Information Utilities (IUs) — centralized repositories of borrowers' financial/credit information.
  • Adjudicating Authority — the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for corporate insolvency.
  • Committee of Creditors (CoC) — drives decisions on resolving the insolvent entity.

Resolution begins on default (any financial or operational creditor can apply), an Insolvency Professional is appointed to run the process within statutory timelines, and if no viable resolution plan is approved, the entity moves to liquidation. This gave banks a faster, more predictable legal route to resolve stressed corporate accounts than the pre-2016 regime (which had relied on BIFR-style mechanisms that largely failed to help banks recover dues — see Topic 5).

3. Key Terms

Price risk
Component of market risk — loss from adverse market-price movements affecting bond portfolios and equity.
Capital (solvency) risk
The summary risk of a bank's ultimate survival, arising when losses from other risks overwhelm the equity capital meant to absorb them.
Gross NPA / Net NPA
Gross NPA = total non-performing principal+interest exposure; Net NPA = Gross NPA minus provisions held against it.
Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR)
Provisions (specific + floating) ÷ Gross NPAs — measures how well-cushioned a bank's bad-loan book is.
IBC, 2016
India's consolidated insolvency law for time-bound resolution of corporate, partnership, and individual insolvency, administered via NCLT/IBBI.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Market risk = price risk + interest rate risk, driven by fluctuating market values.
  • Operational risk covers system failures, fraud, disasters; legal, compliance, reputation, and strategic risk are closely related categories.
  • Capital/solvency risk = the summary risk of institutional failure when other risks overwhelm equity capital; capital adequacy regulation (Basel/CRAR) exists to control it.
  • Net NPA = Gross NPA − Provisions; PCR = Provisions ÷ Gross NPAs.
  • IBC 2016 gave India a time-bound insolvency resolution framework via NCLT, IBBI, IPs, IUs, and the Committee of Creditors — a major current-issue reform for tackling India's NPA problem.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is capital (solvency) risk often described as a "summary" risk rather than an independent risk category? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    Because capital risk arises as a consequence of other risks — bad loans, declining securities values, operational losses, and so on — rather than from an independent source of its own. When losses from these other risk categories overwhelm the equity capital meant to absorb them, the bank faces insolvency. Since its variability stems entirely from other risk types, regulators often don't track it as a separate risk category, even though it represents the ultimate stake: the survival of the institution itself.
  2. Distinguish between legal risk, compliance risk, and reputation risk with an example of each. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Legal risk is variability in earnings from actions of the legal system — e.g. an adverse court judgment or an unenforceable contract increasing expenses. Compliance risk is broader, covering violations of rules and regulations beyond the legal system — e.g. a bank failing to hold adequate regulatory capital, forcing costly corrective action under capital adequacy rules. Reputation risk is the uncertainty from public opinion — e.g. negative publicity about a bank's practices, true or not, driving customers to withdraw funds or avoid the institution, independent of any legal or regulatory violation.
  3. A bank reports Gross NPAs of ₹500 crore against Gross Advances of ₹10,000 crore, and holds provisions of ₹200 crore against these NPAs. Calculate the Gross NPA ratio, the Net NPA amount, and the Provisioning Coverage Ratio. (Numerical)
    Show model answer
    Gross NPA ratio = 500/10,000 = 5%. Net NPA = Gross NPA − Provisions = 500 − 200 = ₹300 crore. PCR = Provisions ÷ Gross NPAs = 200/500 = 40%. This PCR of 40% indicates the bank has cushioned less than half of its bad-loan exposure with provisions, leaving the remaining 60% (₹300 crore) as a potential further hit to capital if these accounts are not recovered.
  4. Name the key institutional players in India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) framework and briefly state each one's role. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    The IBBI (Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India) is the apex regulator promoting transparency and governance under the Code. Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs) enroll and regulate Insolvency Professionals (IPs), who actually conduct the resolution process for a defaulting entity. Information Utilities (IUs) serve as centralized repositories of borrowers' financial and credit information to support the process. The Adjudicating Authority — the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for corporates — oversees the legal process, and the Committee of Creditors (CoC) makes the key decisions on resolving or liquidating the insolvent entity. Together, these players enable a time-bound resolution process, replacing the earlier, largely ineffective BIFR-based framework.

M&A of Banks into the Securities Market

Unit II · Topic 8

1. Overview

This closing topic covers why banks consolidate with each other and expand into securities-market activities — the "universal banking" model — and grounds the discussion in a real Indian case: the 2001 merger of Bank of Madura into ICICI Bank.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Mergers vs. acquisitions vs. amalgamation

A merger results from the mutual decision of two organizations; an acquisition is the takeover of one organization by another. A "forced" merger, or one driven by a survival problem, is termed an amalgamation — e.g. Global Trust Bank's amalgamation with Oriental Bank of Commerce, and Nedungadi Bank's amalgamation with Punjab National Bank, both triggered by the weaker bank's distress (often rising NPAs) rather than a negotiated deal.

2.2 Why banks merge

  • Regulatory pressure toward scale — as RBI implemented Basel II norms, banks needed higher capital adequacy and lower NPAs; "small is no longer beautiful" in a landscape where compliance itself demands scale.
  • Resource constraints — smaller banks lacking the capital and labor to compete with bigger players may be forced to merge with them (the amalgamation route above).
  • Shareholder value via swap ratio — a board may agree to a merger because it offers shareholders a better price through the swap ratio (the ratio at which old-company shares convert into new-company shares) — the negotiated-deal route, as with Bank of Madura/ICICI Bank.
  • Competitive positioning — merging strengthens the acquiring bank to face aggressive multinational competition, even though the resulting concentration can reduce market competitiveness.

Common post-merger outcomes include downsizing, branch relocations, technological change, and employee insecurity — often surfacing as an "us versus them" dynamic, especially where the merging banks have different work cultures or one is seen as procedurally superior to the other.

2.3 Case: Bank of Madura merges into ICICI Bank (2000–01)

Announced 8–11 December 2000, shareholder-approved 19 January 2001, RBI-approved 1 March 2001.

ParameterICICI BankBank of Madura
Established1994 (from ICICI)1943 — 57-year track record
Asset base₹12,000+ crore₹4,400+ crore
CAR19.64%14.25%
Branches104 (technology-driven, all computerized)263 (182 in Tamil Nadu; 132 computerized = 90% of business)
Employees~1,500, all computer-literate2,577, of which 2,000 computer-literate

The swap ratio approved was 2 ICICI Bank shares for every 1 BoM share. Effects of the merger:

  • Distribution reach — ICICI Bank gained BoM's strong rural/semi-urban Tamil Nadu network (87 rural + 88 semi-urban branches), enabling micro-finance lending through self-help groups and priority-sector agricultural lending.
  • Equity dilution vs. EPS gain — the swap ratio diluted ICICI Bank's equity capital by about 12%, but the merger produced roughly a 20% gain in EPS.
  • Capital adequacy — ICICI Bank's comfortable CAR fell from 19.64% to 17.6% post-merger, since BoM's CAR (14.25%) and asset quality were weaker.
  • Asset quality — BoM's Gross NPA/Gross Advances was 11.09% (vs. ICICI's 2.54%) and Net NPA/Net Advances 6.23% (vs. ICICI's 1.53%) in 1999–2000 — the acquiring bank absorbed materially weaker asset quality along with the branch network.
  • Human resources — merging ICICI's small, young, well-paid, urban-focused workforce (~1,500) with BoM's larger, more unionized, lower-career-aspiration workforce (~2,500) into a combined ~4,000-employee entity was a major integration challenge; many BoM employees took voluntary retirement.

2.4 Universal banking — expansion into securities activities

Universal banking refers to combining commercial banking with investment banking (issuing, underwriting, investing, and trading securities), and more broadly to offering the full range of financial services (including insurance) as a "one-stop" supplier. India follows this model.

DriverExplanation
Economies of scale and scopeA bank can lower average costs and improve spreads by expanding scale and diversifying activities, reusing existing expertise, infrastructure, client risk information, and branch network across products.
Cross-selling via lending relationshipsA bank uses its lending relationship to tie in a customer and cross-sell securities and insurance products — insurance and lending are interlinked, so a bank can use one instrument to support the other with the same client.
Customer benefit — one-stop shoppingSaves transaction costs and speeds up economic activity for customers who would otherwise deal with multiple specialized institutions.
Signaling valueA bank's equity stake in a borrower firm signals the firm's health to other investors, since the lending bank is well-positioned to monitor the firm.

Challenges of universal banking

The central drawback is potential conflict between the investment banker's promotional role and the commercial banker's duty to give impartial advice, plus a tendency toward oligopoly/imperfectly competitive market structures as universal banks grow larger and more dominant.

3. Key Terms

Amalgamation
A forced merger driven by one party's survival problem (e.g. rising NPAs), as opposed to a negotiated merger.
Swap ratio
The ratio at which shareholders of the absorbed company receive shares of the surviving company in exchange for their old shares.
Universal banking
A model combining commercial banking, investment banking, and (broadly) insurance/other financial services within one institution.
Economies of scale and scope
Cost efficiencies gained by expanding the scale of one activity, or by diversifying across related activities that share infrastructure/expertise.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • Merger = mutual decision; acquisition = takeover; amalgamation = forced merger from a survival problem (GTB→OBC, Nedungadi→PNB).
  • Bank merger drivers: Basel-driven scale/capital pressure, resource constraints, shareholder value via swap ratio, competitive positioning.
  • BoM/ICICI Bank case: 2:1 swap ratio, ICICI gained rural reach but absorbed weaker CAR (19.64%→17.6%) and NPAs; ~20% EPS gain vs. ~12% equity dilution; major HR integration challenge.
  • Universal banking = commercial + investment banking (+ insurance); driven by economies of scale/scope, cross-selling, one-stop-shopping customer benefit, and equity-stake signaling value.
  • Universal banking's main challenge: conflict between promotional (investment banking) and impartial-advice (commercial banking) roles, plus oligopoly tendencies.

Practice Questions

  1. Distinguish between a merger, an acquisition, and an amalgamation, with one Indian banking example of amalgamation. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    A merger arises from the mutual decision of two organizations to combine; an acquisition is the takeover of one organization by another; an amalgamation is a "forced" merger driven by a survival problem in the weaker entity, rather than a mutually negotiated deal. An Indian banking example of amalgamation is Global Trust Bank's amalgamation with Oriental Bank of Commerce, triggered by GTB's financial distress rather than a negotiated strategic decision.
  2. Using the Bank of Madura–ICICI Bank merger, explain how a merger can simultaneously benefit an acquiring bank's earnings while weakening its capital position. (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    The merger diluted ICICI Bank's equity capital by about 12% (through the 2:1 swap ratio) but produced roughly a 20% gain in EPS, and gave ICICI a much stronger rural/semi-urban distribution network via BoM's Tamil Nadu branches — clear earnings and reach benefits. However, BoM brought a weaker CAR (14.25% vs. ICICI's 19.64%) and significantly worse asset quality (Gross NPA ratio of 11.09% vs. ICICI's 2.54%), which pulled ICICI's post-merger CAR down from 19.64% to 17.6%. This shows a merger can be earnings-accretive while simultaneously importing capital and asset-quality risk from the weaker partner.
  3. What is universal banking, and what are its main benefits to a bank expanding into securities-market activities? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    Universal banking is a model combining commercial banking with investment banking activities (issuing, underwriting, investing, and trading securities), and more broadly offering the full spectrum of financial services including insurance, as a "one-stop" supplier. Key benefits: economies of scale and scope (lower average costs by reusing existing expertise, infrastructure, and client risk information across products); the ability to cross-sell securities and insurance products by leveraging existing lending relationships; customer benefits from one-stop shopping (lower transaction costs, faster service); and the signaling value of a bank's equity stake in a borrower firm, which indicates the firm's health to other investors since the lending bank monitors it closely.
  4. What is the central conflict-of-interest challenge in universal banking, and why does it arise? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The central challenge is the potential conflict between the investment banker's promotional role (e.g. underwriting and promoting a security issue) and the commercial banker's obligation to give impartial advice to the same or related clients. Because a universal bank performs both roles simultaneously, its incentive to promote securities it has underwritten can compromise the objectivity depositors and borrowers expect from its commercial banking relationship — this, alongside a tendency toward oligopolistic market structures as universal banks grow larger, is the main drawback weighed against universal banking's efficiency benefits.

Unit II — Assignments

Two assignments: a CRAR and GAP-analysis numerical problem set, and a bank merger evaluation exercise.

Assignment 1: CRAR and Interest Rate Risk Numerical Set

Task: Solve the following two numerical problems, showing all working.

  1. CRAR: A bank has ₹800 crore in risk-weighted assets, ₹60 crore of Tier 1 capital, and ₹20 crore of Tier 2 capital. Calculate its CRAR. Is it compliant with India's minimum regulatory requirement (Topic 1)? By how much (in ₹ crore of capital) would it need to raise additional capital to reach exactly the minimum, if RWAs stay constant?
  2. GAP analysis: A bank's 0–90 day bucket shows RSAs of ₹620 crore and RSLs of ₹900 crore. Calculate the GAP, classify the bank as asset- or liability-sensitive, and estimate the expected change in NII if rates are expected to fall by 0.75% (Topic 4). Explain in 3–4 sentences what action the ALCO might take in response.

Format: Worked numerical answers with brief written interpretation for each part (400–600 words total plus calculations).

Assignment 2: Bank Merger Evaluation

Task: Using the Bank of Madura–ICICI Bank merger (Topic 8) as your reference case, choose one other real or hypothetical Indian bank merger (e.g. a public-sector bank consolidation, or a private-sector acquisition) and write a short evaluation covering:

  1. Was the merger closer to a negotiated merger or an amalgamation? What evidence supports your classification?
  2. Compare the two banks' pre-merger CAR and asset quality (NPA ratios), if disclosed, and assess what risk the acquiring bank absorbed.
  3. Identify at least two likely integration challenges (branch network, technology, HR/culture) based on the profiles of the two banks.
  4. Would you classify this merger as primarily driven by regulatory/capital pressure, resource constraints, or shareholder value? Justify your answer.

Format: 700–900 words, citing your source for any figures used.

Grading Rubric (applies to both assignments)

CriterionWeightWhat it looks for
Concept understanding25%Correct, precise use of Unit II terminology (CRAR, GAP, RSA/RSL, swap ratio, etc.).
Application / accuracy30%Correct numerical working for Assignment 1; sound reasoning applied to the chosen case in Assignment 2.
Critical analysis25%Goes beyond stating facts to interpreting what the numbers/case mean for the bank's soundness or strategy.
Structure & clarity10%Clearly organized, easy to follow, each step justified.
Use of course material10%Explicit references back to the relevant Unit II topics and concepts used.

Unit II — Quiz

10 questions. Select an answer for each, then click Submit to see your score and which answers were correct.

1. India's minimum CRAR requirement has been what level since 2000?

Correct answer: C. India requires a minimum CRAR of 9%, one percentage point above the international Basel norm of 8%.

2. Which Basel Accord introduced the three-pillar structure and extended minimum capital requirements to cover market and operational risk?

Correct answer: B. Basel II introduced the three pillars (minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline) and extended capital requirements beyond credit risk.

3. In the marginal cost of funds approach to deposit pricing, why can the true cost of matching a competitor's rate rise exceed the nominal rate increase?

Correct answer: A. The marginal cost includes the extra rate paid to depositors who were never at risk of leaving, inflating the true cost well above the nominal rate change.

4. Securities purchased with the intent to sell in the near term, carried at market value with gains/losses hitting the income statement, belong to which investment category?

Correct answer: C. Held for Trading (HFT) securities are bought for near-term sale, marked to market, with gains/losses affecting the income statement.

5. A bank with more Rate Sensitive Liabilities than Rate Sensitive Assets (negative GAP) is termed:

Correct answer: B. Negative GAP (RSL > RSA) means the bank is liability-sensitive and benefits from falling interest rates.

6. In Altman's Z-Score model, a firm is classified as "financially distressed" when Z is:

Correct answer: D. Z < 1.81 classifies a firm as financially distressed or bankrupt; Z > 2.99 is financially sound.

7. Which category of borrower sickness is caused by management incompetence or willful default?

Correct answer: B. Induced sickness is caused by management incompetence or willful default, distinct from sickness at birth (infeasible project) or genuine sickness (beyond the borrower's control).

8. Securities rated below Baa (Moody's) or BBB (S&P) are classified as:

Correct answer: A. Below Baa/BBB is speculative ("junk") grade, not suitable for regulated banks to hold.

9. The Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR) is calculated as:

Correct answer: C. PCR = Provisions (specific + floating) divided by Gross NPAs, indicating how well-cushioned the bad-loan book is.

10. In the Bank of Madura–ICICI Bank merger, what was the approved swap ratio?

Correct answer: B. The approved swap ratio was 2 ICICI Bank shares for every 1 Bank of Madura share.

Case Study — Applying Unit II

Unit II · Capstone case

Note for instructors

This page uses the Yes Bank crisis and RBI-led reconstruction (March 2020) as its worked example — a well-documented, widely-taught episode that ties together capital adequacy failure (Topic 1), credit-concentration and financial-distress signals (Topic 5), solvency/credit risk (Topics 6–7), and the NPA/PCR framework (Topic 7). Swap in any preferred case using the same framework.

Seminar Discussion Agenda (~45–50 min session)

  1. Framing (5 min) — presenter introduces Yes Bank's background (section 2.1) and today's guiding question: how does a bank's own risk-taking, not just a single borrower's default, create systemic distress?
  2. Walk the framework (15 min) — presenter works through case-analysis steps 1–5 (section 1) in order, pausing after each step for class agreement.
  3. Open discussion — Question 1 (8 min) — what early warning signals (Topic 5) were present before the crisis became public?
  4. Open discussion — Question 2 (8 min) — how did capital adequacy (Topic 1) and provisioning coverage (Topic 7) interact in this case?
  5. Open discussion — Question 3 (7 min) — why did RBI choose a reconstruction scheme over liquidation?
  6. Wrap-up (5 min) — class collectively identifies which Unit II risk category (Topics 6–7) was most central to this case, and why.

1. Case Analysis Framework

  1. Identify the risk-taking pattern — what kind of lending/investment concentration built up, and which risk category (Topic 6–7) does it fall under?
  2. Trace the warning signals — what early indicators of financial distress (Topic 5) were visible before the public crisis?
  3. Assess the capital adequacy impact — how did asset quality deterioration interact with CRAR (Topic 1)?
  4. Assess the NPA/provisioning picture — what would Gross NPA, Net NPA, and PCR (Topic 7) have looked like as the crisis unfolded?
  5. Evaluate the regulatory response — what tools did the regulator use, and why not liquidation or a straightforward merger (Topic 8)?

2. Worked Example: The Yes Bank Crisis and Reconstruction (2020)

2.1 Background

Yes Bank, a private sector Indian bank, grew rapidly through the 2010s by aggressively lending to corporate borrowers, including several highly leveraged infrastructure, real estate, and NBFC groups. This concentrated exposure to a relatively small number of large, high-risk corporate accounts left the bank unusually vulnerable when a number of these borrowers came under financial stress simultaneously in the late 2010s.

2.2 Risk category and concentration

The core vulnerability was credit risk (Topic 6) concentrated in a narrow set of large corporate exposures — the opposite of the "diversification of credit risk" objective described for the investment portfolio in Topic 3. When several of these large borrowers deteriorated together, losses were far larger and more correlated than a well-diversified loan book would have produced, illustrating why concentration itself is a risk factor distinct from any single borrower's individual credit quality.

2.3 Early warning signals

Applying Topic 5's warning-signal framework, the pattern that emerged included: a widening gap between the bank's own reported NPA figures and the NPA levels RBI's supervisory Risk-Based Supervision found upon inspection (a divergence later required to be publicly disclosed under RBI norms); rapid loan-book growth concentrated in a few large, high-risk accounts (i.e. the "growth without adequate capital" and "superior competition" style factors flagged in Topic 5 as generic triggers of distress); and deteriorating market confidence reflected in the bank's equity price and its difficulty raising fresh capital — a classic sign, per Topic 5, that a firm's economic (not just accounting) value was falling faster than its books showed.

2.4 Capital adequacy and NPA/provisioning impact

As the concentrated corporate exposures turned into NPAs, the bank's asset quality deteriorated sharply, which — per the CRAR mechanics in Topic 1 — directly eroded the numerator (capital, as losses were provisioned/written off) while the risk-weighted denominator effectively demanded more capital support. Gross NPAs and Net NPAs (Topic 7) rose materially, and the bank's ability to build adequate Provisioning Coverage lagged the pace of asset quality decline, leaving capital increasingly exposed to further loan losses — precisely the "capital/solvency risk" dynamic from Topic 7, where losses from an underlying risk (here, credit risk) eventually threaten the institution's survival.

2.5 The regulatory response — reconstruction, not liquidation or an ordinary merger

Rather than allowing failure or arranging a conventional merger (Topic 8), RBI in March 2020 imposed a moratorium and then implemented a reconstruction scheme: a consortium of banks led by the State Bank of India infused fresh capital in exchange for equity, restoring the bank's capital base above the regulatory minimum while keeping it operating as a going concern. This route was chosen because Yes Bank's franchise (deposit base, branch network) still had value, and depositor protection and financial-system stability were judged better served by recapitalization than by liquidation or an uncontrolled failure — echoing the "too big to fail" concern noted in Topic 8's discussion of bank mergers, but resolved here through regulator-orchestrated recapitalization rather than a market-driven acquisition.

3. Discussion / Practice Questions

  1. Why is a concentrated corporate loan book a distinct risk factor from the credit quality of any individual borrower in it? (Applied)
    Show model answer
    Concentration risk arises because losses across a small number of large, correlated exposures can move together — if several large borrowers in the same sectors (e.g. infrastructure, real estate) come under stress simultaneously, the bank absorbs the combined loss all at once, rather than the losses being smoothed out across a large, diversified pool of smaller, less-correlated borrowers. This is the reverse of the "diversification of credit risk" objective described for investment portfolios in Topic 3 — a lending book concentrated in a few large accounts sacrifices that diversification benefit, so an otherwise-average default rate per borrower can still produce a systemic-scale loss for the bank.
  2. How does capital adequacy (CRAR) mechanically deteriorate when a bank's concentrated NPAs rise sharply? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    CRAR = Regulatory Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets. As concentrated exposures turn into NPAs, the bank must provision for and eventually write off these losses, which directly reduces the numerator (capital, since provisions/write-offs reduce retained earnings and equity). At the same time, the underlying risk-weighted assets don't shrink correspondingly (the loans remain on the books, now classified as NPAs, often with higher risk weights under regulatory norms), so the ratio falls from both directions — a smaller numerator against a still-large or increasing denominator — pushing CRAR toward, or below, the regulatory minimum unless fresh capital is raised.
  3. Why might a Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR) that "lags the pace of asset quality decline" be dangerous for a bank in crisis? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    PCR = Provisions ÷ Gross NPAs, and it indicates how well-cushioned the bank's bad-loan exposure already is. If Gross NPAs rise faster than provisions are built up, PCR falls, meaning a growing share of the bad-loan exposure is uncushioned — any further deterioration in these accounts (lower recovery than expected) then hits the bank's capital directly rather than being absorbed by provisions already set aside, accelerating the erosion of capital adequacy described in the previous question.
  4. Why might a regulator choose a reconstruction/recapitalization scheme over liquidation or a conventional merger for a systemically important bank in distress? (Applied / open-ended)
    Show model answer
    A strong answer weighs: depositor protection (liquidation risks depositor losses and panic beyond the insured limit); financial-system stability (a large bank's failure can trigger contagion, similar to the "too big to fail" concern raised in Topic 8); the surviving value of the bank's franchise (deposit base, branch network, customer relationships) that a going-concern recapitalization preserves but liquidation destroys; and the speed/certainty a regulator-orchestrated scheme offers compared to negotiating a conventional voluntary merger (Topic 8) under crisis conditions, where willing acquirers and swap-ratio negotiations take time the situation may not allow.

Payment Systems in India

Unit III · Topic 1

1. Overview

An efficient, secure payment and settlement system is the backbone of public trust in the financial system. This topic covers how India's payment systems are classified, regulated, and how the major systems — RTGS, ECS, and NEFT — actually work.

2. Detailed Notes

2.1 Regulatory framework

The Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS), set up by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in 2001 by G-10 central banks (RBI is a member), formulates broad supervisory standards for payment systems and defines Systemically Important Payment Systems (SIPS) — systems which, if inadequately protected against credit, liquidity, legal, or operational risk, could transmit disruptions across the financial system. In India, the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 empowered RBI to regulate and supervise payment systems, formulate policy, and provide a legal basis for multilateral netting and settlement finality, operationalized via the Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems Regulations, 2008.

2.2 Classifying payment systems

Classification basisCategories
By modePaper-based (high-value clearing, cheques) vs. electronic (RTGS, ECS, NEFT)
By relative importance/valueLarge-value/bulk (RTGS, high-value clearing, CCIL) — low volume, high value, carries systemic risk, classified as SIPS — vs. retail (MICR/non-MICR cheque clearing, NEFT, ECS, cards, Internet/mobile) — high volume, low value per transaction

Both high-value clearing and RTGS are classified as SIPS under CPSS/BIS standards. Retail payments aren't formally SIPS, but their sheer volume and geographic reach make them critical to the economy nonetheless.

2.3 RTGS — Real Time Gross Settlement

Traditional net-settlement systems (settling at day's end, or 1–2 days later) create credit, liquidity, operational, legal, and systemic risk during the settlement lag. RTGS solves this: it processes and settles fund transfers individually and continuously throughout the day (gross settlement, no netting), so payee banks receive usable funds within minutes rather than up to a day (or a week for cheques).

  • Operationalized in India in March 2004, starting with 4 banks doing interbank-only settlement; extended to customer transactions in 2006; had 105 members by 2009.
  • Owned and operated by RBI; settlement occurs in RBI's own books via a dedicated RTGS settlement account each member funds daily from its RBI current account.
  • Membership types: Type A (commercial banks — can submit customer transactions), Type B (primary dealers), Type D (clearing houses).
  • "High value" for RTGS purposes = transactions of ₹1 lakh and above.
  • Members connect via a dedicated leased line through the INFINET network to RBI's system.

2.4 Paper-based retail instruments

Cheques remain the most common form of "notational money." Related instruments include banker's cheques (drawn by a bank on its own funds — a direct bank obligation) and demand drafts (guaranteed by the drawee bank); both are treated as insured deposits, as are traveller's cheques. Clearing typically takes 2 days (day 1: presented at clearing house; day 2: settled or returned). Cheque truncation — stopping the physical cheque's transit and replacing it with an electronic image en route to the drawee branch — was piloted in the National Capital Region to speed up clearing and cut the cost/risk of physical transit.

2.5 Electronic Clearing Service (ECS)

ECS replaces costly, error-prone bulk paper instruments (like printed dividend/interest warrants) with electronic bulk payments/receipts, available at 75 major centres (2009 figures).

VariantFlowExample
ECS (Credit)One institution pays many retail recipientsDividend/interest payments, salaries
ECS (Debit)Many individuals pay one institutionUtility bill collection via mandate
NECSCentralized version at RBI Mumbai, leveraging member banks' Core Banking Systems nationwideSame credit/debit logic, but pan-India from a single location

Settlement occurs on a T+0/T+1 cycle. Benefits to the paying organization: eliminated printing/dispatch costs, no risk of lost/fraudulently-encashed instruments, automatic reconciliation, easier cash management. Benefits to the customer: on-time payment, no need to visit the bank to deposit a warrant.

2.6 EFT and NEFT

RBI introduced Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) in 1997 for inter-city/intra-city, inter-bank/intra-bank transfers, processing pre-authorized debits/credits within 48 hours. EFT was replaced in November 2005 by NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) — a message-based system using Public Key Infrastructure for end-to-end security, also running over INFINET. NEFT reached about 63,000 bank branches by end-2009, and RBI progressively made it more retail-friendly by permitting walk-in cash-based transactions (not just account-to-account) and credit card payments.

3. Key Terms

SIPS
Systemically Important Payment System — one whose disruption could transmit systemic risk across the financial system; RTGS and high-value clearing qualify in India.
RTGS
Real Time Gross Settlement — continuous, individual (non-netted), same-day settlement of large-value interbank/customer payments, owned and operated by RBI.
ECS/NECS
Electronic Clearing Service (and its centralized version) — bulk electronic credit/debit payment mechanism for repetitive retail payments.
NEFT
National Electronic Funds Transfer — PKI-secured, INFINET-based successor to EFT for retail electronic fund transfers.
Cheque truncation
Stopping a physical cheque's onward transit and substituting an electronic image, to speed clearing and reduce transit risk.

Exam-Prep Summary

  • CPSS (under BIS) sets global SIPS standards; India regulates via the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
  • Two classification axes: paper-based vs. electronic; large-value/SIPS vs. retail.
  • RTGS = continuous, gross (non-netted), real-time settlement; started 2004; owned/operated by RBI; high value = ₹1 lakh+.
  • ECS (Credit/Debit) and its centralized NECS variant handle bulk repetitive retail payments/collections.
  • NEFT (2005) replaced EFT (1997) as the PKI-secured retail electronic transfer system running on INFINET.
  • Cheque truncation replaces physical cheque movement with an electronic image to speed clearing.

Practice Questions

  1. Explain why RTGS is described as a "gross" settlement system, and how this differs from net settlement. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    RTGS is "gross" because each payment instruction is processed and settled individually and continuously as it is received, without netting debits against credits across multiple transactions. Net settlement, by contrast, accumulates transactions and settles only the net balance between parties, typically at the end of the day — meaning payees must wait until that end-of-day settlement to receive usable funds, and the system carries settlement risk throughout the day since obligations remain unsettled until then. RTGS eliminates this waiting period and the associated credit/liquidity risk by settling each transaction in real time.
  2. Distinguish between ECS (Credit) and ECS (Debit), with one example of each. (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    ECS (Credit) facilitates bulk payments where one institution pays many retail recipients — for example, a company paying dividend/interest warrants to many investors, or paying employee salaries — debiting the paying institution's account and crediting many beneficiary accounts. ECS (Debit) is the reverse: many individual customers pay a single institution, such as a utility company collecting bill payments via a standing mandate, debiting many customer accounts and crediting the utility's single account.
  3. What regulatory Act empowered RBI to regulate payment systems in India, and what specific powers did it grant? (Short answer)
    Show model answer
    The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 empowered RBI to regulate and supervise payment and settlement systems in India, formulate relevant policy, and provide a legal basis for multilateral netting and settlement finality. RBI operationalized this through the Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems Regulations, 2008 and the Payment and Settlement Systems Regulations, 2008.
  4. Why are RTGS and high-value clearing classified as Systemically Important Payment Systems (SIPS), while retail systems like NEFT and ECS are not? (Long answer)
    Show model answer
    SIPS classification depends on whether disruption to the system could transmit systemic risk — CPSS criteria include being the principal payment system by aggregate value, handling mostly high-individual-value payments, or being used to settle other financial market/payment systems. RTGS and high-value clearing meet these criteria because they carry relatively low transaction volumes but very high individual transaction values, so a failure could immediately threaten the stability of the broader financial system. Retail systems like NEFT and ECS handle high volumes of comparatively low-value transactions; while their aggregate importance to the economy is significant due to volume and reach, no single retail transaction failure poses the same systemic threat, so CPSS has not set SIPS-equivalent standards specifically for retail payment systems.
